    Let \(x_{1}, x_{2} \in \{0, 1\}\) take all four combinations and let \(y = x_{1}\ \text{XOR}\ x_{2}\), so that \(y = 0, 1, 1, 0\) for \((x_{1}, x_{2}) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)\). Alone, \(x_{1}\) has covariance \((-0.5)(-0.5) + (-0.5)(0.5) + (0.5)(0.5) + (0.5)(-0.5) = 0\) with \(y\), and so does \(x_{2}\): each is uncorrelated with the target and gives no improvement over predicting the mean. Together they predict \(y\) perfectly. Forward selection adds one feature at a time and adds a feature only if it helps by itself, so neither enters and the pair is never tried; a filter that scores features one by one fails the same way. Remedies: build an interaction feature \(x_{1}x_{2}\) or a tree-based model, which can represent the interaction; use a wrapper that also considers pairs, or start from the full set (backward elimination) so that both are present together; or use an embedded method whose model can use interactions.

  13. A pipeline standardises the data, runs PCA, and feeds the top components to a classifier, all three steps carried out on the whole data set before it is split. Where does leakage enter, and what is the correct order?

    Answer

    Leakage enters at each fitted step. (1) Standardising on all rows: \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) include the test rows. This is usually the smallest effect. (2) PCA on all rows: the component directions are chosen to capture the variance of the test rows as well; this is a larger effect, because the directions themselves, and the choice of how many to keep, are learned. (3) Any supervised step on all rows (for example choosing the number of components, or selecting features, by looking at accuracy that includes the test rows) is typically the largest, because the labels of the test set are then used. The correct order is: split first; fit the scaler on the training part; transform the training part; fit the PCA on the scaled training part; transform it; train the classifier on the training components; then apply the stored scaler and PCA to the test part, and evaluate once. In scikit-learn, make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=0.95), model) enforces this order, and refits all three steps inside every cross-validation fold.

Metric Formula Reads as Accuracy \((\text{TP} + \text{TN})/n\) everything over everything Precision \(\text{TP}/(\text{TP} + \text{FP})\) of what I flagged, how much was real Recall \(/ \text{TPR} /\) sensitivity \(\text{TP}/(\text{TP} + \text{FN})\) of what was real, how much I caught Specificity \(/ \text{TNR}\) \(\text{TN}/(\text{TN} + \text{FP})\) recall for the negative class FPR \(\text{FP}/(\text{FP} + \text{TN}) = 1 -\) specificity the x-axis of a ROC curve F1 2PR/(P \(+ R\)) harmonic mean — sits near the smaller one AUC area under TPR vs FPR \(P(a \text{random} \text{positive} \text{outranks} a \text{random} \text{negative})\)

Linkage Distance between clusters Character Single min over pairs long curved shapes; chains through noise Complete max over pairs compact, equal-diameter; outlier-sensitive Average mean over pairs the usual default Ward the merge raising WCSS least spherical, similar sizes

k-means: assign \(\to\) update \(\to\) repeat; the centroid is the mean because the mean minimises squared distance, and that is why it always converges — to a local optimum, so restart it. WCSS falls at every \(k\) and is 0 at \(k = m\), so it can never choose \(k\); use the elbow or maximise the silhouette.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms are listed alphabetically. The bracketed units say where the term is developed: U1 to U5 are the five units of the course (Chapters 1 to 14; see the Preface for the mapping).

Accuracy paradox on imbalanced data the useless majority-class model scores high accuracy, so optimising accuracy pushes you towards it. (U2, U4) AUC area under the ROC curve; the probability a random positive scores above a random negative. (U4) Back-propagation the chain rule organised so each layer's error signal is computed once and reused. (U4) Bias (statistical) error from a model too rigid to represent the pattern; shows as high training error. (U1, U3) Bias term the intercept \(\theta _{0}\) or \(b\). A different meaning of the same word. (U3) Centroid the mean of the points in a cluster. (U5) Chaining single linkage joining two real groups through a thin line of intermediate points. (U5) Classification supervised learning with a categorical target. (U1) Confusion matrix the \(2 \times 2\) table of TP, FP, FN, TN. (U4) Cost function \(J(\theta )\) the loss averaged over the training set; a function of the parameters. (U3) Cross-validation k-fold: each fold is held out once; \(k \times\) candidates model fits in a search. (U3) Curse of dimensionality as \(n\) grows, points become sparse and distances become nearly equal, which breaks k-NN and k-means. (U2) Decision boundary the surface in feature space where the predicted class changes. (U4) Dendrogram the tree of merges; the height of a join is the distance at which it happened. (U5) Design matrix \(X\) \(m \times (n+1)\), one row per example, first column all ones. (U3) Elbow the last \(k\) that buys a large drop in WCSS. (U5) Ensemble combining several models (bagging, random forests, boosting); beyond this syllabus but the usual next step after trees. Entropy \(-\sum p \log_{2}p\), the impurity of a node in bits. (U4) Epoch one pass over the whole training set. (U4) Feature one input column. The target is not a feature. (U1) Feature extraction building new features from combinations of the old (PCA). Contrast selection. (U2) Feature selection keeping a subset of the original columns; filter, wrapper or embedded. (U2) Generalisation performance on data not used in training. The only thing that counts. (U1) Gini index \(1 - \sum p^{2}\), an impurity measure without a logarithm. (U4) Gradient descent \(\theta\) := \(\theta - \alpha \nabla J\), repeated, with all parameters updated simultaneously. (U3) Hinge loss \(\max(0, 1 -\) y·f(x)); exactly zero beyond the margin, which is what makes the SVM sparse. (U4) Hyper-parameter set before training and chosen on validation data: \(\alpha , \lambda\), k, depth, \(C, \gamma\). (U1) Hypothesis space the set of functions an algorithm may choose from. (U1) Imputation filling missing values; the statistic must come from the training fold. (U2) Inductive bias the preference an algorithm has before seeing data, without which learning is impossible. (U1) Information gain impurity before a split minus the weighted impurity after it. (U4) Instance / example one row of the dataset. (U1) k-means++ initialisation that spreads the starting centroids out, reducing poor local optima. (U5) Lasso (L1) penalty \(\lambda \sum |\theta |\); sets coefficients exactly to zero, so it selects features. (U3) Lazy learner one that stores the data and does the work at prediction time; k-NN. (U4) Leakage information from the test set influencing training; the score becomes optimistic by an unmeasurable amount. (U2) Learning curve error against training-set size; a persistent gap means variance, two flat high curves mean bias. (U3) Linkage how the distance between two clusters is defined: single, complete, average, Ward. (U5) Log-loss −[y log \(h + (1-y) \log(1-h)\)]; convex, and unbounded for confident mistakes. (U4) Margin the empty corridor around an SVM boundary, of width \(2/\Vert w\Vert\). (U4) Masking an outlier inflating \(\sigma\) until it hides inside its own band. (U2) Multicollinearity correlated features making the split of credit between their coefficients unstable. (U3) Normal equation \(\theta = (X^{T}X)^{-1}X^{T}y\); exact, no \(\alpha\), but \(O(n^{3})\). (U3) One-hot encoding one binary column per category; drop one level for a linear model. (U2) Overfitting fitting noise; training error low, test error much higher. (U1) PCA rotate to the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix and keep the largest; unsupervised, scale-sensitive, not feature selection. (U2) Perceptron a single threshold unit; converges iff the classes are linearly separable. (U4) Precision \(\text{TP}/(\text{TP} + \text{FP})\). Of what I flagged, how much was real. (U4) Pruning cutting a grown tree back (post-) or stopping it early (pre-). (U4) PVE proportion of variance explained, \(\lambda _{i}/\sum \lambda\). (U2) \(R^{2}\) fraction of variance removed relative to predicting \(\bar{y}\); can be negative on test data. (U3) Recall \(\text{TP}/(\text{TP} + \text{FN})\). Of what was real, how much I caught. (U4) Regression supervised learning with a continuous target. (U1) Regularisation a penalty on parameter size that trades a little bias for a lot of variance. (U3) ReLU \(\max(0\), z); derivative 1 while active, which is why deep networks train. (U4) Residual \(y - \hat{y}\); sums to zero when the model has an intercept. (U3) Ridge (L2) penalty \(\lambda \sum \theta ^{2}\); shrinks smoothly, never to exactly zero, and makes \(X^{T}X + \lambda I\) always invertible. (U3) ROC curve TPR against FPR over every threshold. (U4) Silhouette (\(b -\) a)/max(a, \(b\)) per point; unlike WCSS it has a genuine maximum over \(k\). (U5) SMOTE synthetic minority points interpolated between neighbours; training fold only. (U2) Softmax the multi-class generalisation of the sigmoid; outputs sum to 1. (U4) Standardisation \(z = (x - \mu )/\sigma\); the default scaling. (U2) Stratified split one that preserves the class proportions in each part. (U2) Support vector a training point on or inside the margin; the only points the SVM solution depends on. (U4) Test set opened once, at the end. Looking at it twice makes it a validation set. (U1) \(\text{WCSS} /\) inertia \(\sum \Vert x - \mu \Vert ^{2}\) within clusters; falls at every \(k\), so it cannot choose \(k\). (U5) Underfitting the model cannot represent the pattern; both errors high. (U1) Validation set used to choose hyper-parameters and model family. (U1) Vanishing gradient \(\sigma ' \le 0.25\) multiplied once per layer, so early layers stop learning. (U4) Variance (statistical) how much the fitted model changes with a different training sample; shows as a train–test gap. (U1, U3)

docs.title: Chapter 14: Hierarchical Clustering and Evaluating Clusters
docs.text: K-means needs the number of clusters in advance and produces a single flat partition. Hierarchical clustering produces a whole tree of nested partitions and leaves the choice of the number of clusters until afterwards. This chapter builds that tree by hand, compares the linkage rules, and then returns to the question that unsupervised learning makes hard: how do you know whether a clustering is any good, when there are no labels to check against?

docs.title: 14.1 Hierarchical clustering
docs.text:
Instead of committing to a number of clusters, build the whole family of them at once. Start with every point in its own cluster, repeatedly merge the closest pair, and record the height at which each merge happened. The result is a tree — a dendrogram — and cutting it horizontally at any height gives a clustering. Cut low for many small clusters, high for a few large ones. You never had to choose \(k\) in advance; you choose it afterwards, by looking.

Definition: Agglomerative clustering

  1. Every point is its own cluster.
  2. Merge the two closest clusters, where “closest” is defined by the linkage.
  3. Recompute distances from the new cluster to the rest.
  4. Repeat until one cluster remains.

Divisive clustering goes the other way — start with everything together and split repeatedly — and is far less used, because the first split requires searching over exponentially many ways to divide the data.

Figure 14.1. Eight points and the single-linkage dendrogram built from them. The height of a join records the distance at which the two clusters merged; cutting the tree horizontally gives a clustering. Linkage Distance between clusters Produces Weakness Single the closest pair, min long, curved, non-convex shapes chaining — a thin line of noise joins two separate groups Complete the farthest pair, max compact, roughly equal-diameter clusters a single outlier can hold a merge back Average the mean over all pairs a compromise; the usual default no strong shape preference either way Ward the merge that increases WCSS least similar-sized spherical clusters assumes Euclidean distance

Reading a dendrogram

The height of a join is the distance at which it happened, so a join high above everything else means two genuinely dissimilar groups were finally forced together. Cutting horizontally gives a clustering, and the number of clusters is the number of vertical lines the cut crosses. The natural place to cut is just below the largest vertical gap — the biggest jump in merge distance — which is the hierarchical analogue of the elbow.

# hierarchical clustering, and the dendrogram behind it
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster

for how in ["single", "complete", "average", "ward"]:
    lab = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage=how).fit_predict(Xs)
    print(how, round(silhouette_score(Xs, lab), 3))    # four linkages, four answers

Z = linkage(Xs, method="ward")       # the merge history: [a, b, height, size]
dendrogram(Z, truncate_mode="lastp", p=12)
labels = fcluster(Z, t=3, criterion="maxclust")    # cut the tree into a clustering

The Z matrix is the dendrogram: one row per merge, giving the two clusters joined and the height at which they joined. Everything the figure above draws is in those four columns.

docs.title: 14.2 Evaluating a clustering
docs.text:
There is no accuracy, because there is nothing to be accurate against. Two families of measure exist, and they answer different questions.

Internal

— computed from the data and the clustering alone. WCSS for comparing runs at the same \(k\); the silhouette coefficient; the Davies–Bouldin index (lower is better) and the Calinski–Harabasz score (higher is better), both of which compare within-cluster spread against between-cluster separation.

External

— used when labels do exist, typically to test a clustering algorithm rather than to solve a problem. The Rand index and adjusted Rand index count pairs of points that the clustering and the labels agree about; normalised mutual information measures shared information; purity asks what fraction of each cluster belongs to its most common true class.

Figure 14.2. A silhouette plot: one bar per point, grouped by cluster and sorted, with the average marked by the dashed line. Long bars are points sitting comfortably inside their own cluster.

The plot says more than the single number does. A cluster whose bars are uniformly long is real; one whose bars are short and ragged is a group the algorithm invented to satisfy \(k\); and a negative bar names an individual point that is on average closer to a cluster it was not put in.

Clustering algorithms always return clusters

Run k-means with \(k = 4\) on uniform random noise and you will get four tidy groups with a respectable WCSS. Nothing in the algorithm can tell you that there was no structure to find. That is what the gap statistic tests for, and it is why a clustering result should always be sanity-checked — by plotting it, by looking at cluster profiles, or by asking somebody who knows the domain whether the groups mean anything.

docs.title: Where clustering earns its place
docs.text:
• Customer segmentation. Group by purchase behaviour, then design a campaign per segment. The classic RFM features — recency, frequency, monetary value — need standardising first, because monetary value runs to five figures and frequency to one.
  • Image compression. Cluster the pixel colours into \(k = 16\) groups and store each pixel as a 4-bit cluster index plus a small palette. A 24-bit-per-pixel image becomes 4 bits per pixel, a sixfold saving, and this is exactly k-means with three features.
  • Document grouping. Cluster news articles into topics with cosine distance on TF-IDF vectors — the one place where Euclidean distance is clearly the wrong choice, because it would separate a long article from a short one on the same subject.
  • Gene expression. Group genes with similar expression profiles across conditions; hierarchical clustering with a heat map is the standard presentation, and the dendrogram itself is part of the result.
  • Anomaly detection. Points far from every centroid, or left as singletons late in a dendrogram, are candidates for anomalies — unsupervised detection where no labelled examples of the fault exist.
  • Preprocessing for a supervised model. A cluster label can be a feature. Vector quantisation, and semi-supervised labelling where one member of each cluster is labelled by hand and the label is propagated.

docs.title: Ward's linkage, worked through
docs.text:
Ward's linkage defines the distance between two clusters as the increase in total WCSS that merging them would cause. For clusters of sizes \(n_{a}\) and \(n_{b}\) with means \(\mu_{a}\) and \(\mu_{b}\) that increase has a closed form,

\[\Delta(a, b) = \frac{n_{a} n_{b}}{n_{a} + n_{b}} \, \Vert \mu_{a} - \mu_{b}\Vert^{2}\]

so two clusters are close if their means are close and small clusters are cheaper to absorb than large ones. At each step Ward merges the pair with the smallest \(\Delta\).

Take the four points \(P(1), Q(2), R(5), S(9)\). Merging two single points \(P\) and \(Q\) costs \(\tfrac{1 \cdot 1}{2}(1)^{2} = 0.5\). Then \(\{P,Q\}\) (mean \(1.5\)) with \(R\) costs \(\tfrac{2 \cdot 1}{3}(3.5)^{2} = 8.17\), and \(R\) with \(S\) costs \(\tfrac{1 \cdot 1}{2}(4)^{2} = 8\), which is smaller, so \(\{R, S\}\) forms. The last merge, \(\{P,Q\}\) (mean \(1.5\)) with \(\{R,S\}\) (mean \(7\)), costs \(\tfrac{2 \cdot 2}{4}(5.5)^{2} = 30.25\). The three costs add up to \(0.5 + 8 + 30.25 = 38.75\), which is exactly the WCSS of all four points about their overall mean, \(4.25\), because the tree starts from singletons with WCSS zero and each merge adds its \(\Delta\). The two-cluster cut is \(\{P, Q\}\) and \(\{R, S\}\), a different answer from the single-linkage cut \(\{P, Q, R\}\) and \(\{S\}\) on the same points.

Libraries report the height of a Ward merge as \(\sqrt{2\Delta}\), so that heights are on the scale of a distance. The values for this example are \(1\), \(4\) and \(7.78\), and it is the order of the merges, not the scale, that defines the tree. Ward's linkage is the right default when the clusters are expected to be compact and of similar size, and it requires the Euclidean distance, since \(\Delta\) is derived from squared Euclidean distances.

docs.title: Divisive clustering
docs.text:
Divisive clustering runs the dendrogram in the other direction. All the points start in one cluster, and at each step one cluster is split in two, until every point is alone. To split a cluster optimally one would examine every way of dividing \(m\) points into two non-empty sets, and there are \(2^{m-1} - 1\) of them, which is hopeless beyond a few dozen points. Practical divisive methods therefore split heuristically, and the commonest is bisecting k-means: split the cluster with the largest WCSS (the least cohesive) using 2-means, and repeat.

For the same four points \(\{1, 2, 5, 9\}\) there are \(2^{3} - 1 = 7\) ways to make a first split, and the one with the smallest total WCSS is \(\{1, 2\}\) and \(\{5, 9\}\), with WCSS \(0.5 + 8 = 8.5\). The cluster \(\{5, 9\}\) is then split into its two points, and \(\{1, 2\}\) likewise. The first split reduces the WCSS from \(38.75\) to \(8.5\), a drop of \(30.25\): the same quantity as the last Ward merge, seen from the top. The advantages of working top-down are that one can stop after a few splits without ever building the bottom of the tree, and that the first splits are decided with the whole data in view. The disadvantage is cost, and the fact that, like agglomerative merging, a split is never reconsidered.

docs.title: What the greedy methods cannot undo
docs.text:
K-means moves points between clusters on every iteration, and so can repair an early mistake. Agglomerative clustering cannot: once two clusters are merged they stay merged for every coarser cut, and a divisive split is permanent in the same way. If an early merge is wrong, the error is carried upward through the whole tree. This is the price of a deterministic algorithm and of a result that contains every number of clusters at once.

The memory cost is the other limit. A distance matrix on \(m\) points holds \(m(m-1)/2\) entries, which is \(1770\) for \(60\) points but of the order of \(10^{13}\) for five million, and merging \(m\) points one pair at a time needs about \(m\) steps that each look at that matrix. That is why agglomerative clustering is used on samples of thousands, not millions, of points; a common practice is to run k-means with many clusters to compress a large data set into centroids and then cluster the centroids hierarchically.

docs.title: The Davies–Bouldin index
docs.text:
The Davies–Bouldin index scores a clustering by comparing, for each cluster, its spread against its separation from the most similar other cluster. Let \(s_{i}\) be the mean distance of the points in cluster \(i\) to its centroid, and \(d_{ij}\) the distance between the centroids of clusters \(i\) and \(j\). Then

\[\text{DB} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k} \max_{j \ne i} \frac{s_{i} + s_{j}}{d_{ij}}\]

A tight cluster far from every other has a small ratio, so lower is better, and a value near 0 means compact, well separated clusters. For the one-dimensional clustering \(\{1, 2, 3\}\), \(\{9, 10\}\), \(\{20\}\) the centroids are \(2\), \(9.5\) and \(20\) and the spreads are \(s_{1} = (1 + 0 + 1)/3 = 0.667\), \(s_{2} = 0.5\) and \(s_{3} = 0\). The ratios are \((0.667 + 0.5)/7.5 = 0.156\) for clusters 1 and 2, \(0.667/18 = 0.037\) for 1 and 3, and \(0.5/10.5 = 0.048\) for 2 and 3, so the worst partner of cluster 1 is cluster 2 (0.156), of cluster 2 is cluster 1 (0.156), and of cluster 3 is cluster 2 (0.048). The index is \((0.156 + 0.156 + 0.048)/3 = 0.12\). Like the silhouette, it is computed from the data and the clustering alone, and like every internal index it is useful for comparing clusterings of the same data and not as a certificate that the clusters are real.

docs.title: 14.4 Worked examples
docs.text:
The examples below work through the calculations of this chapter in full. Try each one on paper before reading the steps.

Example 14.1: Agglomerative clustering by hand

Problem. Four points on a line: \(P(1), Q(2), R(5), S(9)\). Build the dendrogram under single linkage and under complete linkage, and give the two-cluster solution in each case.

Step 1 — the distance matrix

\(P\) \(Q\) \(R\) \(S\) \(P\) 0 1 4 8 \(Q\) 1 0 3 7 \(R\) 4 3 0 4 \(S\) 8 7 4 0

The smallest entry is 1, so \(P\) and \(Q\) merge first at height 1 under any linkage — with singletons, every linkage agrees.

Step 2 — single linkage

d({P,Q}, \(R) = \min(4, 3) = 3 \cdot\) d({P,Q}, \(S) = \min(8, 7) = 7 \cdot d(R, S) = 4\)

Smallest is 3, so {P,Q} merges with \(R\) at height 3.

Then d({P,Q,R}, \(S) = \min(8, 7, 4) = 4\), so \(S\) joins at height 4.

Two-cluster solution (cut just below 4): {P, \(Q\), R} and {S}.

Step 3 — complete linkage

d({P,Q}, \(R) = \max(4, 3) = 4 \cdot\) d({P,Q}, \(S) = \max(8, 7) = 8 \cdot d(R, S) = 4\)

There is a tie at 4. Take \(R\) and \(S\): {R,S} merges at height 4.

Then d({P,Q}, {R,S}) \(= \max(4, 8, 3, 7) = 8\), so everything joins at height 8.

Two-cluster solution: {P, Q} and {R, S}.

Answer. Single linkage gives {P,Q,R} and {S}. Complete linkage gives {P,Q} and {R,S}. Same data, same distances, different answer.

Comment. Single linkage grew a chain P–Q–R because each successive link was short, even though \(P\) and \(R\) are 4 apart. Complete linkage refused, because it insists every member be close to every other, and it preferred to pair \(R\) with \(S\). Neither is wrong — but you must say which you used, because the result is meaningless without it.

Example 14.2: Silhouette for one point

Problem. Point \(x\) is in cluster A with two others, at distances 1 and 3. The nearest other cluster B has three members at distances 5, 6 and 7. Compute the silhouette coefficient for \(x\) and interpret it.

Step 1 — a, the cohesion

\(a =\) mean distance to the other members of its own cluster \(= (1 + 3)/2 = 2\). Note \(x\) itself is not counted.

Step 2 — \(b\), the separation

\(b =\) mean distance to all members of the nearest other cluster \(= (5 + 6 + 7)/3 = 6\)

Step 3 — combine

\(s = (b -\) a)/max(a, \(b) = (6 - 2)/6 = 4/6 = 0.667\)

Step 4 — interpret

+0.667 is comfortably positive: \(x\) is three times closer to its own cluster than to the next one, so it is well placed. Values above about 0.5 are generally read as a strong assignment, near 0 as borderline, and negative as misassigned — which happens when \(b < a\), meaning the point is on average nearer to a cluster it does not belong to.

Averaging \(s\) over every point scores the whole clustering, and that average can be maximised over \(k\), which is exactly what WCSS cannot do.

Answer. \(s = 0.667\) — a well-assigned point.

Example 14.3: Diagnose four failed clusterings

Problem. For each situation, name the problem and give the remedy. (a) Two runs of k-means with \(k = 4\) give quite different results. \((b)\) The data is two interlocking crescents and k-means slices both in half. \((c)\) One cluster contains a single point. \((d)\) The clustering appears to be driven entirely by annual income.

(a) Different results each run

Local optima. Lloyd's algorithm converges to a partition determined by where the centroids started. Remedy: run it 10 times with different seeds and keep the lowest WCSS, and use k-means++ so the starts are spread out. scikit-learn's n_init=10 does exactly this by default.

\((b)\) Crescents cut in half

Wrong algorithm, not wrong parameters. k-means assigns each point to the nearest centroid, so its boundaries are perpendicular bisectors — straight lines — and its clusters are convex. A crescent is not convex, so no \(k\) and no initialisation will fix it. Remedy: DBSCAN, spectral clustering, or single-linkage hierarchical, all of which can follow a curved shape.

(c) A cluster of one

An outlier has captured a centroid. Squared distance is dominated by the far-away point, so giving it its own cluster lowers WCSS more than anything else available. Remedy: remove or cap outliers first, or use k-medoids, whose centres must be actual data points and which minimises absolute rather than squared distance.

\((d)\) One feature dominates

Unscaled features. Income runs to \(10^{5}\) and age to \(10^{1}\), so the income term is about \(10^{8}\) times larger in every squared distance and the other features contribute nothing. Remedy: standardise every feature before computing a single distance.

Answer. (a) local optima — restart with k-means++; \((b)\) wrong algorithm — use DBSCAN or spectral; \((c)\) an outlier — remove it or use k-medoids; \((d)\) unscaled features — standardise.

Example 14.4: The same distance matrix, two linkages, two different trees

Problem. Four points have the distance matrix below. Build the agglomerative clustering under single linkage and under complete linkage, give the merge heights, and cut each tree into two clusters.

A B C D A 0 1 4 5 B 1 0 2 6 C 4 2 0 3 D 5 6 3 0

Step 1 — the first merge, the same for both

The smallest entry is \(d(A, B) = 1\), so \(\{A, B\}\) forms at height 1 under either linkage.

Step 2 — single linkage (cluster distance is the minimum)

\(d(\{A,B\}, C) = \min(4, 2) = 2\), \(\quad d(\{A,B\}, D) = \min(5, 6) = 5\), \(\quad d(C, D) = 3\)

The smallest is 2, so \(C\) joins \(\{A, B\}\) at height 2. Then \(d(\{A,B,C\}, D) = \min(5, 3) = 3\), and \(D\) joins at height 3.

The tree is \((((A,B),C),D)\) with heights \(1, 2, 3\). A cut between 2 and 3 gives \(\{A, B, C\}\) and \(\{D\}\).

Step 3 — complete linkage (cluster distance is the maximum)

\(d(\{A,B\}, C) = \max(4, 2) = 4\), \(\quad d(\{A,B\}, D) = \max(5, 6) = 6\), \(\quad d(C, D) = 3\)

The smallest is now \(d(C, D) = 3\), so \(\{C, D\}\) forms at height 3. Then \(d(\{A,B\}, \{C,D\}) = \max(4, 5, 2, 6) = 6\), and the two pairs join at height 6.

The tree is \(((A,B),(C,D))\) with heights \(1, 3, 6\). A cut between 3 and 6 gives \(\{A, B\}\) and \(\{C, D\}\).

Answer. Single linkage: heights \(1, 2, 3\), two clusters \(\{A,B,C\}\) and \(\{D\}\). Complete linkage: heights \(1, 3, 6\), two clusters \(\{A,B\}\) and \(\{C,D\}\).

Comment. The disagreement is in the second merge. Single linkage looked only at the nearest pair, \(B\) and \(C\) at distance 2, and so attached \(C\) to \(\{A, B\}\) even though \(A\) and \(C\) are 4 apart. Complete linkage asked for the farthest pair, saw that \(C\) would then be 4 from \(A\) and only 3 from \(D\), and refused. The top merge heights, 3 and 6, also differ by a factor of 2, so heights from different linkages must never be compared.

Example 14.5: Single, complete and average linkage on five points

Problem. Five points have the distance matrix below. Give the merge order and heights under single, complete and average linkage.

P Q R S T P 0 2 6 10 9 Q 2 0 5 9 8 R 6 5 0 4 5 S 10 9 4 0 3 T 9 8 5 3 0

Step 1 — the two merges all linkages agree on

The smallest entry is \(d(P, Q) = 2\), so \(\{P, Q\}\) forms at height 2. Of the rest, \(d(S, T) = 3\) is smallest, so \(\{S, T\}\) forms at height 3. Singleton distances do not depend on the linkage.

Step 2 — where \(R\) goes

The distances from \(R\) to the other clusters are:

to \(\{P,Q\}\) to \(\{S,T\}\) single (min) \(\min(6, 5) = 5\) \(\min(4, 5) = 4\) complete (max) \(\max(6, 5) = 6\) \(\max(4, 5) = 5\) average \((6 + 5)/2 = 5.5\) \((4 + 5)/2 = 4.5\)

Under each linkage \(R\) is nearest to \(\{S, T\}\), so it joins them at height 4 (single), 5 (complete) or 4.5 (average). The distance between \(\{P, Q\}\) and \(\{S, T\}\) is at least 8 under every linkage, so it is not the smaller one.

Step 3 — the final merge

\(\{P, Q\}\) joins \(\{R, S, T\}\). The six cross distances are \(d(P,R) = 6\), \(d(P,S) = 10\), \(d(P,T) = 9\), \(d(Q,R) = 5\), \(d(Q,S) = 9\), \(d(Q,T) = 8\).

Single: the minimum, \(5\). Complete: the maximum, \(10\). Average: \((6 + 10 + 9 + 5 + 9 + 8)/6 = 47/6 = 7.83\).

Answer.

linkage merge 1 merge 2 merge 3 merge 4 single \(PQ\) at 2 \(ST\) at 3 \(R\) joins \(ST\) at 4 \(PQ\) joins \(RST\) at 5 complete \(PQ\) at 2 \(ST\) at 3 \(R\) joins \(ST\) at 5 \(PQ\) joins \(RST\) at 10 average \(PQ\) at 2 \(ST\) at 3 \(R\) joins \(ST\) at 4.5 \(PQ\) joins \(RST\) at 7.83

Comment. The merge order, and so the tree shape, is the same for all three; only the heights differ, and they are ordered single \(\le\) average \(\le\) complete in every row. That ordering always holds, because the minimum of a set of numbers is at most their mean, which is at most their maximum. A cut that yields two clusters gives \(\{P,Q\}\) and \(\{R,S,T\}\) in each case.

Example 14.6: Single linkage on points in the plane

Problem. Cluster \(A(1,2),\; B(2,1),\; C(4,4),\; D(5,4),\; E(2,5)\) by single linkage with Euclidean distance. Give the distance matrix, the merges with their heights, and the two-cluster solution.

Step 1 — the distance matrix

\(d(A,B) = \sqrt{1 + 1} = 1.414\), \(\quad d(A,C) = \sqrt{9 + 4} = 3.606\), \(\quad d(A,D) = \sqrt{16 + 4} = 4.472\), \(\quad d(A,E) = \sqrt{1 + 9} = 3.162\)

\(d(B,C) = \sqrt{4 + 9} = 3.606\), \(\quad d(B,D) = \sqrt{9 + 9} = 4.243\), \(\quad d(B,E) = \sqrt{0 + 16} = 4\)

\(d(C,D) = \sqrt{1 + 0} = 1\), \(\quad d(C,E) = \sqrt{4 + 1} = 2.236\), \(\quad d(D,E) = \sqrt{9 + 1} = 3.162\)

A B C D E A 0 1.414 3.606 4.472 3.162 B 1.414 0 3.606 4.243 4 C 3.606 3.606 0 1 2.236 D 4.472 4.243 1 0 3.162 E 3.162 4 2.236 3.162 0

Step 2 — merge \(C\) and \(D\)

The smallest entry is \(d(C, D) = 1\), so \(\{C, D\}\) forms at height 1. The updated distances, each the smaller of two entries, are \(d(\{C,D\}, A) = \min(3.606, 4.472) = 3.606\), \(d(\{C,D\}, B) = \min(3.606, 4.243) = 3.606\) and \(d(\{C,D\}, E) = \min(2.236, 3.162) = 2.236\).

Step 3 — merge \(A\) and \(B\)

The smallest entry is now \(d(A, B) = 1.414\), so \(\{A, B\}\) forms at height 1.414. Then \(d(\{A,B\}, \{C,D\}) = \min(3.606, 3.606) = 3.606\) and \(d(\{A,B\}, E) = \min(3.162, 4) = 3.162\).

Step 4 — merge \(E\) into \(\{C, D\}\)

The smallest remaining is \(d(\{C,D\}, E) = 2.236\), so \(E\) joins \(\{C, D\}\) at height 2.236. Now \(d(\{A,B\}, \{C,D,E\}) = \min(3.606, 3.162) = 3.162\).

Step 5 — the last merge, and the cut

\(\{A, B\}\) joins \(\{C, D, E\}\) at height 3.162, the single link being \(A\) to \(E\). The merge heights are \(1,\ 1.414,\ 2.236,\ 3.162\). A cut between 2.236 and 3.162 crosses two branches.

Answer. Two clusters: \(\{A, B\}\) and \(\{C, D, E\}\). Merge heights \(1,\ 1.414,\ 2.236,\ 3.162\).

Comment. The last link is \(A\) to \(E\), at \(3.162\), not the larger \(3.606\) that connects both \(A\) and \(B\) to \(C\). Single linkage uses only the smallest cross distance, so a single pair of points, one from each side, decided how the two halves were joined.

Example 14.7: Reading the elbow from a table

Problem. Running k-means for several values of \(k\) gives the following WCSS. Use the elbow method to choose \(k\).

\(k\) 1 2 3 4 5 WCSS 500 220 90 75 65

Step 1 — the drop bought by each extra cluster

step drop as a fraction of the previous WCSS \(1 \to 2\) \(500 - 220 = 280\) \(280/500 = 56\%\) \(2 \to 3\) \(220 - 90 = 130\) \(130/220 = 59\%\) \(3 \to 4\) \(90 - 75 = 15\) \(15/90 = 17\%\) \(4 \to 5\) \(75 - 65 = 10\) \(10/75 = 13\%\)

Step 2 — find the bend

The first two extra clusters each cut the WCSS by more than half. After \(k = 3\) the gains drop abruptly to a handful of units and stay small. The curve bends at \(k = 3\).

Answer. \(k = 3\).

Comment. The elbow is a judgement, not a calculation: the evidence here is the sharp change between the second and third rows of the table. When the curve falls smoothly, with no visible bend, the elbow gives no answer, and the silhouette or the purpose of the analysis has to decide. The elbow also cannot confirm that the clusters are real; it only locates the point of diminishing returns.

Example 14.8: Average silhouette for a whole clustering

Problem. The six points \(1, 2, 3, 9, 10, 20\) on a line are clustered in two ways: \(k = 2\) gives \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) and \(\{9, 10, 20\}\), and \(k = 3\) gives \(\{1, 2, 3\}\), \(\{9, 10\}\) and \(\{20\}\). Compute the average silhouette of each and compare.

Step 1 — silhouettes for \(k = 2\)

For each point, \(a\) is its mean distance to the others in its own cluster, \(b\) is its mean distance to the other cluster, and \(s = (b - a)/\max(a, b)\).

point \(a\) \(b\) \(s\) 1 \((1+2)/2 = 1.5\) \((8+9+19)/3 = 12\) \(10.5/12 = 0.875\) 2 \((1+1)/2 = 1\) \((7+8+18)/3 = 11\) \(10/11 = 0.909\) 3 \((2+1)/2 = 1.5\) \((6+7+17)/3 = 10\) \(8.5/10 = 0.850\) 9 \((1+11)/2 = 6\) \((8+7+6)/3 = 7\) \(1/7 = 0.143\) 10 \((1+10)/2 = 5.5\) \((9+8+7)/3 = 8\) \(2.5/8 = 0.313\) 20 \((11+10)/2 = 10.5\) \((19+18+17)/3 = 18\) \(7.5/18 = 0.417\)

The average is \((0.875 + 0.909 + 0.850 + 0.143 + 0.313 + 0.417)/6 = 3.506/6 = 0.584\).

Step 2 — silhouettes for \(k = 3\)

point \(a\) \(b\) (nearest other cluster) \(s\) 1 1.5 \((8+9)/2 = 8.5\) \(7/8.5 = 0.824\) 2 1 \((7+8)/2 = 7.5\) \(6.5/7.5 = 0.867\) 3 1.5 \((6+7)/2 = 6.5\) \(5/6.5 = 0.769\) 9 1 \((8+7+6)/3 = 7\) \(6/7 = 0.857\) 10 1 \((9+8+7)/3 = 8\) \(7/8 = 0.875\) 20 undefined \(0\) by convention

For the point 9 the nearest other cluster is \(\{1,2,3\}\) (mean distance 7), not \(\{20\}\) (distance 11). The singleton \(\{20\}\) has no other member to measure \(a\) against, and the convention is \(s = 0\).

The average is \((0.824 + 0.867 + 0.769 + 0.857 + 0.875 + 0)/6 = 4.192/6 = 0.699\).

Step 3 — compare, and check against the WCSS

\(k = 3\) has the higher average silhouette (\(0.699\) against \(0.584\)). The WCSS agrees: with \(k = 2\) the cluster \(\{9, 10, 20\}\) has centroid 13 and contributes \(16 + 9 + 49 = 74\), giving a total of \(76\); with \(k = 3\) the total is \(2 + 0.5 + 0 = 2.5\).

Answer. Average silhouette \(0.584\) for \(k = 2\) and \(0.699\) for \(k = 3\), so \(k = 3\) is preferred.

Comment. The weak silhouettes in the \(k = 2\) table, \(0.143\) and \(0.313\) for the points 9 and 10, point straight at the problem: the point 20 is far from 9 and 10 and does not belong with them. This is the per-point diagnostic the average hides. Isolating 20 raised the silhouettes of 9 and 10 from \(0.143\) and \(0.313\) to \(0.857\) and \(0.875\), and the singleton's own \(s = 0\) costs the average little. So check whether a singleton cluster is a genuine anomaly or only an artefact of choosing \(k\) too large.

Example 14.9: Comparing a clustering with known labels

Problem. Ten items have true classes A or B, and a clustering puts them in two clusters, giving the counts below. Compute the purity and the Rand index.

class A class B cluster size cluster 1 4 1 5 cluster 2 1 4 5

Step 1 — purity

Each cluster is credited with its most common class: 4 in cluster 1 and 4 in cluster 2. Purity \(= (4 + 4)/10 = 0.8\).

Step 2 — the Rand index counts pairs

There are \(\binom{10}{2} = 45\) pairs of items. Each pair is either together or apart in the clustering, and together or apart in the true classes.

  • Together in both: cluster 1 has \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) pairs both of class A, and cluster 2 has \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) both of class B. Total \(12\).
  • Together in the clustering: \(\binom{5}{2} + \binom{5}{2} = 20\) pairs, so \(20 - 12 = 8\) of them are together in the clusters but of different classes.
  • Together in the classes: \(\binom{5}{2} + \binom{5}{2} = 20\) pairs, so \(20 - 12 = 8\) are of the same class but split between the clusters.
  • Apart in both: \(45 - 12 - 8 - 8 = 17\).

Step 3 — the index

\(\text{Rand} = \dfrac{12 + 17}{45} = \dfrac{29}{45} = 0.644\)

The adjusted Rand index corrects this for chance agreement. It uses the expected number of agreeing pairs for random labels, \(20 \times 20/45 = 8.89\):

\(\text{ARI} = \dfrac{12 - 8.89}{\tfrac{1}{2}(20 + 20) - 8.89} = \dfrac{3.11}{11.11} = 0.28\)

Answer. Purity \(0.8\), Rand index \(0.644\), adjusted Rand index \(0.28\).

Comment. Purity of \(0.8\) sounds good and the adjusted index of \(0.28\) sounds poor, and both describe the same table. Purity ignores how the errors fall and rises trivially as the number of clusters grows (it is 1 when every point is its own cluster), while the adjusted index starts from 0 for a random labelling. Neither measure cares which cluster is called 1 and which 2, so permuting the cluster names leaves them unchanged.

docs.title: 14.5 Common mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
Each of the following is a mistake that costs marks in an examination or accuracy in practice.

  • Do not report a hierarchical clustering without naming the linkage. Single and complete can give completely different trees from the same distances.
  • Do not read the horizontal order of leaves in a dendrogram as meaningful. Any branch can be swapped without changing the tree; only the heights carry information.
  • Do not assume clusters exist. Every algorithm here will return clusters from pure noise.
  • Do not confuse clustering with classification. There is no accuracy here, and a cluster is not a class until a human decides what it means.

docs.title: 14.6 Summary
docs.text:
After working through this chapter you should be able to do the following.

  • Choose \(k\) with the elbow and the silhouette, and you can explain in one sentence why WCSS alone can never do it.
  • Build an agglomerative clustering under three linkages, show that they give different answers on the same data, read a dendrogram's heights, and cut it to get any \(k\) you like.
  • Recall that evaluation here is genuinely harder: internal measures compare runs, and external ones need labels you usually do not have. You also know that every algorithm in this unit will happily return clusters from pure noise. That is why the last check is always a human one.

docs.title: 14.7 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Cluster \(P = \{p_{1}, p_{2}\}\) and \(Q = \{q_{1}, q_{2}\}\) with distances \(d(p_{1},q_{1})=3, d(p_{1},q_{2})=6, d(p_{2},q_{1})=4, d(p_{2},q_{2})=9\). Give the single, complete and average linkage distances.

    Answer

    Single: the minimum, \(3\). Complete: the maximum, \(9\). Average: \((3 + 6 + 4 + 9)/4 = 22/4 = 5.5\).

  2. Five points on a line at 0, 1, 4, 9, 10. Build the single-linkage dendrogram and give the two-cluster solution.

    Answer

    The smallest gaps are \(0\)–\(1\) and \(9\)–\(10\), both \(1\), so those two pairs form at height \(1\). The nearest points between \(\{0, 1\}\) and the point \(4\) are \(1\) and \(4\), so \(4\) joins at height \(3\). The last merge joins \(\{0, 1, 4\}\) to \(\{9, 10\}\) through the pair \(4\) and \(9\), at height \(5\).

    Cutting between heights 3 and 5 gives the two clusters \(\{0, 1, 4\}\) and \(\{9, 10\}\).

  3. A point has \(a = 4\) and \(b = 3\). Compute its silhouette and say what it means.

    Answer

    \(s = (b - a)/\max(a, b) = (3 - 4)/4 = -0.25\). A negative value means the point is on average nearer to another cluster than to its own, so it is probably in the wrong cluster.

  4. Four points have the distance matrix with \(d(A,B) = 2\), \(d(A,C) = 6\), \(d(A,D) = 10\), \(d(B,C) = 5\), \(d(B,D) = 9\), \(d(C,D) = 4\). Give the merge order and merge heights under single, complete and average linkage, and the two-cluster solution.

    Answer

    The smallest distance is \(d(A,B) = 2\), so \(\{A,B\}\) forms first at height 2 under every linkage. Then \(d(\{A,B\}, C)\) is \(5\), \(6\) or \(5.5\) and \(d(\{A,B\}, D)\) is \(9\), \(10\) or \(9.5\) (single, complete, average), both larger than \(d(C,D) = 4\), so \(\{C,D\}\) forms second at height 4.

    The last merge joins \(\{A,B\}\) and \(\{C,D\}\) through the cross distances \(6, 10, 5, 9\): single \(= \min = 5\), complete \(= \max = 10\), average \(= 30/4 = 7.5\).

    The order is the same for all three, with heights \(2, 4, 5\) (single), \(2, 4, 10\) (complete) and \(2, 4, 7.5\) (average). The two-cluster solution is \(\{A,B\}\) and \(\{C,D\}\) in every case, from a cut just below the last merge.

  5. The one-dimensional points are \(A = 2\), \(B = 4\), \(C = 7\), \(D = 9\). Cluster them by complete linkage, and also by single linkage, giving the heights. There is a tie: does it matter which tied pair is merged first?

    Answer

    The distances are \(d(A,B) = 2\), \(d(C,D) = 2\), \(d(B,C) = 3\), \(d(A,C) = 5\), \(d(B,D) = 5\), \(d(A,D) = 7\).

    The smallest value, \(2\), occurs twice, for \(A\)–\(B\) and \(C\)–\(D\). The two merges involve different points and do not interfere, so whichever is done first, both clusters form at height 2 and the order does not matter.

    Complete linkage: the last merge is \(\max(5, 7, 3, 5) = 7\), so the heights are \(2, 2, 7\). Single linkage: the last merge is \(\min(5, 7, 3, 5) = 3\), so the heights are \(2, 2, 3\). Both give the two clusters \(\{A,B\}\) and \(\{C,D\}\) if cut between 2 and the final height.

  6. The points are \(A = (1, 2)\), \(B = (2, 4)\) and \(C = (5, 8)\). By single linkage, which two clusters form first, and at what heights?

    Answer

    \(d(A,B) = \sqrt{1 + 4} = \sqrt{5} = 2.236\), \(d(B,C) = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5\), \(d(A,C) = \sqrt{16 + 36} = \sqrt{52} = 7.211\).

    The smallest is \(d(A,B)\), so \(\{A, B\}\) forms first at height \(2.236\). Then \(d(\{A,B\}, C) = \min(7.211, 5) = 5\), so \(C\) joins at height \(5\).

  7. A dendrogram on five points has merge heights \(0.5, 0.8, 2.0, 3.5\) (bottom to top). (a) What does the height of a merge represent? (b) How many clusters result from a cut between 0.8 and 2.0, and how many from a cut between 2.0 and 3.5? (c) Why is the left-to-right order of the leaves not meaningful?

    Answer

    (a) The distance, in the linkage being used, between the two clusters at the moment they were merged.

    (b) A cut between 0.8 and 2.0 lies above the two lowest merges and below the other two, so two merges have happened and \(5 - 2 = 3\) clusters remain. A cut between 2.0 and 3.5 lies above three merges, so \(5 - 3 = 2\) clusters remain.

    (c) At every merge the two branches can be swapped without changing which points are joined or at what height. A tree on five points therefore has \(2^{4} = 16\) equivalent drawings. Only the heights, and which branches are joined, carry information. Two leaves drawn side by side are not necessarily similar.

  8. Compute the silhouette coefficient for (i) \(a = 1.5\), \(b = 4.5\) and (ii) \(a = 2.8\), \(b = 3.0\), and interpret each.

    Answer

    (i) \(s = (4.5 - 1.5)/4.5 = 3/4.5 = 0.667\). The point is three times nearer its own cluster than the next one, so it is well assigned.

    (ii) \(s = (3.0 - 2.8)/3.0 = 0.067\). The point is almost equally close to both clusters, so it lies on a fuzzy boundary; the assignment is barely better than the alternative. A silhouette of exactly 0 would mean \(a = b\).

  9. One algorithm splits \(N\) points into two clusters of \(N/2\) each and another splits the same points into clusters of \(N/4\) and \(3N/4\). Which is better? Name an evaluation measure you would use.

    Answer

    The sizes alone say nothing about quality. Equal clusters are not better than unequal ones, since the true groups may well be of unequal size, and an algorithm that forces equal sizes can cut a natural group in two.

    Compare the two clusterings with a measure computed from the data and the clusters: the average silhouette (higher is better) or the Davies–Bouldin index (lower is better), and the WCSS if the two have the same \(k\), as they do here. If true labels are available, use an external measure such as the adjusted Rand index or purity. Prefer the clustering with the better score, and then look at the groups to see whether they make sense for the application.

  10. (a) You must cluster 5 million web-log records, and you roughly know how many groups you want. (b) A biologist has 60 samples and wants to see the hierarchy of relationships between them. Recommend k-means or agglomerative clustering for each, and justify it.

    Answer

    (a) K-means. Its cost is linear in the number of records, \(O(mkni)\). Agglomerative clustering needs all pairwise distances, about \(m^{2}/2 = 1.25 \times 10^{13}\) of them for \(m = 5 \times 10^{6}\), which is roughly 100 terabytes at 8 bytes each, so it is out of the question. The number of groups is roughly known, which is the one thing k-means needs.

    (b) Agglomerative clustering. There are only \(60 \times 59/2 = 1770\) pairs, so the cost is trivial, and the dendrogram is exactly the hierarchy the biologist wants. No \(k\) has to be fixed in advance, and the result is deterministic, so the same samples always give the same tree.

  11. K-means is run for \(k = 1, \dots, 6\) and gives WCSS of \(1200, 640, 310, 270, 250, 240\). Find the elbow, and say what you would check before accepting it.

    Answer

    The drops are \(560, 330, 40, 20, 10\). The gains are large up to \(k = 3\) and small afterwards, so the elbow is at \(k = 3\).

    Before accepting it, check the average silhouette at \(k = 2\) to \(5\) to see that \(k = 3\) is also a good value there; look at the clusters or their profiles to see whether they mean something for the application; and remember that the elbow only locates diminishing returns. It does not prove that the data has three clusters.

  12. (a) Explain in what sense Ward's linkage is the hierarchical cousin of k-means, giving one practical advantage of each. (b) The cost of merging two clusters under Ward's linkage is \(\dfrac{n_{a} n_{b}}{n_{a} + n_{b}} \Vert \mu_{a} - \mu_{b}\Vert^{2}\). Compute it for merging \(\{1, 2\}\) and \(\{5\}\), and check it against the WCSS.

    Answer

    (a) Both try to keep the WCSS small. Ward merges, at each step, the two clusters whose union raises the total WCSS the least, which builds a tree of compact, similar-sized clusters of the kind k-means produces. K-means has the advantage of speed, linear in the number of points, and of letting points move between clusters at every iteration. Ward gives the whole hierarchy at once, with no need to fix \(k\) in advance and a deterministic result, but its merges are greedy and never undone, and it costs at least \(O(m^{2})\).

    (b) The means are \(1.5\) and \(5\) and the sizes \(2\) and \(1\), so the cost is \(\dfrac{2 \cdot 1}{3} (3.5)^{2} = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 12.25 = 8.167\). Check: the WCSS of \(\{1, 2, 5\}\) about its mean \(8/3\) is \(\tfrac{25 + 4 + 49}{9} = 8.667\), and the WCSS of \(\{1, 2\}\) is \(0.5\), so merging raises it by \(8.667 - 0.5 = 8.167\).

  13. A clustering of 30 items into three clusters, compared with their three true classes, has the counts shown. Compute the purity and say which cluster is weakest.

    class 1 class 2 class 3 cluster 1 9 1 0 cluster 2 1 6 3 cluster 3 0 1 9 Answer

    Each cluster is credited with its largest count: \(9, 6, 9\). Purity \(= (9 + 6 + 9)/30 = 24/30 = 0.8\).

    Cluster 2 is the weakest: its purity is \(6/10 = 0.6\), and it mixes all three classes, with 3 items of class 3. Clusters 1 and 3 are each \(0.9\) pure.

    Purity should be read with care: it rises as the number of clusters rises and is 1 when every item is its own cluster. The adjusted Rand index for this table is \(0.50\), a chance-corrected measure that does not have that weakness.

  14. Define the chaining effect. The points \(0, 1, 2\) and \(6, 7, 8\) form two groups. At what height does single linkage join them? Add a stray point at \(4\) and repeat. Does the final merge height of complete linkage change?

    Answer

    Chaining is single linkage's tendency to merge two clusters through a thin bridge of intermediate points, because it looks only at the nearest pair and so lets a chain of short links join groups that are far apart overall.

    Without the stray point the groups are joined by the pair \(2\) and \(6\), at height \(4\). With a point at \(4\) the gaps \(2\) to \(4\) and \(4\) to \(6\) are both \(2\), so single linkage joins the groups through the bridge at height \(2\), half the earlier height, and the clear gap between the groups has disappeared from the tree.

    Complete linkage uses the farthest pair, so its final merge is at \(|0 - 8| = 8\) in both cases, and the stray point does not change it. This is why complete linkage resists chaining.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Learning from Data
docs.text:
Ordinary programming works by explicit instruction. You study a problem, work out the rules yourself, and write them down. To separate spam from real mail that way you might begin with if "lottery" in subject: mark_as_spam(). That works for a dozen obvious cases and then falls apart. Spammers change their words. Genuine mail mentions transfers and prizes. The rulebook grows into a thicket nobody can maintain, and it is still wrong.

Machine learning turns this around. You do not write the rules. You supply examples instead — thousands of messages already marked spam or not — and an algorithm works the rules out for itself. You write the recipe for learning; the data supplies the specifics. That is the whole inversion, and everything in this course is a variation on it.

One warning before you start, because it decides how you should read every later unit. A model that reproduces its training data perfectly has proved nothing. A lookup table can do that. The only question that matters is how the model behaves on data it has never seen. That property is called generalisation, and everything that looks like decoration in this course — splitting the data, regularisation, cross-validation, pruning — exists to protect it.

Learning outcomes of Unit 1

  • Say precisely what distinguishes machine learning from ordinary programming, and state Mitchell's \(T / P / E\) definition for a system you have just been described.
  • Name the parts of a learning problem — instance, feature, label, model, hypothesis space, parameter, hyper-parameter, loss, generalisation — and point to each one in a real dataset.
  • Classify any task as supervised (classification or regression), unsupervised (clustering or dimensionality reduction) or reinforcement learning, and defend the choice.
  • Explain why training error is not evidence of anything, and diagnose underfitting and overfitting from a pair of error numbers.
  • Lay out the end-to-end pipeline from raw data to a deployed model, and say what goes wrong if any two steps are swapped.

docs.title: 1.1 What machine learning is
docs.text:
There is a famous informal definition, usually credited to Arthur Samuel. In 1959 he wrote a checkers program that got better than he was by playing itself, and he described the field as the study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed. It is a good slogan and a poor specification — it does not tell you what to build or how to tell whether it worked. Tom Mitchell's 1997 version does.

Definition: Mitchell's definition of learning

A computer program is said to learn from experience \(E\) with respect to some class of tasks \(T\) and performance measure \(P\), if its performance at tasks in \(T\), as measured by \(P\), improves with experience \(E\).

The value of this definition is that it forces you to name three things, and naming them turns a wish into an engineering problem. “Build something that detects fraud” is a wish. The three-part version is a specification you can start work on tomorrow.

Spam filter Handwriting recognition Flat-price predictor \(T\) — the task label an incoming email spam / not spam identify which digit 0–9 an image shows predict the sale price of a flat \(P\) — the measure fraction of mail classified correctly, or recall on spam at a fixed false-alarm rate percentage of digits recognised correctly root mean squared error in lakhs \(E\) — the experience a corpus of mail users have already marked 60 000 labelled digit images 12 000 past sales with area, rooms, locality

Key idea

If you cannot state \(P\), you cannot tell whether the system is improving, and you have no way to choose between two models. Half the disasters in applied machine learning are not modelling failures at all — they are projects that optimised a P nobody had thought about carefully. A cancer screen with 99% accuracy on a population where 1% have cancer may be detecting nothing whatsoever.

Traditional programming Machine learning A human studies the problem and works out the rules. The rules are unknown, or too many to write down. Rules + data go in; answers come out. Data + answers go in; a model comes out. Every case must be anticipated in advance. Cases nobody anticipated are handled by generalisation. Behaviour is fully inspectable: you can read the rule. Behaviour may be opaque — a neural network is not a rule you can read. Changing the world means rewriting the code. Changing the world means retraining on new data. Right when the rules are genuinely known — payroll, tax, a compiler, a sorting routine. Right when patterns exist, are hard to hand-code, and data is available — spam, faces, speech, demand.

The third bullet on each side is the honest trade. A rule-based system is exactly as good as the rules you wrote, and no better; a learned model can handle a case you never imagined, and can also fail on one for reasons you cannot see.

When is machine learning the right tool?

Three conditions have to hold together. A pattern exists — there is some real relation between the inputs and the target, otherwise you are fitting noise. You cannot write it down — if you can, write it down; a rule is faster, cheaper and auditable. Data is available — enough examples, of the right kind, with labels if the task is supervised. If all three hold, learning is likely the best available tool. If any fails, it is the wrong one.

docs.title: AI, machine learning, deep learning, data science
docs.text: These four names are used loosely in public and precisely in exams, so it is worth fixing them. Artificial intelligence is the broadest: any technique that makes machines behave in ways we would call intelligent, rule-based expert systems and search algorithms included. Machine learning is the subset of AI in which the behaviour is learned from data rather than programmed. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers, which learn the features as well as the model. Data science is not a subset of anything — it is a wider practice of getting value out of data, using machine learning as one tool alongside statistics, databases, visualisation and domain knowledge.

docs.title: 1.2 The anatomy of a learning problem
docs.text:
Every algorithm in Units 2 to 5 is assembled from the same handful of parts. Learn the parts once here and each new algorithm becomes a rearrangement of things you already know rather than a fresh subject.

A dataset, with everything named

# area (sq ft) bedrooms age (years) price (lakh) 1 1 100 2 8 62 2 1 450 3 3 91 3 900 2 15 48 4 1 800 4 1 128 … … … … …
  • Instance / example — one row. Row 4 is one example, written \(x^{(4)}\) together with its answer \(y^{(4)}\).
  • Feature — one input column. Here there are \(n = 3\) features. The price column is the target, not a feature; miscounting this is the single commonest slip in the first month of the course.
  • Feature vector — one row's features taken together: \(x^{(4)} = (1800, 4, 1)\). It is a point in a 3-dimensional feature space, and thinking of examples as points in space is what makes k-NN, k-means and SVM intuitive later.
  • Target / label — the answer column \(y\). Continuous \(\to\) regression; categorical \(\to\) classification.
  • \(m\) — the number of examples. \(n\) — the number of features. The design matrix \(X\) is therefore \(m \times n\).

Definition: Model, hypothesis and hypothesis space

A model (or hypothesis) \(h_{\theta }\) is a function that maps a feature vector to a prediction: \(\hat{y} = h_{\theta }(x)\). The hypothesis space \(H\) is the set of all functions the algorithm is allowed to consider — for example, every straight line, or every decision tree of depth \(\le 4\). Learning is a search of \(H\) for the member that fits the data best.

\[ \hat{y} = h_{\theta }(x) = \theta _{0} + \theta _{1}x_{1} + \theta _{2}x_{2} + \theta _{3}x_{3} \]

the hypothesis for the table above: choose \(\theta\), and you have chosen a model

  • Parameters \(\theta\) are learned from the data — the four numbers above. You never set them by hand.
  • Hyper-parameters are set before learning and control how learning happens: the learning rate \(\alpha\), the \(k\) in k-NN, the depth of a tree, the \(\lambda\) of a regulariser. They are chosen on a validation set, never on the test set.
  • Loss measures how wrong one prediction is; cost \(J(\theta )\) is the loss averaged over the training set. Fitting means finding the \(\theta\) that minimises \(J\).
  • Training is the search for \(\theta\). Inference is using the fixed \(\theta\) on new data. They have wildly different costs: training a large model can take days, inference milliseconds — except for k-NN, which reverses this and does all its work at inference.
Figure 1.1. The learning loop of every supervised learner. Data feed a model, a loss scores its predictions, an optimiser adjusts the parameters and the loop repeats; only at the end is the model checked on a test set that was held back from the start. Later chapters change only what sits inside the model box and what the loss looks like.
  1. Training data ((x, y) pairs). \(m\) examples, each an n-dimensional feature vector with its known answer. This is the experience \(E\).
  2. Model hθ(x) (a guess at the rule). A function with adjustable parameters \(\theta\). Choosing the family of function — line, tree, network — fixes the hypothesis space, and that choice is the inductive bias.
  3. Prediction ŷ. What the current parameters say the answer is for each training example.
  4. Loss J(θ) (how wrong we are). A single number summarising the gap between \(\hat{y}\) and \(y\) over the whole training set. This is the thing that gets minimised.
  5. Optimiser (adjust θ). Gradient descent, or a closed-form solution. It changes \(\theta\) in the direction that lowers \(J\), then the loop repeats.
  6. Test set (the verdict). Data held out from the very beginning and never used for fitting or tuning. Performance here is the only honest estimate of how the model will behave in the world.

docs.title: 1.3 The three paradigms
docs.text: Almost every problem you will meet falls into one of three families, and the family is decided by what the data contains, not by the subject matter. Medicine, finance and images appear in all three.

docs.title: Supervised learning — every example carries its answer
docs.text:
You are given pairs (x, y) and asked to learn the mapping. The word supervised refers to the labels acting as a teacher: for each input the correct output is known while training, so the model's error can be measured directly.

Classification — \(y\) is a category. Spam or not; benign or malignant; the digit 0–9. The model carves the feature space into regions, and the surface between them is the decision boundary. Units 4 is entirely about this.

Regression — \(y\) is a number on a continuous scale. Price, temperature, demand, days of stay. The model is a surface through the points rather than a fence between them. Unit 3 is entirely about this.

Figure 1.2. The same ten points, read two ways. Regression asks how high the surface is at a new x; classification asks on which side of a fence a new x falls. The data look the same, but the loss, the metrics and the algorithms differ.

docs.title: Unsupervised learning — no answers at all
docs.text:
You are given only \(x\). There is no \(y\) to be right or wrong about, so the algorithm has to find structure that is already there.

  • Clustering — group similar examples. Customer segments, document topics, gene-expression groups. Unit 5.
  • Dimensionality reduction — describe the same data with fewer numbers, by finding the directions along which it actually varies. PCA, in Unit 2.
  • Association rule mining — find items that co-occur, the “customers who bought this also bought” pattern. Outside this syllabus, but part of the family.

Evaluating unsupervised results is genuinely harder, because there is no answer key to compare against. That difficulty is not a detail; it is the defining feature of the paradigm, and Unit 5 spends real time on it.

docs.title: Reinforcement learning — learning from consequences
docs.text:
An agent takes actions in an environment, which returns a reward and a new state. There is no dataset of correct actions; there is only the reward, often arriving long after the action that earned it. A robot learning to walk, a program learning Go by self-play, an advertising system learning what to show. The characteristic difficulty is credit assignment — which of the two hundred moves you made was the one that won the game? — and the characteristic trade-off is exploration versus exploitation: try something new, or repeat what has worked?

The distinction that is actually tested

Do not classify by domain. “Medical data” is not a paradigm. Ask instead: does the training data contain the answers? If yes \(\to\) supervised, then ask whether the answer is a category or a number. If no \(\to\) unsupervised. If there is no fixed dataset at all, only a stream of actions and rewards \(\to\) reinforcement. A fourth case worth knowing: semi-supervised learning, where a small labelled set is combined with a large unlabelled one — which is the realistic situation far more often than the tidy textbook version, because labelling is expensive and raw data is cheap.

Supervised Unsupervised Reinforcement Data: (x, y) pairs Data: \(x\) only Data: states, actions, rewards Goal: learn \(x \to y\) Goal: find structure Goal: a policy that maximises long-run reward Feedback: the correct answer, for every example Feedback: none Feedback: delayed and evaluative, not instructive Classification: spam, digits, diagnosis Clustering: segments, topics Games, robotics, control Regression: price, demand, temperature Dimensionality reduction: PCA Explore vs exploit is the central tension Evaluated against held-out labels Evaluated indirectly — WCSS, silhouette, or a human Evaluated by total reward earned

docs.title: 1.4 Generalisation, and the two ways to fail
docs.text:
A student who memorises last year's question paper scores brilliantly on last year's question paper. Whether they have learned any physics is a separate question, and the only way to find out is to hand them a paper they have not seen. Machine learning has exactly this problem, and exactly this remedy.

Definition: Generalisation

A model generalises if it performs well on data drawn from the same distribution as the training data but not used for training. The gap between training performance and test performance is the generalisation gap, and it is the number that tells you whether learning happened or memorising did.

Two failures sit at opposite ends of one scale.

Underfitting (high bias)

— the hypothesis space is too small to contain any good answer. A straight line through a curve. Training error is already high, and test error is no better. More data does not help; you need a more flexible model or better features.

Overfitting (high variance)

— the hypothesis space is rich enough to fit the noise as well as the signal. Training error is tiny, test error is large, and the gap between them is the symptom. Cures: more data, fewer parameters, regularisation, early stopping.

Figure 1.3. Underfitting. A straight line (degree 1) fitted to twelve noisy training points cannot follow the true function (dashed); the error is large on the training points and on unseen test points (pale) alike. A very flexible polynomial would instead thread through every training point and fail on the test points: overfitting.

Notice what the degree of the polynomial is really controlling: the size of the hypothesis space. A degree-1 space contains only straight lines. A degree-10 space contains every degree-10 polynomial, including some that pass through all twelve points exactly. Richer is not better — a hypothesis space large enough to fit anything tells you nothing when it fits your data, because it would have fitted random data just as well.

Key idea — inductive bias

Infinitely many functions pass through any finite set of points. To choose one, an algorithm must prefer some functions over others before it sees any data at all, and that preference is its inductive bias: linear regression prefers straight lines, decision trees prefer axis-parallel boxes, k-NN prefers that nearby points share a label. Learning without a bias is impossible, not merely difficult — this is the content of the no free lunch theorem, which says that averaged over all possible problems, every algorithm is equally good. There is no best algorithm; there is only a bias that suits your problem.

docs.title: 1.5 The pipeline, end to end
docs.text:
An applied project is not one step but eight, and the modelling step — the one this course spends most of its time on — is rarely the one that decides success.

Figure 1.4. The eight steps from a question to a deployed model, and the loop back to the start. The steps that most often sink a project are the first and the last: solving the wrong problem, and a model whose world changes underneath it.
  1. 1 Frame the problem. What exactly is being predicted, from what, and what does a mistake cost? Fix \(T\) and \(P\) before touching data. A model optimised for the wrong \(P\) is worse than no model, because it will be trusted.
  2. 2 Collect data. Gather examples that resemble the ones the model will meet in production. Data collected under different conditions than deployment is the deepest and least visible source of failure.
  3. 3 Explore. Plot everything. Distributions, correlations, missing values, impossible values. Ten minutes of plotting saves a week of debugging a model that was fitting a data-entry error.
  4. 4 Preprocess. Clean, encode, scale, select, reduce. Unit 2 in full. Split FIRST, then fit every transformation on the training part alone.
  5. 5 Train. Choose a model family, fit the parameters, tune the hyper-parameters on a validation set or by cross-validation. Units 3, 4 and 5.
  6. 6 Evaluate. On the held-out test set, with a metric that matches what a mistake actually costs. Compare against a trivial baseline — the majority class, or the mean — and report both.
  7. 7 Deploy. The model now meets data nobody curated. The preprocessing must travel with it, identically; a scaler fitted at training time must be the one used at prediction time.
  8. 8 Monitor. Distributions drift, behaviour changes, the model itself changes the world it predicts. Watch the live metric, and retrain when it slips. A model is a perishable good.

Definition: Train, validation, test

The data is cut three ways. The training set fits the parameters. The validation set chooses the hyper-parameters and the model family. The test set is opened once, at the end, to report a number. A typical split is \(60 / 20 / 20\), or \(80 / 20\) with k-fold cross-validation carving the validation set out of the training part.

The test set is not a leaderboard

If you look at the test score, change the model, and look again, you have begun tuning on the test set, and it has quietly become a validation set. The number you eventually report will be optimistic by an amount nobody can estimate. This mistake is easy, invisible, and made by nearly everyone once.

# the split, which everything else in this course depends on
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
    X, y,
    test_size=0.2,        # 20% held back and not looked at until the end
    random_state=42,      # so the split is the same every run — reproducibility
    stratify=y)           # keep the class proportions in both halves

print(X_tr.shape, X_te.shape)     # (m_train, n)  (m_test, n)
print(y_tr.mean(), y_te.mean())   # with stratify, these two agree

Three arguments, three ideas from this unit. test_size is the train/test split itself; random_state is what makes a result you can defend in a viva rather than one that changes on every run; and stratify matters the moment a class is rare — without it a 2% positive class can land almost entirely in one half.

docs.title: 1.6 Where it is actually used
docs.text:
• Healthcare. Tumour detection in scans (classification), length-of-stay prediction (regression), patient sub-typing (clustering). The metric is almost never accuracy — a missed tumour and a false alarm cost wildly different things, so recall at a controlled false-positive rate is the number that matters.
  • Finance. Credit scoring, fraud detection, algorithmic trading. Fraud is the textbook imbalanced problem: perhaps 0.1% of transactions, so a model that says “genuine” every time is 99.9% accurate and worthless.
  • Retail and web. Recommendation, demand forecasting, customer segmentation, churn prediction. Segmentation is unsupervised; churn is supervised classification; demand is regression — one business, all three paradigms.
  • Vision and speech. Face recognition, OCR, speech to text, self-driving perception. These are the tasks where deep learning displaced hand-designed features entirely, because nobody could write down what a cat looks like as a rule.
  • Agriculture and public data. Yield prediction from soil and weather, disease detection from leaf photographs. India's data.gov.in and the UCI repository are the sources this course's practicals draw on.
  • And where it should not be used. When the rule is known and simple; when a wrong answer must be explainable in a court; when the training data encodes a historical injustice that the model will then reproduce at scale and with an air of objectivity.

docs.title: A short history, and why now
docs.text:
The ideas in this course are older than most of its users. In the 1950s Turing wrote of "learning machines", and Arthur Samuel's checkers program, which improved by playing itself, gave the field its name in 1959. Rosenblatt's perceptron (1957 onwards) was the first trainable classifier; its limits, set out by Minsky and Papert at the end of the 1960s, helped bring on the first "winter" in artificial-intelligence research, a period in which funding and interest fell away. The 1980s and 1990s brought back-propagation into wide use, together with decision trees, support vector machines and a statistical view of learning that made machine learning a rigorous, data-driven discipline. A revival of neural networks around 2006 to 2012 (called deep learning, because the networks have many layers) reached public attention when AlexNet won the ImageNet image-recognition contest in 2012; since 2016, systems such as AlphaGo (reinforcement learning) and large language models have reached or passed human performance on hard tasks.

Period Milestone Why it matters 1950s learning machines; Samuel's checkers program; the name "machine learning" (1959) programs can improve with experience 1957–69 the perceptron; its limits exposed first trainable classifier, and the first winter 1980s–90s back-propagation; trees, SVMs; statistical learning a rigorous, data-driven discipline 2006–12 deep-learning revival; AlexNet (2012) neural networks leap ahead in vision and speech 2016 onwards AlphaGo; large language models super-human performance on some hard tasks

If the theory is decades old, why did machine learning take off only recently? Three forces arrived together. Data grew explosively, from the web, sensors and phones. Compute became cheap and parallel, with graphics processors and cloud services. Software improved, with open libraries such as scikit-learn, TensorFlow and PyTorch that put good algorithms in anyone's hands. The recipe was known; the fuel and the engine were recent.

docs.title: What the learner does not do for you
docs.text: A common misconception is that "the computer programs itself" with no human effort. Machine learning automates one thing, the discovery of rules from examples. People still choose the task, collect and clean the data, decide which features and which model family to use, tune the settings and judge the results. "Garbage in, garbage out" holds with more force here than almost anywhere in computing: a flexible learner trained on mislabelled or unrepresentative data will learn the mistakes faithfully. This is why Chapter 2 is devoted to preparing the data, and why the pipeline in Section 1.5 has eight steps and only one of them is "train".

docs.title: Reinforcement learning: the vocabulary
docs.text:
Section 1.3 named the agent, the environment, the reward and the exploration trade-off. Reinforcement learning has four more terms, and exams ask for all of them.

At each step the agent observes a state \(s_{t}\) (a description of the current situation), chooses an action \(a_{t}\), and the environment replies with a reward \(r_{t+1}\) and a new state \(s_{t+1}\). The agent's strategy, a rule that maps states to actions, is its policy \(\pi\): "in this position, make that move". Learning means improving the policy so as to maximise not the next reward but the return, the total of all future rewards, usually discounted so that rewards far in the future count for less:

\[ G_{t} = r_{t+1} + \gamma\, r_{t+2} + \gamma ^{2} r_{t+3} + \cdots , \qquad 0 \le \gamma \le 1 . \]

For example, with \(\gamma = 0.9\) a game that gives \(0\) for two moves and \(+10\) for winning on the third has return \(0 + 0.9 \times 0 + 0.9^{2} \times 10 = 8.1\). The return, not the single reward, is what makes a quiet, patient move worth making, and it is why credit assignment is hard: the \(+10\) arrives only at the end, and the learner must work out which of the earlier moves earned it.

Term Self-driving delivery robot Game-playing program agent the controller the program environment the roads, traffic and pedestrians the game and its rules state a snapshot of the sensor readings the current board position action steer, accelerate, brake a legal move reward positive for progress, negative for a collision \(+1\) for a win, \(-1\) for a loss, \(0\) otherwise policy the rule from sensor snapshot to action the rule from position to move

The dilemma of exploration versus exploitation deserves one picture. Each evening you can go to the restaurant you know is good (exploit) or try a new one that might be better or worse (explore). Someone who only exploits never discovers a better favourite; someone who only explores eats many poor meals. Good agents explore a lot early, when they know little, and settle down as they learn.

docs.title: Association rules
docs.text:
The third task of unsupervised learning, besides clustering and dimensionality reduction, looks for items that occur together. A rule such as \(\{\text{bread}, \text{butter}\} \Rightarrow \{\text{jam}\}\) says that baskets containing bread and butter often contain jam too. Two numbers describe a rule. Its support is the fraction of all baskets that contain every item in it; its confidence is the fraction of baskets containing the left-hand side that also contain the right-hand side.

Basket Items 1 bread, butter, jam 2 bread, butter 3 bread, butter, jam, milk 4 milk 5 bread, jam

Three of the five baskets hold bread and butter, and two of those also hold jam. So the support of the rule is \(2/5 = 0.40\) and its confidence is \(2/3 \approx 0.67\). Nobody told the algorithm to look for bread and jam; the pattern surfaced from the records alone, which is what makes this an unsupervised task. Market-basket analysis and recommendation use it; the course returns to it no further.

docs.title: 1.8 Worked examples
docs.text:
The examples below work through the calculations of this chapter in full. Try each one on paper before reading the steps.

Example 1.1: Turning a wish into a specification

Problem. A college wants to “use AI to reduce dropouts”. Turn this into a well-posed learning problem, naming T, P and \(E\), and say which paradigm it belongs to.

Step 1 — decide what is being predicted, and when

“Reduce dropouts” is an action, not a prediction. The predictable quantity is whether a given student will fail to enrol next semester, and it must be predicted early enough to act on — say, by the end of week six. That timing constraint also decides which features are allowed: anything not available in week six cannot be used, however predictive it is.

Step 2 — \(T\)

Given a student's attendance, internal marks, fee-payment status and prior academic record as of week six, classify them as at risk or not at risk of not enrolling next semester. Two categories, so this is supervised classification.

Step 3 — \(P\), chosen from the cost of each mistake

A false negative is a student who drops out unnoticed — the failure the project exists to prevent. A false positive is a mentoring conversation with someone who was fine, which costs an hour. The costs are wildly asymmetric, so accuracy is the wrong measure. Use recall on the at-risk class, reported at a false-positive rate the mentoring staff can absorb. If 200 students can be contacted, the real question is what fraction of true dropouts appear in the top 200 by risk score.

Step 4 — \(E\)
