Records of past students, each with the week-six features and the known outcome. Note the labels take a semester to arrive, so the dataset can only be built from history.

Answer. \(T\): classify a student at week six as at-risk / not. \(P\): recall on at-risk at a fixed number of contacts. \(E\): past students' week-six features with known outcomes. Supervised classification.

Comment. Everything hard about this problem appeared before any algorithm was mentioned — the timing, the asymmetric costs, the label delay. That is typical.

Example 1.2: Counting the parts of a dataset

Problem. A CSV has 5 000 rows and 13 columns. One column is a unique student ID, one is the final grade (A–F) to be predicted, and one is 80% empty. State \(m\) and \(n\), name the target type, and say what you would do with the ID and the sparse column.

Step 1 — \(m\) and \(n\)

\(m = 5 000\) examples. Of the 13 columns, one is the target and one is an identifier, leaving 11 candidate features — so \(n = 11\), not 13 and not 12.

Step 2 — the target

A–F is categorical and ordered, so this is classification with six classes — multi-class, not binary. The ordering is real information: predicting B when the truth is A is a smaller error than predicting \(F\), and a plain multi-class classifier will not know that. Either accept the loss of that information or use an ordinal method.

Step 3 — the ID column

Drop it. An identifier is unique per row, so a flexible model can use it to memorise the training set perfectly and will learn nothing that transfers. Tree-based models are especially prone to this. IDs also often encode admission order or batch, which leaks information that will not exist for a future student.

Step 4 — the 80%-empty column

Three options, in order of preference. Drop it if the remaining 20% is not clearly informative. Keep it with an explicit “missing” indicator if the fact of being missing is itself meaningful — an unfilled optional field may say a great deal. Impute only if the missingness is plausibly random; imputing 80% of a column mostly manufactures a constant, and the imputation value must be computed on the training fold alone.

Answer. \(m = 5 000, n = 11\) usable features; six-class ordinal classification; drop the ID; drop or flag the sparse column.

Example 1.3: Reading two error numbers

Problem. Three models are trained on the same data. Their errors are: A — train 0.42, test 0.44; B — train 0.02, test 0.39; \(C\) — train 0.11, test 0.13. Which would you deploy, and what would you try next for the other two?

Step 1 — read the gaps

A: both high, gap \(\approx 0\). B: training near zero, gap 0.37. \(C\): both low, gap 0.02.

Step 2 — diagnose

A is underfitting: it cannot even fit the data it was shown, so the model is too rigid or the features carry too little signal. B is overfitting: perfect on what it saw, poor on what it did not. \(C\) generalises.

Step 3 — act

Deploy \(C\). For A: a richer model, polynomial or interaction features, less regularisation. For B: more training data, fewer parameters, stronger regularisation, early stopping, or pruning if it is a tree.

Answer. Deploy \(C\). A underfits — add capacity. B overfits — restrain it.

Comment. Note that B has the best training error of the three and is the worst model. Reporting training error is not merely uninformative; it points the wrong way.

Example 1.4: Which paradigm, and which kind of task?

Problem. For each scenario say whether it is supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement learning. For the supervised ones, say whether the task is regression or classification, and whether a classification is binary or multi-class.

Scenario (a) Predict a flat's sale price from its size, locality and age, using 5 000 past sales with their prices. (b) Group 10 000 news articles by topic when no topic labels exist. (c) A robot learns to walk by trying movements and receiving a reward for distance covered. (d) Flag a card transaction as fraud or not fraud, using past transactions that have been labelled. (e) Detect unusual readings from factory sensors when no example of "unusual" is available. (f) Predict how many customers will visit a shop tomorrow. (g) Decide whether a photograph shows a cat, a dog or a horse. (h) Predict the PIN-code area (a six-digit number) of a delivery address from the text of the address.

Step 1 — ask the three questions, in this order

  1. Does the training data contain the answer for every example? If yes, the problem is supervised.
  2. If not, is there a stream of actions that earn rewards, with no fixed dataset? If yes, it is reinforcement learning.
  3. If neither, there are only inputs, and the task is to find structure: unsupervised.

For a supervised problem, one more question: is the target a quantity on a numeric scale (regression) or a member of a finite set of categories (classification)?

Step 2 — apply them

Labels? Target Paradigm and task (a) yes, the price continuous number supervised, regression (b) no none unsupervised, clustering (c) no; only a reward none reinforcement (agent = robot, reward = distance) (d) yes, fraud / not two categories supervised, binary classification (e) no labelled anomalies none unsupervised, anomaly detection (find points unlike the rest) (f) yes, past counts a count, treated as a quantity supervised, regression (g) yes, the animal three unordered categories supervised, multi-class classification (h) yes, the area code numbers used only as names supervised, multi-class classification

Step 3 — the two cases that tempt a wrong answer

In (f) a count is technically discrete, but it is an ordered quantity with a meaningful size, and a prediction of 41 when the truth is 40 is nearly right. That is regression. In (h) the target is written as a number, but "twice the PIN code" and "halfway between two PIN codes" mean nothing, so the numbers are labels. The test is whether twice and in between make sense for the target.

Answer. (a) supervised regression; (b) unsupervised clustering; (c) reinforcement; (d) supervised binary classification; (e) unsupervised; (f) supervised regression; (g) supervised multi-class classification; (h) supervised multi-class classification.

Comment. Scenario (e) would become supervised classification the moment a set of labelled faults existed. The paradigm is decided by what the data contains, not by the application.

Example 1.5: Reading a hypothesis — features, label, parameters, and one prediction

Problem. A bank records, for each applicant, annual income (in lakh), loan amount (in lakh), credit score and years in current employment, and whether the applicant later defaulted (yes or no). A student proposes

\[ h_{\theta }(x) = \sigma (\theta _{0} + \theta _{1}\,\text{income} + \theta _{2}\,\text{loan} + \theta _{3}\,\text{score} + \theta _{4}\,\text{years}), \qquad \sigma (z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}. \]

Name the features, label, hypothesis and parameters; give \(n\); say what \(m\) is; and evaluate the hypothesis for two applicants using the illustrative values \(\theta = (-1,\,-0.15,\,0.2,\,-0.004,\,-0.1)\).

Step 1 — match each name to the problem

Term In this problem features \(x\) income, loan amount, credit score, years employed label \(y\) defaulted, coded 1 for yes and 0 for no hypothesis \(h_{\theta }\) the formula above, mapping a feature vector to a number in \((0, 1)\) parameters \(\theta\) \(\theta _{0}, \theta _{1}, \theta _{2}, \theta _{3}, \theta _{4}\) \(n\) 4 \(m\) the number of applicants in the training set

There are \(n + 1 = 5\) parameters, because every feature has a weight and the intercept \(\theta _{0}\) is the extra one. The features are data we are given; the parameters are numbers the algorithm chooses. The sigmoid \(\sigma\) squeezes the output into \((0, 1)\), which is why this is a classification hypothesis (a probability of default) rather than plain linear regression.

Step 2 — applicant 1: income 6, loan 10, score 650, 4 years

With \(x_{0} = 1\) for the intercept,

\(z = -1 + (-0.15)(6) + (0.2)(10) + (-0.004)(650) + (-0.1)(4)\)

\(z = -1 - 0.9 + 2.0 - 2.6 - 0.4 = -2.9\)

\(h_{\theta }(x) = 1/(1 + e^{2.9}) = 0.052\)

Step 3 — applicant 2: income 3, loan 14, score 520, 1 year

\(z = -1 + (-0.15)(3) + (0.2)(14) + (-0.004)(520) + (-0.1)(1)\)

\(z = -1 - 0.45 + 2.8 - 2.08 - 0.1 = -0.83\)

\(h_{\theta }(x) = 1/(1 + e^{0.83}) = 0.304\)

Step 4 — turn probabilities into decisions

With the usual threshold of \(0.5\), both applicants are predicted not to default. The signs are sensible: a larger loan raises the risk, while a higher income, score and employment record lower it. The threshold is itself a choice: if a missed default costs far more than a rejected good applicant, a threshold of \(0.25\) would flag applicant 2 and not applicant 1.

Answer. Features: income, loan, score, years (\(n = 4\)). Label: default indicator. Parameters: five numbers \(\theta _{0}, \dots , \theta _{4}\). \(m\) is the number of applicants in the training set. Predicted probabilities of default: \(0.052\) and \(0.304\).

Comment. The values of \(\theta\) here were chosen for illustration; in practice they are found by minimising a loss on the training set (Chapter 8). Notice also that no number in the table of features is a parameter, and no parameter appears in the data.

Example 1.6: The cost of a hypothesis, and what fitting means

Problem. Study hours \(x\) and test scores \(y\) for three students are \((1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 4)\). Using \(J(\theta ) = \dfrac{1}{2m}\sum _{i=1}^{m}\left(h_{\theta }(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\right)^{2}\), compute the cost of (i) \(h(x) = x\) and (ii) \(h(x) = 0.5 + x\). Then find the line with the smallest cost.

Step 1 — set up the table for \(h(x) = x\)

Here \(m = 3\).

\(x\) \(y\) \(h(x) = x\) error \(h - y\) error\(^{2}\) 1 2 1 \(-1\) 1 2 2 2 0 0 3 4 3 \(-1\) 1

Sum of squared errors \(= 1 + 0 + 1 = 2\), so \(J = \dfrac{2}{2 \cdot 3} = \dfrac{1}{3} = 0.333\).

Step 2 — the line \(h(x) = 0.5 + x\)

\(x\) \(y\) \(h(x)\) error error\(^{2}\) 1 2 1.5 \(-0.5\) 0.25 2 2 2.5 \(0.5\) 0.25 3 4 3.5 \(-0.5\) 0.25

Sum \(= 0.75\), so \(J = \dfrac{0.75}{6} = 0.125\). Shifting the line up by \(0.5\) cut the cost from \(0.333\) to \(0.125\).

Step 3 — the best straight line

The least-squares line has slope \(\theta _{1} = \dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})(y - \bar{y})}{\sum (x - \bar{x})^{2}}\) and intercept \(\theta _{0} = \bar{y} - \theta _{1}\bar{x}\).

\(\bar{x} = 2, \ \bar{y} = 8/3\). The numerator is \((-1)(2 - 8/3) + (0)(2 - 8/3) + (1)(4 - 8/3) = 2/3 + 0 + 4/3 = 2\), and the denominator is \(1 + 0 + 1 = 2\).

\(\theta _{1} = 1, \quad \theta _{0} = 8/3 - 2 = 2/3\)

The errors of \(h(x) = \tfrac{2}{3} + x\) are \(-\tfrac{1}{3}, +\tfrac{2}{3}, -\tfrac{1}{3}\), with squares \(\tfrac{1}{9}, \tfrac{4}{9}, \tfrac{1}{9}\) and sum \(\tfrac{6}{9} = \tfrac{2}{3}\). Then \(J = \dfrac{2/3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{9} = 0.111\).

Answer. \(J = 0.333\) for \(h(x) = x\); \(J = 0.125\) for \(h(x) = 0.5 + x\); the best line is \(h(x) = \tfrac{2}{3} + x\) with \(J = \tfrac{1}{9} \approx 0.111\).

Comment. Each choice of \((\theta _{0}, \theta _{1})\) is one hypothesis, and each has its own cost: fitting is the search for the pair with the smallest \(J\). The cost of \(0.111\) is the best any straight line can do on these three points, not zero; the points do not lie on a line. Chapter 4 replaces this hand calculation with a formula and with gradient descent.

Example 1.7: Three disjoint sets, and why a rare class needs a stratified split

Problem. You have 1 000 labelled examples of which 20 (2%) are positive. You need to fit parameters, choose between three candidate models, and report an honest final accuracy. (i) Propose a split and say what each part is for. (ii) How many positives would a test set of 150 hold if the split were random? (iii) What goes wrong with a purely random split, and how is it avoided?

Step 1 — the split

Use three disjoint parts, for example \(700 / 150 / 150\) (that is \(70\%, 15\%, 15\%\), and \(700 + 150 + 150 = 1000\)).

Part Size Used for training 700 fitting the parameters \(\theta\) of each candidate model validation 150 comparing the three models and tuning hyper-parameters test 150 one final measurement, after every decision has been made

The test set is used once. If it were used to choose among the three models, the winner would be the one that happened to suit those 150 examples, and its score on them would be optimistic. A set used to make a choice has become a validation set, and no honest estimate remains.

Step 2 — how many positives in the test set

On average, a test set of 150 from 1 000 examples holds \(150/1000 = 15\%\) of the positives: \(0.15 \times 20 = 3\).

Step 3 — the risk of a purely random split

The chance that a random draw of 150 contains no positive at all is

\[ P(0) = \frac{\binom{980}{150}}{\binom{1000}{150}} \approx 0.037, \]

close to \((1 - 0.15)^{20} = 0.039\). So there is about a 1 in 27 chance that the test set contains no positive example and recall cannot even be computed. With 3 expected positives, a result of 1 or 6 is entirely plausible, and a recall measured on three cases can only be 0, 33%, 67% or 100%.

Step 4 — the remedy

A stratified split forces each part to keep the class proportions: each of the three parts receives its share of the 20 positives, so the 150-example test set holds \(20 \times 0.15 = 3\) positives every time, and the training set holds \(20 \times 0.70 = 14\). In scikit-learn this is the argument stratify=y.

Answer. Split \(700 / 150 / 150\) for fitting, choosing and reporting; stratify so each part keeps the 2% positive rate (14, 3 and 3 positives). A random split leaves about a 3.7% chance of no positive in the test set.

Comment. Even a perfectly stratified test set of 3 positives is a very small sample. The proper response to a rare class is a larger test set, or cross-validation, as well as a metric such as recall that looks at the rare class and not at overall accuracy.

docs.title: 1.9 Common mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
Each of the following is a mistake that costs marks in an examination or accuracy in practice.

  • Do not count the target column as a feature. A table of 13 columns with one target and one ID has 11 features.
  • Do not classify a problem by its domain. “Healthcare” is not a paradigm; the presence or absence of labels in the data is.
  • Do not call a numeric target classification because it happens to be written as an integer. Predicting the number of days is regression; predicting which of five wards is classification.
  • Do not report training accuracy as if it were a result. It is a diagnostic, and it can always be driven to 100% by memorising.
  • Do not tune anything on the test set — not the model, not a threshold, not a hyper-parameter. Once you have looked at it twice, it is a validation set.
  • Do not confuse parameters with hyper-parameters. \(\theta\) is learned; \(k, \alpha , \lambda\) and depth are chosen.
  • Do not assume more data fixes everything. It cures overfitting; it does nothing at all for underfitting.
  • Do not treat a model as finished when it is deployed. Distributions drift and accuracy decays, which is why step 8 exists.
  • Do not say “the algorithm found a correlation, therefore \(X\) causes Y”. Every model in this course learns association. Causation requires an experiment or an argument, and no amount of accuracy substitutes for either.

docs.title: 1.10 Summary
docs.text:
After working through this chapter you should be able to do the following.

  • Define machine learning against ordinary programming: rules and data go into one, data and answers go into the other. You can also state Mitchell's \(T / P / E\) for any system described to you. That is what turns a vague brief into something buildable.
  • Name every part of a learning problem in a real table. There are \(m\) examples and \(n\) features, and one of the columns is the target. A row is a feature vector, which is a point in feature space. The model \(h_{\theta }\) is drawn from a hypothesis space. Parameters are learned; hyper-parameters are chosen. Loss is measured on one example, cost over the whole set. And training finds the parameters, while inference uses them.
  • Place any task in one of three paradigms by asking what the data contains rather than what field it comes from, and you know the two sub-families of each: classification and regression; clustering and dimensionality reduction.
  • Recall that the only meaningful measure of success is performance on unseen data, that underfitting shows as two high errors and overfitting as a wide gap, and that more data cures one and not the other.
  • Explain why an algorithm must have an inductive bias before it sees any data, what the no-free-lunch theorem says about the search for a best algorithm, and therefore why this course teaches you a toolbox rather than a favourite.
  • Lay out the eight-step pipeline, defend the three-way split of the data, and explain why the test set is opened exactly once.

docs.title: 1.11 Exercises
docs.text:
1. State \(T\), \(P\) and \(E\) for a system that predicts which of five bus routes a commuter will take tomorrow. Which paradigm, and why?

    Answer

    \(T\): given the day, the time and the weather, say which of the five routes the commuter will take. \(P\): the fraction of days on which the predicted route is the route actually taken. \(E\): a record of the commuter's past journeys, each with its day, time and weather and the route that was chosen. The paradigm is supervised multi-class classification: every past journey carries its answer (the route), and that answer is one of five unordered categories, not a number on a scale.

  2. A dataset has 800 rows and 20 columns, of which one is the target and three are 80% empty. Give \(m\), the number of usable features under each of the three policies for a sparse column, and say which you would choose.

    Answer

    \(m = 800\). One column is the target, so there are \(19\) candidate features, three of which are sparse. Each of those has \(0.8 \times 800 = 640\) empty cells and only \(160\) filled ones.

    • Drop the three sparse columns: \(19 - 3 = 16\) features.
    • Impute them (for example with the training median): \(19\) features. Four-fifths of each column is then a manufactured constant.
    • Impute and add a "was missing" indicator for each: \(19 + 3 = 22\) columns.

    Unless there is a reason to think the fact of being missing is itself informative, drop them: the remaining 160 values are few, and imputing 640 cells mostly adds a constant. If missingness plausibly carries information (an optional form field left blank, say), use the imputed column together with its indicator, and let validation performance decide. Whichever policy is used, any imputation value must be computed on the training part alone.

  3. Model A scores 0.95 training accuracy and 0.61 test accuracy; model B scores 0.72 and 0.70. Which is better, and what would you try next for each?

    Answer

    B is better, because test performance is what predicts behaviour on new data: \(0.70 > 0.61\). Model A's gap is \(0.95 - 0.61 = 0.34\), the signature of overfitting; model B's gap is only \(0.02\), so B generalises, but its training accuracy of \(0.72\) is itself modest, which suggests it is somewhat too rigid. For A: restrain it with fewer parameters, regularisation, early stopping or pruning, and more training data if available. For B: add capacity, with a richer model, extra or better-engineered features, or less regularisation.

  4. A hospital's data has 2% positive cases. A model predicts "negative" always. Give its accuracy, precision and recall.

    Answer

    Take 1 000 patients: 20 are positive and 980 negative. The model gets all 980 negatives right and all 20 positives wrong, so it has \(TP = 0\), \(FN = 20\), \(FP = 0\), \(TN = 980\).

    Accuracy \(= (0 + 980)/1000 = 98\%\). Recall \(= TP/(TP + FN) = 0/20 = 0\). Precision \(= TP/(TP + FP) = 0/0\), which is undefined, because the model never predicts a positive. The 98% accuracy is exactly the share of negatives, the baseline that any useful model must beat, and the model detects nothing.

  5. Give one task from your own experience for each of the three paradigms, and say what data would have to exist for each.

    Answer

    Any well-chosen triple will do; here is one. Supervised: predict from a student's first three internal marks whether they will pass the course (classification); it needs past students' marks together with the pass or fail outcome. Unsupervised: group the books in a library by borrowing pattern; it needs only the loan records, with no category labels. Reinforcement: a thermostat that learns when to switch heating on to keep a room comfortable at low energy cost; it needs no dataset at all, but an environment it can act in and a reward that scores comfort and energy use after each action. In every case the test is what the data contains: answers, nothing, or rewards for actions.

  6. Explain in three sentences why a hypothesis space that can fit any dataset is useless, referring to inductive bias.

    Answer

    A hypothesis space that can fit every possible dataset fits random noise as readily as it fits a real pattern, so a perfect fit to your data tells you nothing about whether a pattern exists. Learning from finitely many examples needs an inductive bias, an assumption that prefers some functions to others before any data are seen, because infinitely many functions pass through the same points and only the assumption chooses among them. A space with no such preference cannot choose, and one that merely memorises the training set will predict arbitrarily on every new input.

  7. An engineer scales the whole dataset, splits it, trains and reports 94% test accuracy. Name the error and say in which direction the reported number is wrong.

    Answer

    The error is data leakage, through preprocessing: the scaling statistics (mean and standard deviation, or minimum and maximum) were computed from all rows, test rows included, so information about the test set entered the training pipeline. The test set was therefore not truly unseen, and the reported 94% is optimistic: the true accuracy on new data is likely to be lower (typically only slightly for scaling, much more for steps such as feature selection). The correct order is to split first, fit the scaler on the training part alone, and apply those stored numbers to both parts.

  8. Why can training error not be used to choose between a degree-2 and a degree-9 polynomial, when test error can?

    Answer

    The degree-9 family contains every degree-2 polynomial (set the higher coefficients to zero), so its best fit to the training data can never be worse than the degree-2 best fit, and with noisy data it is almost always strictly better. Training error therefore falls as the degree rises, and would always select the most complex model, whether or not it has learned a real pattern. Test error is measured on points the fit did not see, so the degree-9 curve is penalised exactly where it has followed noise; it typically falls and then rises as the degree grows, and its minimum picks a degree that generalises. (In practice the choice is made on a validation set, and the test set is kept for the final report.)

  9. Hours studied \(x\) and marks \(y\) are \((1, 3), (2, 4), (4, 8)\). For the hypothesis \(h(x) = 2x\), compute the cost \(J = \dfrac{1}{2m}\sum _{i}\left(h(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\right)^{2}\), showing every step.

    Answer

    \(m = 3\). The predictions are \(h(1) = 2\), \(h(2) = 4\), \(h(4) = 8\). The errors \(h - y\) are \(2 - 3 = -1\), \(4 - 4 = 0\), \(8 - 8 = 0\), with squares \(1, 0, 0\). The sum of squared errors is \(1\), so

    \[ J = \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3} \times 1 = \frac{1}{6} \approx 0.167. \]

    The line passes through two of the three points exactly and misses the first by one mark.

  10. Classify each of the following as a parameter or a hyper-parameter, and say how its value is decided: (a) the slope of a fitted line; (b) the learning rate \(\alpha\); (c) the weights of a trained neural network; (d) \(k\) in k-NN; (e) the maximum depth of a decision tree; (f) the intercept \(\theta _{0}\).

    Answer

    (a) Parameter: learned by minimising the cost on the training data. (b) Hyper-parameter: set by the practitioner before training and tuned on a validation set. (c) Parameters: learned during training by gradient descent. (d) Hyper-parameter: chosen before the algorithm runs, by comparing validation performance for several values of \(k\). (e) Hyper-parameter: it fixes the size of the hypothesis space, and is chosen by validation or cross-validation. (f) Parameter: learned along with the slope. The rule: parameters are the numbers inside the fitted model that the algorithm finds; hyper-parameters control how the search is carried out or how rich the model may be, and are set from outside.

  11. Name the learning paradigm in each case, with a one-sentence reason. (A1) A spam filter learns from thousands of emails already marked spam or not spam. (A2) A self-driving car learns to hold its lane through a reward for staying in lane and a penalty for swerving, without being told the correct steering angle. (A3) A news site groups articles into topics using only the words they contain, with no topic labels.

    Answer

    (A1) Supervised (binary classification): each training email carries its label. (A2) Reinforcement: an agent acts, receives only a reward or penalty, and learns a policy; no correct action is ever supplied. (A3) Unsupervised (clustering): only the inputs, the words, are available, and the groups must be discovered.

  12. A bank trains a model to predict whether a loan will default. Among the input features is a column "amount recovered after default". What is wrong with it, what is the problem called, and what happens when the model is deployed?

    Answer

    The amount recovered after a default is known only after the outcome has happened, and it is non-zero only for loans that did default. It therefore carries the answer inside the inputs: this is data leakage, sometimes called label leakage. The model will appear near-perfect on the training and test data, because the leaked column nearly gives the label away. In deployment, when a new application is assessed, the column does not exist yet (nothing has been recovered from a loan that has not been made), so the model's main input is missing and its predictions are worthless. The remedy is to build features only from information available at the moment the prediction must be made.

  13. A spam filter is retrained every month on the most recent emails with exactly the same procedure, yet over a year its test accuracy slowly declines. Give two plausible explanations rooted in this chapter and say how you would detect the problem.

    Answer

    (1) The data drift. Spammers change their wording and tactics, and ordinary language and mail patterns also change, so the distribution of the inputs and the relation between inputs and labels move away from what the model learned. The model is a perishable good, which is why monitoring is the last step of the pipeline. (2) The test set may no longer match the world, if it is a fixed old sample while the training data are always recent, or the other way round; in either case the measured number is about a different distribution from the one the model will meet. Other causes include a change in the labelling practice and spammers adapting to the filter itself. To detect it: track the live metric (recall on spam, false-positive rate) on fresh, freshly labelled mail, compare feature distributions (word frequencies, mail length) between months, and set an alert and a retraining trigger when either slips.

docs.title: Chapter 9: k-Nearest Neighbours
docs.text: Every classifier so far has built a model from the training data and then thrown the data away. The k-nearest-neighbour classifier does the opposite: there is no training step at all, and a new example is classified by looking up the most similar examples already stored. It is the simplest classifier to describe, a useful baseline, and a clear illustration of the bias-variance trade-off and of why feature scaling matters.

docs.title: 9.1 k-nearest neighbours
docs.text:
To classify something new, look at the \(k\) training examples closest to it and take a vote. There is no training step at all: the model is the dataset. It is called a lazy or instance-based learner, and it postpones every calculation to prediction time.

Figure 9.1. k-NN with the query point shown as a diamond and its k nearest neighbours ringed; the shading is the decision region. A small k gives a jagged boundary with an island around every stray point (low bias, high variance); a large k smooths it until real structure is ignored. \(k\) Boundary Bias Variance Failure mode 1 jagged, follows every point low high a single mislabelled point creates a whole wrong region \(\sqrt{m}\), roughly reasonable moderate moderate the usual starting guess, then tuned by cross-validation \(m\) none — one flat prediction maximal zero always predicts the majority class

Three things k-NN insists on

Scaling, because a distance is a sum over features and the largest-numbered feature otherwise decides every neighbour. An odd \(k\) for two classes, so a vote cannot tie. And a modest number of features: in high dimensions all pairwise distances converge towards each other, so “nearest” stops meaning anything — the curse of dimensionality hurts k-NN more than any other algorithm in this course.

Variants worth knowing: distance-weighted voting, where a neighbour's vote is divided by its distance so that close neighbours count more; and k-NN regression, which averages the neighbours' values instead of voting. The cost is \(O(\text{mn})\) per query, which is why large deployments use a k-d tree or a ball tree to avoid comparing against every point.

# k-NN: no training, so all the cost is in predict()
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

for k in [1, 3, 5, 11, 21]:
    pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k))
    print(k, cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean().round(3))

# run it once WITHOUT the scaler to see the whole of Unit 2 in one number
print(cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(5), X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean())

Definition: Getting boolean features into a distance

k-NN needs a numeric vector, because it computes a distance. Boolean attributes are made numeric by binarisation: True \(\to 1\), False \(\to 0\), one column each. The class label is not binarised — it is what is being predicted.

Two things follow, and both are worth stating in an answer. All columns are then on the same 0/1 scale, so no further scaling is needed. And on 0/1 vectors the squared Euclidean distance is exactly the number of positions that differ, so \(d = \sqrt{\text{mismatches}}\) — the Hamming distance under a square root. Ranking by Euclidean distance and ranking by Hamming distance therefore give the same neighbours.

Example 9.1: Three boolean toppings

Problem. Five pizzas were recorded as liked or not, described by Pepperoni, Pineapple and Pickled-onion. Classify \(\langle \text{False}\), True, \(\text{True}\rangle\) with \(k = 3\).

Step 1 — binarise

Pizza Pepperoni Pineapple Pickled-onion Liked P1 1 1 1 No P2 1 0 0 Yes P3 0 1 1 No P4 0 1 0 Yes P5 1 0 0 Yes query 0 1 1 ?

Step 2 — count the mismatches

Pizza Positions that differ Distance Liked P1 1 (pepperoni) \(\sqrt{1} = 1.0000\) No P2 3 \(\sqrt{3} = 1.7321\) Yes P3 0 0.0000 No P4 1 (pickled-onion) \(\sqrt{1} = 1.0000\) Yes P5 3 \(\sqrt{3} = 1.7321\) Yes

Step 3 — vote

The three nearest are P3 (0.0000, No), P1 (1.0000, No) and P4 (1.0000, Yes). No 2, Yes \(1 \to\) not liked.

Two remarks the examiner is looking for. P3 is an exact match at distance 0. And at \(k = 5\) the vote becomes Yes 3, No 2 and the answer flips — which is why \(k\) is chosen by validation, why it is kept odd, and why distance-weighted voting (weight 1/d) is often preferred, since it would let the exact match dominate.

Answer. Neighbours \(P3, P1, P4 \to\) not liked

docs.title: Distance measures for k-NN
docs.text:
"Nearest" means nearest under some distance, and the choice is part of the model. For two vectors \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{x}'\) with \(n\) features, the family used most often is

\[ d_{p}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \left( \sum_{j=1}^{n} |x_{j} - x'_{j}|^{p} \right)^{1/p}, \]

the Minkowski distance of order \(p\). For \(p = 2\) it is the Euclidean distance, the straight-line distance and the usual default; for \(p = 1\) it is the Manhattan (city-block) distance, the sum of the absolute differences; and as \(p\) grows it approaches the Chebyshev distance, the single largest coordinate gap. For two points whose coordinates differ by \(3\), \(4\) and \(0\), for instance, the distances are \(\sqrt{9 + 16 + 0} = 5\) (Euclidean), \(3 + 4 + 0 = 7\) (Manhattan) and \(4\) (Chebyshev). Squaring makes the Euclidean distance sensitive to one large difference, while the Manhattan distance is more forgiving of it. For yes/no or categorical features, the Hamming distance simply counts the positions at which two vectors differ. The distances are met again, with the cosine measure, in the unit on clustering.

None of these choices can compensate for features on different scales, and which distance ranks the neighbours best is an empirical matter that can be settled by cross-validation like the choice of \(k\).

docs.title: Weighted votes and k-NN regression
docs.text:
Let \(N_{k}(\mathbf{q})\) be the \(k\) training examples nearest to the query \(\mathbf{q}\), and give neighbour \(i\) the weight \(w_{i} = 1/d(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{x}_{i})\), or \(1/d^{2}\) for a steeper fall-off. In classification the weights of each class are added and the class with the larger total wins,

\[ \hat{y} = \arg\max_{c} \sum_{i \in N_{k}(\mathbf{q}),\; y_{i} = c} w_{i}, \]

and with \(w_{i} = 1\) this is the plain majority vote. In regression the prediction is the weighted mean of the neighbours' targets,

\[ \hat{y} = \frac{\sum_{i \in N_{k}(\mathbf{q})} w_{i}\, y_{i}}{\sum_{i \in N_{k}(\mathbf{q})} w_{i}}, \]

which is the plain average when all weights are 1. If the query coincides with a training point, \(d = 0\) and the weight is undefined; the usual convention is to return that point's label or value directly.

docs.title: Ties, and scaling done properly
docs.text:
Ties arise in two ways. The vote itself can tie, which an odd \(k\) prevents for two classes but not for three or more; the remedies are to let the nearer neighbours decide, to use distance weights, or to reduce \(k\) by one. The distances can also tie at the \(k\)-th place, so that there are more than \(k\) candidates for the last place; either all of the tied points are admitted or a fixed rule (such as the order of the rows) breaks the tie. A query that lies exactly midway between two classes, as in the exercise below, is tied however the votes are counted, and the correct reply is that the data do not decide it.

Scaling is carried out in one of two standard ways. Min-max scaling maps a feature onto \([0, 1]\),

\[ x' = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}, \]

and standardisation subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, \(x' = (x - \mu)/\sigma\). In both, the constants are computed on the training set only, and the same constants are then applied to every new query; scaling a query with its own minimum and maximum, or letting test data into the statistics, gives a distance that means nothing. Binary 0/1 features need no scaling.

docs.title: 9.3 Worked examples
docs.text:
The examples below work through the calculations of this chapter in full. Try each one on paper before reading the steps.

The examples below fix the details that decide a k-NN answer: the value of \(k\), whether the vote is weighted, whether the features are on one scale, and what changes when the target is a number.

Example 9.2: The same point, three values of \(k\)

Problem. Six training points are given with their classes.

Point P1 P2 P3 P4 P5 P6 \(x_1\) 4 3 5 2 8 7 \(x_2\) 3 3 5 4 8 2 Class B A A A B B

Classify \(Q = (4, 4)\) with \(k = 1\), \(k = 3\) and \(k = 5\) using Euclidean distance, and say what happens at \(k = 6\).

Step 1 — the distances from \(Q = (4, 4)\)

For P1: \(d = \sqrt{(4-4)^{2} + (4-3)^{2}} = \sqrt{1} = 1.000\). For P2: \(d = \sqrt{1 + 1} = \sqrt{2} = 1.414\). All six, sorted:

Rank Point \((\Delta x_{1})^{2} + (\Delta x_{2})^{2}\) Distance Class 1 P1 (4, 3) \(0 + 1 = 1\) 1.000 B 2 P2 (3, 3) \(1 + 1 = 2\) 1.414 A 3 P3 (5, 5) \(1 + 1 = 2\) 1.414 A 4 P4 (2, 4) \(4 + 0 = 4\) 2.000 A 5 P6 (7, 2) \(9 + 4 = 13\) 3.606 B 6 P5 (8, 8) \(16 + 16 = 32\) 5.657 B

P2 and P3 are equally far away; both are class A, so their order does not affect any answer.

Step 2 — vote for each \(k\)

\(k = 1\): the nearest is P1, class B.

\(k = 3\): P1 (B), P2 (A), P3 (A) give A 2, B 1, class A.

\(k = 5\): P1 (B), P2 (A), P3 (A), P4 (A), P6 (B) give A 3, B 2, class A.

\(k = 6\): all six points vote, A 3 and B 3, a dead tie that has nothing to do with where \(Q\) is.

Answer. \(k = 1\) gives B; \(k = 3\) and \(k = 5\) give A; \(k = 6\) gives a tie.

Comment. P1 is a lone B sitting among A's, and may be noise or a mislabelled record. With \(k = 1\) the model trusts it completely (high variance, overfitting). Raising \(k\) lets the surrounding A's outvote it. If \(k\) grows to the size of the whole set, the prediction is simply the overall majority wherever \(Q\) lies (high bias, underfitting). A sensible starting point is \(k \approx \sqrt{m}\), rounded to an odd number, and then tuned by cross-validation.

Example 9.3: Plain majority against a distance-weighted vote

Problem. A clinic records two scaled measurements for eight patients and whether each turned out to be diabetic.

Patient P1 P2 P3 P4 P5 P6 P7 P8 \(x_1\) (glucose index) 5 4 7 5 2 8 1 5 \(x_2\) (BMI index) 4 6 5 8 4 8 5 10 Diabetic Yes No Yes No No Yes No Yes

A new patient has \(Q = (5, 5)\). Classify with (a) \(k = 3\), (b) \(k = 5\), and (c) \(k = 5\) with each vote weighted by \(1/d^{2}\).

Step 1 — squared distances

Work with \(d^{2}\) and take the root only for display. For P1: \(d^{2} = (5-5)^{2} + (5-4)^{2} = 1\).

Patient \(d^{2}\) \(d\) Diabetic P1 (5, 4) 1 1.000 Yes P2 (4, 6) 2 1.414 No P3 (7, 5) 4 2.000 Yes P4 (5, 8) 9 3.000 No P5 (2, 4) 10 3.162 No P7 (1, 5) 16 4.000 No P6 (8, 8) 18 4.243 Yes P8 (5, 10) 25 5.000 Yes

Step 2 — (a) \(k = 3\)

The three nearest are P1 (Yes), P2 (No), P3 (Yes): Yes 2, No 1, so Yes.

Step 3 — (b) \(k = 5\)

Add P4 (No) and P5 (No): Yes 2, No 3, so No. The two extra neighbours were both No and flipped the result.

Step 4 — (c) \(k = 5\) weighted by \(1/d^{2}\)

Neighbour Class \(d^{2}\) Weight \(1/d^{2}\) P1 Yes 1 1.0000 P2 No 2 0.5000 P3 Yes 4 0.2500 P4 No 9 0.1111 P5 No 10 0.1000

\(\text{Yes} = 1.0000 + 0.2500 = 1.2500, \qquad \text{No} = 0.5000 + 0.1111 + 0.1000 = 0.7111\)

\(1.2500 > 0.7111\), so the weighted vote says Yes.

Answer. (a) Yes (2 votes to 1). (b) No (3 votes to 2). (c) Yes (weight 1.2500 against 0.7111).

Comment. In (b) the three No neighbours are at distances 1.414, 3.000 and 3.162, while the two Yes neighbours are at 1.000 and 2.000. A plain majority throws that information away; a neighbour three times farther off still gets one whole vote. Weighting restores it: the very close P1 alone (weight 1.0) outweighs the two distant No votes together (0.211). Weighting also makes exact ties in the vote practically impossible.

Example 9.4: Why the features must be rescaled first

Problem. A shop records four customers.

Customer Age (years) Salary (thousand rupees) Segment C1 20 500 A C2 25 800 A C3 60 520 B C4 55 900 B

A new customer is 24 years old and earns 890 thousand. (a) Classify with \(k = 1\) and \(k = 3\) from the raw numbers. (b) Apply min-max scaling and classify again. (c) Which answer is to be trusted?

Step 1 — (a) raw distances from \(Q = (24, 890)\)

For C1: \(d^{2} = (24-20)^{2} + (890-500)^{2} = 16 + 152100 = 152116\), so \(d = 390.02\).

Customer \(\Delta\)age \(\Delta\)salary \(d^{2}\) \(d\) Segment C4 \(-31\) \(-10\) \(961 + 100 = 1061\) 32.57 B C2 \(-1\) 90 \(1 + 8100 = 8101\) 90.01 A C3 \(-36\) 370 \(1296 + 136900 = 138196\) 371.75 B C1 4 390 \(16 + 152100 = 152116\) 390.02 A

\(k = 1\): C4, segment B. \(k = 3\): C4 (B), C2 (A), C3 (B), segment B.

The result deserves suspicion. C4 is 55 years old and the query is 24, a gap of 31 years, yet C4 is the nearest customer. In its \(d^{2}\) the age term contributes 961 and the salary term only 100; across the table, salary differences are in the hundreds and age differences at most 36, so salary drowns age.

Step 2 — (b) min-max scaling

\(x' = \dfrac{x - \min}{\max - \min}\), with Age: min 20, max 60, range 40, and Salary: min 500, max 900, range 400. The query is scaled with the training minimum and maximum. For C2: age \((25-20)/40 = 0.125\), salary \((800-500)/400 = 0.750\).

Age Salary C1 0.000 0.000 C2 0.125 0.750 C3 1.000 0.050 C4 0.875 1.000 Q 0.100 0.975

For C2: \(d^{2} = (0.100 - 0.125)^{2} + (0.975 - 0.750)^{2} = 0.000625 + 0.050625 = 0.051250\), so \(d = 0.2264\). In full:

Customer \(d^{2}\) \(d\) Segment C2 0.051250 0.2264 A C4 \(0.600625 + 0.000625 = 0.601250\) 0.7754 B C1 \(0.010000 + 0.950625 = 0.960625\) 0.9801 A C3 \(0.810000 + 0.855625 = 1.665625\) 1.2906 B

\(k = 1\): C2, segment A. \(k = 3\): C2 (A), C4 (B), C1 (A), segment A.

Step 3 — (c) which to trust

The query is young with a high salary. C2 is 25 with 800: young, high salary, segment A. C4 is 55 with 900. Common sense, and the scaled calculation, say C2 is the better match.

Answer. Raw numbers give B for both \(k\); after scaling both give A. Trust the scaled answer, segment A.

Comment. Standardising (subtracting the mean and dividing by the population standard deviation: means 40 and 680, standard deviations 17.68 and 173.78) gives the same neighbours in the same order, C2, C4, C1, C3, so the conclusion does not depend on which of the two scalings is used. k-NN has no idea what a year or a rupee is; it sees only numbers, and a column with bigger numbers silently wins. Compute the scaling constants on the training set and apply the same constants to every query.

Example 9.5: k-NN for a number: Manhattan distance and weighting

Problem. Five houses have recently been sold.

House Size (100 sq ft) Bedrooms Price (lakh) H1 10 2 30 H2 12 3 38 H3 15 3 45 H4 20 4 60 H5 22 4 66

Estimate the price of a house of size 14 with 3 bedrooms by k-NN regression with \(k = 3\) and the Manhattan distance, then refine the estimate by weighting each neighbour by \(1/d\).

Step 1 — Manhattan distances from \(Q = (14, 3)\)

\(d = |14 - \text{size}| + |3 - \text{bedrooms}|\). For H1: \(|14 - 10| + |3 - 2| = 4 + 1 = 5\).

House \(\lvert\Delta\text{size}\rvert\) \(\lvert\Delta\text{bedrooms}\rvert\) \(d\) Price H3 1 0 1 45 H2 2 0 2 38 H1 4 1 5 30 H4 6 1 7 60 H5 8 1 9 66

Step 2 — the unweighted average of the three nearest

The nearest three are H3, H2 and H1. For regression the neighbours' values are averaged instead of voted on:

\(\hat{y} = \dfrac{45 + 38 + 30}{3} = \dfrac{113}{3} = 37.67 \text{ lakh}\)

Step 3 — weighting by \(1/d\)

The weights are \(w_{3} = 1/1 = 1.000\), \(w_{2} = 1/2 = 0.500\) and \(w_{1} = 1/5 = 0.200\), so

\(\hat{y} = \dfrac{1(45) + 0.5(38) + 0.2(30)}{1 + 0.5 + 0.2} = \dfrac{45 + 19 + 6}{1.7} = \dfrac{70}{1.7} = 41.18 \text{ lakh}\)

Answer. The unweighted estimate is 37.67 lakh and the weighted estimate is 41.18 lakh.

Comment. The weighted estimate is higher because H3, the most similar house, now dominates the average. Here the Manhattan and Euclidean distances rank the five houses in the same order, but they need not: Manhattan adds the differences without squaring them, so one large difference counts for less. Size is measured in hundreds and bedrooms in single digits, so a real model would scale both columns first.

docs.title: 9.4 Common mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
Each of the following is a mistake that costs marks in an examination or accuracy in practice.

  • Do not run k-NN, SVM or a neural network on unscaled features.
  • Do not use an even \(k\) in two-class k-NN.

docs.title: 9.5 Summary
docs.text:
After working through this chapter you should be able to do the following.

  • Classify by hand with k-NN, describe how \(k\) trades bias against variance, and name the three conditions it insists on — scaling, an odd \(k\), and not too many dimensions.

docs.title: 9.6 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Training points \((1,1) \to A\), \((2,2) \to A\), \((4,4) \to B\), \((5,5) \to B\). Classify \((3,3)\) with \(k = 1\) and with \(k = 3\), and explain the tie.

    Answer

    The distances from \((3,3)\) are \(\sqrt{2} = 1.414\) to both \((2,2)\) and \((4,4)\), and \(\sqrt{8} = 2.828\) to both \((1,1)\) and \((5,5)\). The query sits exactly midway between the two classes, and the data are symmetric about it.

    \(k = 1\): the nearest neighbours are \((2,2)\), class A, and \((4,4)\), class B, at exactly the same distance. Neither is nearer, so the data do not decide the class; a program would choose whichever it meets first, which is an accident of row order.

    \(k = 3\): the two nearest points are \((2,2)\) (A) and \((4,4)\) (B), and the third place is again a tie between \((1,1)\) (A) and \((5,5)\) (B). The vote is A 2, B 1 or A 1, B 2 depending on the tie-break, so it does not settle the question either. Weighting the votes by \(1/d\) does not help: A receives \(1/\sqrt{2} + 1/\sqrt{8}\) and so does B.

    A tie of this kind is a property of the geometry and not a flaw in the method; the honest answer is that the query is undecided. In practice one would prefer a \(k\) that does not cut through a group of equidistant points, or break the tie by a stated rule such as choosing the class with the larger prior.

  2. Five points and a query \(q = (5, 5)\) are given.

    Point \((x_1, x_2)\) Class A (4, 5) Red B (6, 6) Blue C (5, 7) Blue D (1, 2) Red E (7, 3) Red

    Classify \(q\) for \(k = 1\) and \(k = 3\) using Euclidean distance.

    Answer

    Squared distances from \((5,5)\): A \(1 + 0 = 1\); B \(1 + 1 = 2\); C \(0 + 4 = 4\); E \(4 + 4 = 8\); D \(16 + 9 = 25\). The distances are 1.000, 1.414, 2.000, 2.828 and 5.000.

    \(k = 1\): the nearest is A (1.000), class Red.

    \(k = 3\): the nearest three are A (Red), B (Blue), C (Blue), so Blue 2 and Red 1, class Blue.

    The answer changes with \(k\), which is why \(k\) is a hyper-parameter to be chosen by validation.

  3. The points \(A(1,2)\), \(B(2,3)\) and \(F(2,1)\) are of class Black and \(C(3,3)\), \(D(6,5)\) and \(E(7,8)\) are of class White. Classify \(q = (3,4)\) with the Euclidean distance for (a) \(k = 1\) and (b) \(k = 3\), showing the distances and the votes.

    Answer

    Squared distances from \((3,4)\): C \(0 + 1 = 1\); B \(1 + 1 = 2\); A \(4 + 4 = 8\); D \(9 + 1 = 10\); F \(1 + 9 = 10\); E \(16 + 16 = 32\). The distances are C 1.00, B 1.41, A 2.83, D 3.16, F 3.16, E 5.66.

    (a) \(k = 1\): the nearest is C, so White.

    (b) \(k = 3\): C (White), B (Black), A (Black) give Black 2, White 1, so Black. (D and F tie for fourth place but lie outside the three.)

  4. A clothing company records the size worn by six past customers.

    Customer A B C D E F Height (cm) 158 158 163 165 168 170 Weight (kg) 58 59 61 61 62 68 Size M M M L L L

    Predict the size of a new customer of height 161 cm and weight 61 kg by k-NN with \(k = 3\) and Euclidean distance.

    Answer

    Squared distances from \((161, 61)\): A \(9 + 9 = 18\); B \(9 + 4 = 13\); C \(4 + 0 = 4\); D \(16 + 0 = 16\); E \(49 + 1 = 50\); F \(81 + 49 = 130\). The distances are A 4.243, B 3.606, C 2.000, D 4.000, E 7.071, F 11.402.

    The nearest three are C (2.000, M), B (3.606, M) and D (4.000, L): M 2, L 1, so the predicted size is M. Customer D, a size L, is among the three nearest, which shows that k-NN needs a majority and not unanimity. With \(k = 2\) there would have been a tie, which is one reason for an odd \(k\).

  5. A laboratory classifies patients as High or Low risk from glucose (\(x_1\)) and BMI (\(x_2\)).

    Patient Glucose BMI Risk P1 100 18 Low P2 110 22 Low P3 105 25 Low P4 135 32 High P5 150 35 High

    A new patient has glucose 130 and BMI 28. (a) Classify with \(k = 3\) and the raw Euclidean distance. (b) Repeat after min-max scaling of both features, using the training minimum and maximum. Comment.

    Answer

    (a) Squared distances from \((130, 28)\): P4 \(25 + 16 = 41\); P2 \(400 + 36 = 436\); P5 \(400 + 49 = 449\); P3 \(625 + 9 = 634\); P1 \(900 + 100 = 1000\). The distances are 6.40, 20.88, 21.19, 25.18 and 31.62. The nearest three are P4 (High), P2 (Low) and P5 (High): High 2, Low 1, so High.

    (b) Glucose runs from 100 to 150 (range 50) and BMI from 18 to 35 (range 17). The query becomes \((0.600, 0.588)\) and the patients \((0, 0)\), \((0.2, 0.235)\), \((0.1, 0.412)\), \((0.7, 0.824)\), \((1, 1)\). The distances are P4 0.256 (High), P3 0.530 (Low), P2 0.533 (Low), P5 0.574 (High), P1 0.840 (Low). The nearest three are P4, P3 and P2: Low 2, High 1, so Low.

    The prediction flips. In raw units the glucose gaps (tens) dwarf the BMI gaps (single digits), and P5 sneaks into the top three on its glucose alone. After scaling both features carry equal weight. The scaled answer is the one to trust, though the margin is small (P5 at 0.574 is only just outside), so with so few patients the answer is fragile whichever scaling is used.

  6. Calculate the Euclidean and the Manhattan distance between \(p_1 = (2, 4, 6)\) and \(p_2 = (5, 8, 6)\).

    Answer

    The coordinate differences are 3, 4 and 0. Euclidean: \(\sqrt{9 + 16 + 0} = \sqrt{25} = 5\). Manhattan: \(3 + 4 + 0 = 7\). The Euclidean distance is never larger than the Manhattan distance, which is a useful check on the arithmetic.

  7. Eight students have the following hours of study, attendance and exam score.

    Student S1 S2 S3 S4 S5 S6 S7 S8 Hours 2 3 5 6 8 9 4 7 Attendance (%) 60 70 75 80 85 90 65 95 Score 40 50 62 70 82 88 55 78

    Predict the score of a student with 6 hours and 82% attendance by k-NN regression with (a) \(k = 3\), (b) \(k = 5\), and (c) \(k = 3\) with \(1/d\) weights. Which feature dominates the distance, and why does that matter?

    Answer

    Squared distances from \((6, 82)\): S4 \(0 + 4 = 4\); S5 \(4 + 9 = 13\); S3 \(1 + 49 = 50\); S6 \(9 + 64 = 73\); S2 \(9 + 144 = 153\); S8 \(1 + 169 = 170\); S7 \(4 + 289 = 293\); S1 \(16 + 484 = 500\). The distances are 2.00, 3.61, 7.07, 8.54, 12.37, 13.04, 17.12, 22.36.

    (a) S4, S5, S3: \((70 + 82 + 62)/3 = 214/3 = 71.33\).

    (b) Add S6 (88) and S2 (50): \((70 + 82 + 62 + 88 + 50)/5 = 352/5 = 70.40\).

    (c) Weights \(1/2.00 = 0.5000\), \(1/3.61 = 0.2774\), \(1/7.07 = 0.1414\), total \(0.9188\). \(\hat{y} = (0.5000 \times 70 + 0.2774 \times 82 + 0.1414 \times 62)/0.9188 = 66.514/0.9188 = 72.39\).

    Going from \(k = 3\) to \(k = 5\) pulls in S2, who scored only 50, and drags the average down; weighting raises the estimate because S4 and S5 carry 85% of the total weight. Attendance (range 60 to 95) dominates hours (range 2 to 9): for S1 it contributes 484 of the squared distance 500. Strictly the two columns should be scaled before the distances are computed.

  8. Describe what happens to the k-NN decision boundary, and to the bias and the variance of the model, as \(k\) increases from 1 to \(m\), the number of training examples. What does \(k = m\) predict for every query?

    Answer

    With \(k = 1\) the boundary is jagged and follows every training point, including noisy ones: bias is low and variance high, and a single mislabelled point creates a wrong region around itself. As \(k\) increases the vote averages over more neighbours, the boundary becomes smoother, variance falls and bias rises. At \(k = m\) every query is compared with the whole training set, so the prediction is the majority class of the training data whatever the query: a single flat prediction, maximal bias and zero variance. The best \(k\) lies between these extremes and is chosen by cross-validation, with \(\sqrt{m}\) as a starting guess.

  9. A student applies k-NN with raw Euclidean distance to a data set with the features age (18 to 70) and annual income in rupees (200 000 to 2 000 000), and gets poor results. Find the mistake, explain why it damages k-NN in particular, and give the cure.

    Answer

    The mistake is to leave the features unscaled. The distance is a sum of squared differences, and an income difference of tens of thousands of rupees is squared into the hundreds of millions while an age difference is at most 52 and squares to at most 2704. The distance is therefore essentially the income difference and age is ignored. A tree is unaffected by this, because it only compares a feature with a threshold, but k-NN has nothing but the distance, so a badly scaled distance is a badly wrong model.

    The cure is to rescale: min-max scaling to \([0, 1]\) or standardisation to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, using statistics computed from the training set only and applied to every query.

  10. Compare a decision tree and k-NN on training cost, prediction cost, interpretability, need for feature scaling and behaviour in high dimensions.

    Answer Decision tree k-NN Training cost a greedy search for splits, so a real cost none: the data are simply stored Prediction cost very cheap: follow one path of tests high: a distance to every stored example, \(O(mn)\) per query without an index Interpretability high: readable if-then rules low: no model, only the neighbours of each query Feature scaling not needed, since only thresholds on one feature at a time are used essential, since the distance mixes all the features High dimensions copes better, because it only uses the few features it splits on degrades badly: all distances become nearly equal and "nearest" loses its meaning

  11. True or false, with a reason: "k-NN does most of its computation during training and very little when it predicts."

    Answer

    False. k-NN is a lazy learner: there is no training step beyond storing the data, and all the work, computing distances to the stored examples and sorting them, happens at prediction time. A decision tree is the opposite: costly to build and very cheap to use.

  12. Name two distance measures used in k-NN, say why feature scaling matters, and give two limitations of the method.

    Answer

    Euclidean distance (the straight line) and Manhattan distance (the sum of absolute differences); Hamming distance for categorical or 0/1 features is a third.

    Scaling matters because the distance sums contributions from every feature, so a feature measured in large numbers outweighs the rest and decides the neighbours regardless of how informative it is.

    Limitations include: the cost of every prediction grows with the size of the training set, and the whole set must be kept in memory; accuracy falls in high dimensions, where the distances to the nearest and the farthest points become similar; and the result depends on the choices of \(k\) and of the distance, and is easily upset by irrelevant features and by unscaled ones.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
docs.text:
You have some flats with their areas and their sale prices, and you want a rule that turns an area into a price. Draw the points on paper; they scatter around something roughly straight. Lay a ruler across them. You have just done regression.

Everything else is making that precise. Which line? The one that makes the total error smallest — and once you write down what “error” means, the best line is determined, and there is a formula for it. How do you find it when there are twenty features and no formula is practical? You start anywhere and repeatedly step downhill on the error surface, which is gradient descent, and it is the same algorithm that trains every neural network in Unit 4. How do you stop the line from being too clever? That is regularisation. How do you know whether any of it worked? That is the metrics section.

This unit is the longest in the course for a reason: every idea in it reappears in Unit 4 with a different loss function bolted on the front. Learn the machinery here and classification becomes a variation rather than a new subject.

Learning outcomes of Unit 3

  • Derive and apply the closed-form least-squares line, and read its slope and intercept in the language of the problem.
  • Write down \(J(\theta )\), say why the error is squared and why the ½ is there, and describe the shape of the surface.
  • Perform one step of gradient descent by hand, diagnose a learning rate from a cost curve, and explain why feature scaling changes the number of iterations but not the answer.
  • Move to many variables in vector form, use the normal equation, and say when it is the wrong tool.
  • Fit polynomial features and recognise the moment they start fitting noise.
  • Explain bias and variance as a decomposition of expected error, and place any model on that axis.
  • Apply ridge and lasso, explain geometrically why only lasso gives exact zeros, and choose \(\lambda\) honestly.
  • Compute MSE, RMSE, \(\text{MAE}, R^{2}\) and adjusted \(R^{2}\), and argue for one of them given what a mistake costs.

docs.title: 4.1 Linear regression with one variable
docs.text:
Definition: Simple linear regression

\(h_{\theta }(x) = \theta _{0} + \theta _{1}x\), where \(\theta _{0}\) is the intercept (the prediction when \(x = 0\)) and \(\theta _{1}\) is the slope (the change in \(\hat{y}\) for a one-unit change in \(x\)). The residual for example i is \(e_{i} = y_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}\): what the model missed by, with sign.

“Best” has to be defined before it can be found. Least squares defines it as minimising the sum of squared residuals, and the minimum has a closed form.

\[ \theta _{1} = \sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})(y_{i} - \bar{y}) / \sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})^{2} \quad \theta _{0} = \bar{y} - \theta _{1}\bar{x} \]

the least-squares line, obtained by setting both partial derivatives of the cost to zero

The second formula says something worth noticing: the fitted line always passes through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\). Substitute \(x = \bar{x}\) and you get exactly \(\bar{y}\). It is a free check on any calculation you do by hand, and a useful mental image — the line pivots about the centre of the data as the slope changes.

Figure 4.1. A line through eight points. Each shaded square has side equal to a residual, so its area is that point's squared error and the total shaded area is the SSE. The least-squares line is the one that makes this total as small as possible.

docs.title: Why squared, and not something else
docs.text:
Four reasons, in increasing order of depth. Squaring makes every error positive, so errors above and below the line cannot cancel — that rules out plain \(\sum e\). It is differentiable everywhere, unlike |e|, whose kink at zero makes calculus awkward. It punishes a few large misses more than many small ones, which is often what you want. And it has a probabilistic pedigree: minimising the squared error is exactly maximum likelihood estimation if the noise is Gaussian with constant variance.

Figure 4.2. Three ways to charge for an error. Squared error curves upwards, so an error of 4 costs sixteen times an error of 1; absolute error charges in proportion and is robust to outliers, at the price of a kink at zero; Huber squares small errors and switches to absolute error for large ones.

docs.title: Correlation is not regression
docs.text:
They are related and not the same. The correlation coefficient \(r\) is symmetric and unitless: it measures how tightly the points cluster about a line, and swapping \(x\) and \(y\) leaves it unchanged. The regression slope is directional and carries units — lakh per hundred square feet — and regressing \(x\) on \(y\) gives a different line from regressing \(y\) on \(x\). The link is \(\theta _{1} = r \cdot (s_{y}/s_{x})\), and \(r^{2}\) is exactly the \(R^{2}\) of the simple-regression fit.

Example 4.1: Deriving the least-squares line

Problem. Where do \(\theta _{1} = \sum (x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y})/\sum (x-\bar{x})^{2}\) and \(\theta _{0} = \bar{y} - \theta _{1}\bar{x}\) come from? Nothing is assumed here except that we want the \(\theta\) making the total squared error smallest.

Step 1 — write down what is being minimised

\(J(\theta _{0}, \theta _{1}) = \sum _{i} (\theta _{0} + \theta _{1}x_{i} - y_{i})^{2}\). It is a smooth function of two variables and a sum of squares, so it is bounded below and has a minimum. At that minimum both partial derivatives are zero.

Step 2 — differentiate with respect to \(\theta _{0}\)

Each term is the square of something linear in \(\theta _{0}\), so the chain rule gives \(2(\theta _{0} + \theta _{1}x_{i} - y_{i}) \times 1\):

\(\partial J/\partial \theta _{0} = 2 \sum (\theta _{0} + \theta _{1}x_{i} - y_{i}) = 0\)

Divide by 2 and split the sum: \(m\theta _{0} + \theta _{1}\sum x_{i} - \sum y_{i} = 0\). Divide by \(m\) and use \(\bar{x} = \sum x_{i}/m\) and \(\bar{y} = \sum y_{i}/m\):

\(\theta _{0} + \theta _{1}\bar{x} = \bar{y}\), that is, \(\theta _{0} = \bar{y} - \theta _{1}\bar{x}\).

Read that again: it says the fitted line passes through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\). The second formula was never a separate fact — it is the first normal equation.

Step 3 — differentiate with respect to \(\theta _{1}\)

Now the inner derivative is \(x_{i}\):

\(\partial J/\partial \theta _{1} = 2 \sum (\theta _{0} + \theta _{1}x_{i} - y_{i}) x_{i} = 0\)

Step 4 — eliminate \(\theta _{0}\)

Substitute \(\theta _{0} = \bar{y} - \theta _{1}\bar{x}\) into step 3 and divide by 2:

\(\sum (\bar{y} - \theta _{1}\bar{x} + \theta _{1}x_{i} - y_{i}) x_{i} = 0\)

Group the \(\theta _{1}\) terms: \(\sum (y_{i} - \bar{y})x_{i} = \theta _{1} \sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})x_{i}\), so \(\theta _{1} = \sum (y_{i} - \bar{y})x_{i} / \sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})x_{i}\).

Step 5 — put it in the centred form

One identity finishes it: \(\sum (x_{i} - \bar{x}) = 0\), because \(\sum x_{i} = m\bar{x}\). Multiplying that zero by any constant is still zero, so we may subtract \(\bar{x}\sum (y_{i} - \bar{y})\) from the numerator and \(\bar{x}\sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})\) from the denominator without changing either. They become \(\sum (y_{i} - \bar{y})(x_{i} - \bar{x})\) and \(\sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})^{2}\).

Answer. \(\theta _{1} = \sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})(y_{i} - \bar{y}) / \sum (x_{i} - \bar{x})^{2}\) and \(\theta _{0} = \bar{y} - \theta _{1}\bar{x}\)

Comment. Two things fall out for free. The numerator is the sample covariance and the denominator the variance of \(x\), so \(\theta _{1} = r\cdot (s_{y}/s_{x})\) — the link between correlation and regression. And step 2 says the residuals sum to zero whenever the model has an intercept, which is the fastest check on any fit you do by hand.

docs.title: 4.2 The cost function
docs.text:
\[ J(\theta _{0}, \theta _{1}) = (1/2m) \sum _{i=1..m} ( h_{\theta }(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} )^{2} \]

the mean squared error, halved

The 1/m makes the cost comparable across datasets of different size. The ½ is pure convenience: differentiating the square brings down a factor of 2 which the ½ cancels, so the gradient comes out clean. Neither changes where the minimum is, only what number sits there.

Key idea

\(J\) is a function of the parameters, not of \(x\). Every point \((\theta _{0}, \theta _{1})\) in the plane is one candidate line, and the height above it is how badly that line fits. For linear regression \(J\) is a convex quadratic bowl — one minimum, no local traps — which is why linear regression is a solved problem and neural network training is not.

Figure 4.3. Contours of the cost J over the two parameters of a straight line; every point on one ring is a line with the same SSE. Gradient descent starts at the red point and walks towards the minimum (green), crossing contours at right angles.

docs.title: 4.3 Gradient descent
docs.text:
Definition: Batch gradient descent

Repeat until convergence, updating every parameter simultaneously:

\(\theta _{j}\) := \(\theta _{j} - \alpha \partial J/\partial \theta _{j}\)

For the squared cost above, the partial derivatives are

\(\partial J/\partial \theta _{0} = (1/m) \sum (h(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)})\) \(\partial J/\partial \theta _{1} = (1/m) \sum (h(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}) x^{(i)}\)

Read the update in words: look at how wrong you are, and move each parameter in the direction that reduces that wrongness, by an amount proportional to how steeply it reduces it. The learning rate \(\alpha\) controls the size of the step and nothing else.

Simultaneous update

Compute both gradients from the current \(\theta\), then assign both. Computing the new \(\theta _{0}\) and then using it inside the gradient for \(\theta _{1}\) is a different algorithm that does not descend the cost you wrote down. It is the most common bug in a hand-written implementation, and it usually still converges — to the wrong place, or more slowly — which is what makes it hard to spot.

Figure 4.4. Gradient descent on a cost with one parameter. The slope at the current point (dashed tangent) says which way is downhill, and each step is proportional to the slope, so steps shrink automatically near the bottom. Variant Examples per update Character Batch all \(m\) smooth, exact descent; one update costs a full pass over the data Stochastic (SGD) 1 noisy path, very fast per step, escapes shallow local minima, never quite settles Mini-batch 32–256 the practical compromise, and what everything real uses

Why scaling changes the number of iterations

If \(x_{1}\) runs to 2 000 and \(x_{2}\) to 5, the cost contours are a long thin ravine rather than round rings. The gradient points steeply across the ravine and only slightly along it, so descent zig-zags between the walls and creeps towards the minimum. Standardise both features and the ravine becomes a bowl: the gradient points at the minimum and descent walks straight there. The answer is identical either way — scaling changes the route, not the destination.

Here is the same descent written out, so that nothing is hidden. This is the entire algorithm — nine lines, and every one of them is a line of the derivation above.

# batch gradient descent from scratch, for one feature or many
def gradient_descent(X, y, alpha=0.05, iters=1000):
    m, n  = X.shape
    X     = np.c_[np.ones(m), X]      # the x0 = 1 column, so the intercept is a weight
    theta = np.zeros(n + 1)
    history = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        error = X @ theta - y         # shape (m,)
        grad  = (X.T @ error) / m     # (1/m) sum (h - y) x
        theta = theta - alpha * grad  # every parameter updated together
        history.append((error ** 2).sum() / (2 * m))
    return theta, history

theta, J = gradient_descent(X_scaled, y, alpha=0.1)
# always plot J: it rises only when alpha is too large

Read theta \(=\) theta - alpha \(*\) grad once more

The whole vector is replaced at once — that is what a simultaneous update looks like in code, and writing the loop one element at a time is exactly where the classic bug gets in.

1 000 iterations is an optimistic default

When the features are correlated the valley is the long thin ravine described above, and descent crawls along it. On the diabetes dataset with \(\alpha = 0.1\) the coefficients are still 15.4 away from the exact least-squares answer after 1 000 iterations, 1.2 away after 4 000, and correct to four decimals only after about 20 000 — while the largest true coefficient is 37.7, so that first error is not small. And \(J\) looks flat long before \(\theta\) has settled, because the cost near a minimum changes quadratically while the parameters still have a long way to travel. Judge convergence by how much \(\theta\) moves, not by eye on the cost curve — and while \(n\) is small enough, check against the closed form.

Example 4.2: Deriving the gradient-descent update

Problem. Why is \(\partial J/\partial \theta _{1} = (1/m)\sum (h(x_{i}) - y_{i})x_{i}\), and what happened to the ½?

Step 1 — the cost, with its constants

\(J(\theta ) = (1/2m) \sum _{i} (h_{\theta }(x_{i}) - y_{i})^{2}\), with \(h_{\theta }(x) = \theta _{0} + \theta _{1}x\).

Step 2 — differentiate one term by the chain rule

Write \(e_{i} = h_{\theta }(x_{i}) - y_{i}\). Then \(\partial (e_{i}^{2})/\partial \theta _{j} = 2e_{i} \cdot \partial e_{i}/\partial \theta _{j}\).

The inner derivative is easy because \(h\) is linear: \(\partial e_{i}/\partial \theta _{0} = 1\) and \(\partial e_{i}/\partial \theta _{1} = x_{i}\). (\(y_{i}\) is data, not a variable, so it differentiates to zero.)

Step 3 — sum, and cancel the 2

\(\partial J/\partial \theta _{0} = (1/2m) \sum 2e_{i} = (1/m) \sum (h(x_{i}) - y_{i})\)

\(\partial J/\partial \theta _{1} = (1/2m) \sum 2e_{i}x_{i} = (1/m) \sum (h(x_{i}) - y_{i}) x_{i}\)

That is the whole job of the ½: it cancels the 2 that squaring produces. It moves nothing — the minimum of \(J\) sits at the same \(\theta\) either way — and it makes every formula after it cleaner.

Step 4 — the general case, in one line

With the convention \(x_{0} = 1\) the two formulas become one: \(\partial J/\partial \theta _{j} = (1/m) \sum (h(x_{i}) - y_{i}) x_{\text{ij}}\). Descend by subtracting \(\alpha\) times it, simultaneously for every \(j\).

Answer. \(\theta _{j}\) := \(\theta _{j} - (\alpha /m) \sum _{i} (h(x_{i}) - y_{i}) x_{\text{ij}}\)

Comment. Remember the shape: error \(\times\) input, averaged. You meet it twice more in this course — it is exactly the logistic-regression gradient with \(h\) redefined as \(\sigma (\theta ^{T}x)\), and it is the last step of back-propagation, where the error is \(\delta\) and the input is the activation arriving at that weight.

docs.title: 4.4 Many variables at once
docs.text:
\[ h_{\theta }(x) = \theta _{0} + \theta _{1}x_{1} + \theta _{2}x_{2} + \ldots + \theta _{n}x_{n} = \theta ^{T}x \]

with the convention \(x_{0} = 1\), so the intercept is just another weight

The \(x_{0} = 1\) trick is not cosmetic — it lets one matrix expression cover the intercept and every slope together, which is what makes the vector form and the normal equation possible.

Definition: The normal equation

\(\theta = (X^{T}X)^{-1}X^{T}y\), where \(X\) is the \(m \times (n+1)\) design matrix whose first column is all ones.

It is exact, needs no learning rate and no iteration, and requires no feature scaling. Its cost is the matrix inversion: roughly \(O(n^{3})\), which is nothing for \(n = 20\) and impossible for \(n = 50 000\). The crossover in practice is around \(n \approx 10^{4}\).

\(X^{T}X\) fails to be invertible in exactly two situations, and both are diagnosable. The first is redundant features: one column is a linear combination of others — height in cm beside height in inches, or all \(c\) one-hot columns kept alongside the intercept. The second is more features than examples, \(n > m\). The fixes are to drop the redundancy, collect more data, or add a ridge penalty, which makes \(X^{T}X + \lambda I\) invertible for every \(\lambda > 0\).

docs.title: Reading coefficients, and one trap
docs.text:
Each \(\theta _{j}\) is a partial effect: the change in \(\hat{y}\) for a one-unit change in \(x_{j}\) with every other feature held fixed. Two warnings follow. Coefficient magnitudes cannot be compared unless the features are standardised — a feature measured in thousands gets a small coefficient regardless of its importance. And when features are correlated, “holding the others fixed” is partly fictional. Area and bedrooms move together, so the split of credit between their coefficients becomes unstable. Small changes in the data can then swing them wildly, and occasionally even reverse a sign. That instability is multicollinearity, and it is one of the two things ridge regression was invented to fix.

# Unit 3, in the form you will actually write it
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

reg = LinearRegression().fit(X_tr, y_tr)      # solves the normal equation internally
print(reg.coef_, reg.intercept_)              # the slopes, and the intercept apart

pred = reg.predict(X_te)
mse  = mean_squared_error(y_te, pred)
print("MSE", mse, "RMSE", np.sqrt(mse),
      "MAE", mean_absolute_error(y_te, pred),
      "R2",  r2_score(y_te, pred))

LinearRegression does not iterate — it solves the normal equations, through a numerically safer routine than forming an explicit inverse. Notice that coef_ and intercept_ are kept apart: that is the library reminding you \(\theta _{0}\) is not penalised once you move to ridge.

Example 4.3: Deriving the normal equation

Problem. Show that the \(\theta\) minimising \(\Vert X\theta - y\Vert ^{2}\) is \(\theta = (X^{T}X)^{-1}X^{T}y\), and say exactly when that inverse fails to exist.

Step 1 — the cost in matrix form

Stack the residuals into a vector \(r = X\theta - y\). The sum of squared residuals is the dot product of \(r\) with itself: \(J(\theta ) = r^{T}r = (X\theta - y)^{T}(X\theta - y)\).

Step 2 — expand

\(J = \theta ^{T}X^{T}X\theta - \theta ^{T}X^{T}y - y^{T}X\theta + y^{T}y\)

The two middle terms are scalars, and a scalar equals its own transpose, so \(\theta ^{T}X^{T}y = y^{T}X\theta\) and they combine: \(J = \theta ^{T}X^{T}X\theta - 2\theta ^{T}X^{T}y + y^{T}y\).

Step 3 — differentiate with respect to the vector \(\theta\)

Two standard identities are all that is needed: \(\partial (\theta ^{T}A\theta )/\partial \theta = 2A\theta\) for symmetric A — and \(X^{T}X\) is symmetric, since \((X^{T}X)^{T} = X^{T}X\) — and \(\partial (\theta ^{T}b)/\partial \theta = b\). The last term has no \(\theta\) in it. So \(\nabla J = 2X^{T}X\theta - 2X^{T}y\).

Step 4 — set it to zero

\(X^{T}X\theta = X^{T}y\) — the normal equations. When \(X^{T}X\) is invertible, \(\theta = (X^{T}X)^{-1}X^{T}y\). It is a minimum and not a maximum because the second derivative \(2X^{T}X\) is positive semi-definite: \(v^{T}X^{T}\text{Xv} = \Vert \text{Xv}\Vert ^{2} \ge 0\) for every \(v\).

Step 5 — when the inverse does not exist

\(\Vert \text{Xv}\Vert ^{2} = 0\) for some \(v\) ≠ 0 exactly when the columns of \(X\) are linearly dependent, which happens in precisely two situations: a redundant feature (height in cm beside height in inches; all \(c\) one-hot columns kept alongside the intercept), or \(n > m\), since \(n + 1\) columns cannot be independent in \(m\) dimensions.

A ridge penalty replaces \(X^{T}X\) by \(X^{T}X + \lambda I\), and \(v^{T}(X^{T}X + \lambda I)v = \Vert \text{Xv}\Vert ^{2} + \lambda \Vert v\Vert ^{2} > 0\) for every \(v\) ≠ 0 and every \(\lambda > 0\). So ridge always has a unique solution, even where ordinary least squares has none — the second, less advertised reason to use it.

Answer. \(\theta = (X^{T}X)^{-1}X^{T}y\), singular exactly when the columns of \(X\) are linearly dependent

Comment. The geometric reading is worth carrying away. \(X^{T}X\theta = X^{T}y\) says \(X^{T}(X\theta - y) = 0\): the residual vector is orthogonal to every column of \(X\). Least squares projects \(y\) perpendicularly onto the space the features can span, and what is left over is, by construction, the part no feature could have explained.

Figure 4.5. Forty refits of a model whose two features are strongly correlated; the true coefficients are (2, 1). The fitted pairs stretch into a streak along the dashed line on which their sum is constant: the sum is stable but each coefficient on its own is unreliable.

That is the whole of multicollinearity in one picture. The data has seen \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) rise and fall together, so it has no way to tell which of them earned the weight. It knows only what they earn together — which is why the sum is pinned down while each part is not, and why the forecast survives even when the explanation does not.

docs.title: Choosing the learning rate and reading the cost curve
docs.text:
The learning rate is the one number in gradient descent that you must choose, and the cost-versus-iteration curve is the instrument that tells you whether you chose well. Plot it on every run. The figure shows the descent on the three points \((1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 5)\) of the worked examples, which lie exactly on \(y = 2x - 1\), so the true minimum cost is zero. The three curves use \(\alpha = 0.01, 0.1\) and \(0.4\), and the vertical axis is logarithmic so that all three fit.

Figure 4.6. Cost against iteration for gradient descent on the points (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 5), on a logarithmic scale. With alpha 0.01 the cost falls but is still far from zero after forty iterations; with alpha 0.1 it falls fast and then settles into a slow tail; with alpha 0.4 every step overshoots and the cost grows by a constant factor per iteration.

Three shapes are worth recognising. A curve that falls but has barely bent after many iterations means \(\alpha\) is too small: the method is correct and merely slow. A curve that falls quickly and then flattens is the good case. A curve that rises, or zig-zags upwards, means \(\alpha\) is too large, and on a log scale a diverging run appears as a straight line climbing, because the cost is multiplied by the same factor at every step.

The reason for the boundary between the second and third shapes is the one-parameter argument of the worked example on three learning rates, carried to many parameters. The Hessian of the cost is \(X^{T}X/m\), a symmetric matrix with non-negative eigenvalues, and along the direction belonging to an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) each iteration multiplies the remaining distance to the minimum by \(1 - \alpha\lambda\). Descent is stable only if every such factor lies between \(-1\) and \(1\), that is

\[ \alpha < \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}} \]

For these three points the eigenvalues of \(X^{T}X/m\) are \(5.546\) and \(0.120\), so the threshold is \(2/5.546 = 0.361\): \(\alpha = 0.1\) is safe and \(\alpha = 0.4\) is not. The small eigenvalue explains the slow tail. At \(\alpha = 0.1\) its direction shrinks by only \(1 - 0.1(0.120) = 0.988\) per iteration, so after forty iterations about \(0.988^{40} = 62\%\) of the distance along it remains. The ratio of the two eigenvalues, \(5.546/0.120 = 46\), is the elongation of the valley.

Centring the feature shows what scaling does. Replacing \(x = 1, 2, 3\) by \(x - 2 = -1, 0, 1\) changes nothing about the model, only about the surface: the eigenvalues become \(1\) and \(0.667\), a ratio of \(1.5\), and the valley is almost a bowl. With the same \(\alpha = 0.1\) and forty iterations the cost reaches \(0.0063\) instead of \(0.0676\). This is the precise sense in which scaling speeds descent: it shrinks the ratio of the largest eigenvalue to the smallest, which is the number that decides how many iterations are needed.

docs.title: Epochs, stopping rules and learning-rate schedules
docs.text:
One epoch is one full pass through the training data. Batch descent makes one update per epoch, stochastic descent makes \(m\) updates per epoch, and mini-batch descent makes about \(m\) divided by the batch size. Training length is therefore usually quoted in epochs, not in updates, so that runs with different batch sizes can be compared.
