Gradient descent needs a rule for when to stop, and three are in common use. The simplest is a fixed maximum number of iterations or epochs, which guarantees termination but not accuracy. The second is a tolerance: stop when the cost improves by less than a small \(\varepsilon\) between iterations, or better, when the parameters themselves move by less than \(\varepsilon\), since the cost flattens long before the parameters settle (the warning earlier in this chapter). The third, used when a validation set is available, is early stopping: watch the error on the validation set and stop when it stops improving, even though the training error is still falling. It is a form of regularisation, taken up in the next chapter.

A constant \(\alpha\) is a compromise between speed early and precision late. In stochastic and mini-batch descent it is a real problem, because the noise in each gradient stops \(\theta\) from settling however long you run. A learning-rate schedule lowers \(\alpha\) as training proceeds, for example \(\alpha_{t} = \alpha_{0}/(1 + kt)\) after \(t\) updates, or by halving it every fixed number of epochs. Large steps early cover the ground quickly and small steps late average out the noise. For batch descent on a convex cost with a well-chosen constant \(\alpha\) no schedule is needed.

docs.title: Categorical predictors as dummy variables
docs.text:
Regression needs numbers, but some predictors are categories: whether a flat has a lift, the city a house is in. A dummy variable codes a two-valued category as 0 or 1, for example \(d = 1\) if the flat has a lift and \(d = 0\) otherwise. In the model \(\hat{y} = \theta_{0} + \theta_{1}x + \theta_{2}d\) the coefficient \(\theta_{2}\) is the shift in the prediction between the two groups at the same \(x\): the line for flats with a lift is the line for flats without one moved up or down by \(\theta_{2}\). The slope \(\theta_{1}\) is shared.

A category with \(c\) values needs \(c - 1\) dummy columns, not \(c\). The omitted category becomes the baseline absorbed in the intercept, and each coefficient measures the difference from it. If all \(c\) columns are kept beside the intercept, they add up to the column of ones: one column is then a linear combination of the others and \(X^{T}X\) is singular, which is the redundant-feature case of Section 4.4, usually called the dummy-variable trap. Libraries avoid it by dropping the first category (drop="first" in the scikit-learn one-hot encoder), or the penalty of ridge regression removes the ambiguity if all columns are kept.

Dummy variables shift the intercept only. If the slope should also differ between the groups, the model needs the product \(x \cdot d\) as a further feature, an interaction term, which the next chapter takes up with the other ways of enlarging the feature set.

docs.title: 4.6 Worked examples
docs.text:
The examples below work through the calculations of this chapter in full. Try each one on paper before reading the steps.

Example 4.4: Fit a line and interpret it

Problem. Hours studied \(x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\) with marks \(y = 52, 55, 61, 64, 68\). Fit the least-squares line, predict for 6 hours, and state what the slope means.

Step 1 — the means

\(\bar{x} = 15/5 = 3, \bar{y} = 300/5 = 60\)

Step 2 — the two sums

\(x\) \(y\) \(x-\bar{x}\) \(y-\bar{y}\) \((x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y})\) \((x-\bar{x})^{2}\) 1 52 −2 −8 16 4 2 55 −1 −5 5 1 3 61 0 1 0 0 4 64 1 4 4 1 5 68 2 8 16 4 \(\sum\) 41 10

Step 3 — the coefficients

\(\theta _{1} = 41/10 = 4.1 \cdot \theta _{0} = 60 - 4.1(3) = 60 - 12.3 = 47.7\)

Check: does the line pass through (3, 60)? \(47.7 + 4.1(3) = 60\). ✓

Step 4 — predict and interpret

\(\hat{y}(6) = 47.7 + 4.1(6) = 72.3\) marks

The slope says: each additional hour of study is associated with about 4.1 more marks, over the range 1–5 hours observed. The intercept, 47.7, is the predicted mark for zero hours, which here is inside a plausible range. In many problems it is not: the intercept extrapolates to a value of \(x\) that never occurs, and then it should not be interpreted at all.

Note “associated with”, not “causes”. And note that predicting for \(x = 20\) hours would be extrapolation far outside the data, where a straight line has no authority whatsoever — it would predict 129 marks.

Answer. \(\hat{y} = 47.7 + 4.1x\); \(\hat{y}(6) = 72.3\)

Example 4.5: Two steps of gradient descent, in full

Problem. Data (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6). Start at \(\theta _{0} = \theta _{1} = 0\) with \(\alpha = 0.1\) and \(J = (1/2m)\sum (h - y)^{2}\). Perform two iterations.

Iteration 1 — predictions and errors

With \(\theta = (0, 0), h = 0\) for every point, so the errors \(h - y\) are −2, −4, −6.

\(\partial J/\partial \theta _{0} = (-2 - 4 - 6)/3 =\) −12/3 \(= -4\)

\(\partial J/\partial \theta _{1} =\) ((−2)(1) + (−4)(2) + (−6)(3))/3 \(= (-2 - 8 - 18)/3 =\) −28/3 \(= -9.333\)

Iteration 1 — update, both together

\(\theta _{0}\) := \(0 - 0.1(-4) = 0.4 \cdot \theta _{1}\) := \(0 - 0.1(-9.333) = 0.9333\)

Both gradients were negative, so both parameters increased. Gradient descent subtracts the gradient; when the gradient is negative that is an increase.

Iteration 2 — predictions with the new \(\theta\)

\(h(1) = 0.4 + 0.9333 = 1.3333\), error −0.6667

\(h(2) = 0.4 + 1.8667 = 2.2667\), error −1.7333

\(h(3) = 0.4 + 2.8 = 3.2\), error −2.8

\(\partial J/\partial \theta _{0} = (-0.6667 - 1.7333 - 2.8)/3 =\) −5.2/3 \(= -1.7333\)

\(\partial J/\partial \theta _{1} =\) ((−0.6667)(1) + (−1.7333)(2) + (−2.8)(3))/3 \(= (-0.6667 - 3.4667 - 8.4)/3 = -4.1778\)

Iteration 2 — update

\(\theta _{0}\) := \(0.4 + 0.17333 = 0.5733 \cdot \theta _{1}\) := \(0.9333 + 0.41778 = 1.3511\)

Answer. After two steps: \(\theta _{0} \approx 0.573, \theta _{1} \approx 1.351\)

Comment. The exact answer here is \(\theta _{0} = 0, \theta _{1} = 2\), and the descent is heading towards it — \(\theta _{1}\) is climbing steadily while \(\theta _{0}\) overshoots slightly and will come back down. Note also that the gradients shrank between the two iterations, from −4 to −1.73: as the fit improves, the steps get smaller on their own. You never need to reduce \(\alpha\) by hand for this reason.

The first two examples are least-squares lines, the next two follow gradient descent by hand, and the last three solve normal equations: for a straight line, for two predictors and for a quadratic.

Example 4.6: A line, its residuals and its \(R^{2}\)

Problem. A firm records the amount spent on advertising (\(x\), in lakh) and the sales achieved (\(y\), in lakh) over five months.

\(x\) 1 2 3 4 5 \(y\) 2 4 5 4 5

Fit \(y = \theta_{0} + \theta_{1}x\) by least squares, estimate the sales when \(x = 6\), and compute the coefficient of determination \(R^{2}\).

Step 1 — means and the two sums

\(\bar{x} = 15/5 = 3, \ \bar{y} = 20/5 = 4\)

\(x\) \(y\) \(x-\bar{x}\) \(y-\bar{y}\) \((x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y})\) \((x-\bar{x})^{2}\) 1 2 −2 −2 4 4 2 4 −1 0 0 1 3 5 0 1 0 0 4 4 1 0 0 1 5 5 2 1 2 4 \(\sum\) 6 10

Step 2 — the line

\(\theta_{1} = 6/10 = 0.6, \quad \theta_{0} = 4 - 0.6(3) = 2.2\), so \(\hat{y} = 2.2 + 0.6x\).

At \(x = 6\): \(\hat{y} = 2.2 + 0.6(6) = 5.8\).

Step 3 — residuals

\(x\) \(y\) \(\hat{y}\) \(e = y - \hat{y}\) \(e^{2}\) \((y-\bar{y})^{2}\) 1 2 2.8 −0.8 0.64 4 2 4 3.4 0.6 0.36 0 3 5 4.0 1.0 1.00 1 4 4 4.6 −0.6 0.36 0 5 5 5.2 −0.2 0.04 1 \(\sum\) 0 2.40 6

The residuals sum to zero, as they must for a line with an intercept.

Step 4 — \(R^{2}\)

\(\text{SS}_{\text{res}} = 2.40, \ \text{SS}_{\text{tot}} = 6\), so \(R^{2} = 1 - 2.40/6 = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6\).

Answer. \(\hat{y} = 2.2 + 0.6x\); the estimate at \(x = 6\) is 5.8 lakh; \(R^{2} = 0.6\).

Comment. The line explains 60% of the variation in sales. For a single predictor \(R^{2}\) equals the square of the correlation coefficient: \(r = 6/\sqrt{10 \times 6} = 0.7746\) and \(r^{2} = 36/60 = 0.6\). The estimate at \(x = 6\) lies just one step outside the data, which is mild extrapolation; the further from \(1\)–\(5\) the less it can be trusted.

Example 4.7: Unequal spacing, MSE and an estimate far outside the data

Problem. Four observations are given.

\(x\) 2 6 7 11 \(y\) 25 24 28 29

Find the least-squares line, compute the MSE and \(R^{2}\), and predict \(y\) at \(x = 18\).

Step 1 — means and deviations

\(\bar{x} = 26/4 = 6.5, \ \bar{y} = 106/4 = 26.5\)

\(x-\bar{x}\) −4.5 −0.5 0.5 4.5 \(y-\bar{y}\) −1.5 −2.5 1.5 2.5 product 6.75 1.25 0.75 11.25 \((x-\bar{x})^{2}\) 20.25 0.25 0.25 20.25

\(\sum(x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y}) = 20, \quad \sum(x-\bar{x})^{2} = 41\)

Step 2 — coefficients

\(\theta_{1} = 20/41 = 0.4878, \quad \theta_{0} = 26.5 - 0.4878(6.5) = 26.5 - 3.1707 = 23.3293\)

Step 3 — fitted values and residuals

\(x\) \(y\) \(\hat{y}\) \(e\) \(e^{2}\) 2 25 24.3049 0.6951 0.4832 6 24 26.2561 −2.2561 5.0899 7 28 26.7439 1.2561 1.5778 11 29 28.6951 0.3049 0.0930 \(\sum\) 0 7.2439

\(\text{MSE} = 7.2439/4 = 1.811\)

Step 4 — \(R^{2}\)

\(\text{SS}_{\text{tot}} = 2.25 + 6.25 + 2.25 + 6.25 = 17\), so \(R^{2} = 1 - 7.2439/17 = 1 - 0.4261 = 0.574\).

Step 5 — the prediction

\(\hat{y}(18) = 23.3293 + 0.4878(18) = 23.3293 + 8.7805 = 32.11\)

Answer. \(\hat{y} = 23.33 + 0.4878x\); MSE \(= 1.811\); \(R^{2} = 0.574\); \(\hat{y}(18) \approx 32.1\).

Comment. The data stop at \(x = 11\), so \(x = 18\) is far beyond them and the number 32.1 has no support from the data. With \(R^{2} = 0.57\) even the fit inside the range leaves almost half the variation unexplained. Note too that the means are not whole numbers here; the table of deviations makes the arithmetic painless all the same.

Example 4.8: Two iterations of gradient descent, with the cost tracked

Problem. Fit \(h(x) = \theta_{0} + \theta_{1}x\) to the points \((1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 5)\) by batch gradient descent with \(J = (1/2m)\sum(h - y)^{2}\). Start at \(\theta_{0} = \theta_{1} = 0\), take \(\alpha = 0.1\) and perform two iterations, showing \(J\) each time.

Step 1 — the starting cost

At \(\theta = (0, 0)\) every prediction is 0, so the errors \(h - y\) are \(-1, -3, -5\).

\(J = \dfrac{1}{6}\left[(-1)^{2} + (-3)^{2} + (-5)^{2}\right] = \dfrac{35}{6} = 5.8333\)

Step 2 — iteration 1: gradients and update

\(\partial J/\partial\theta_{0} = (-1 - 3 - 5)/3 = -3.0000\)

\(\partial J/\partial\theta_{1} = \left[(-1)(1) + (-3)(2) + (-5)(3)\right]/3 = -22/3 = -7.3333\)

\(\theta_{0} := 0 - 0.1(-3.0000) = 0.3000, \qquad \theta_{1} := 0 - 0.1(-7.3333) = 0.7333\)

Step 3 — iteration 1: the new cost

Predictions \(h = 1.0333, 1.7667, 2.5000\); errors \(0.0333, -1.2333, -2.5000\).

\(J = (0.0011 + 1.5211 + 6.2500)/6 = 7.7722/6 = 1.2954\)

Step 4 — iteration 2: gradients and update

\(\partial J/\partial\theta_{0} = (0.0333 - 1.2333 - 2.5000)/3 = -3.7000/3 = -1.2333\)

\(\partial J/\partial\theta_{1} = \left[(0.0333)(1) + (-1.2333)(2) + (-2.5000)(3)\right]/3 = -9.9333/3 = -3.3111\)

\(\theta_{0} := 0.3000 + 0.1(1.2333) = 0.4233, \qquad \theta_{1} := 0.7333 + 0.1(3.3111) = 1.0644\)

Step 5 — iteration 2: the new cost

Predictions \(h = 1.4878, 2.5522, 3.6167\); errors \(0.4878, -0.4478, -1.3833\).

\(J = (0.2379 + 0.2005 + 1.9136)/6 = 2.3520/6 = 0.3920\)

Answer. After two iterations \(\theta_{0} = 0.4233\) and \(\theta_{1} = 1.0644\); the cost has fallen \(5.8333 \to 1.2954 \to 0.3920\).

Comment. The three points lie exactly on \(y = 2x - 1\), so the true minimum is \(\theta = (-1, 2)\) with \(J = 0\). The cost drops fast at first and then slows: the intercept has to travel from \(0.42\) to \(-1\) and does so slowly, because the unscaled column \(x = 1, 2, 3\) makes the cost surface a narrow valley. Even after forty iterations at this \(\alpha\) the cost is still \(0.068\). Watching \(J\) fall is the check that \(\alpha\) is acceptable; watching \(\theta\) settle is the check that the algorithm has finished.

Example 4.9: Three learning rates on one function

Problem. Minimise \(J(\theta) = \theta^{2} - 4\theta + 5\) by gradient descent from \(\theta = 0\), using the update \(\theta := \theta - \alpha\,dJ/d\theta\). Compare \(\alpha = 0.1, 0.5\) and \(1.1\) over three iterations, and say for which \(\alpha\) the method converges.

Step 1 — the update rule and the exact minimum

\(dJ/d\theta = 2\theta - 4\), so \(\theta_{\text{new}} = \theta - \alpha(2\theta - 4) = (1 - 2\alpha)\theta + 4\alpha\).

Setting \(2\theta - 4 = 0\) gives the minimiser \(\theta^{*} = 2\), with \(J(2) = 4 - 8 + 5 = 1\).

Step 2 — a one-line description of every iteration

Subtract 2 from both sides of the update:

\(\theta_{\text{new}} - 2 = (1 - 2\alpha)(\theta - 2)\)

So each step multiplies the distance to the minimum by \(1 - 2\alpha\). Also \(J(\theta) = (\theta - 2)^{2} + 1\), which makes the cost easy to read off.

Step 3 — the three runs

iteration \(\alpha = 0.1\): \(\theta\) \(J\) \(\alpha = 0.5\): \(\theta\) \(J\) \(\alpha = 1.1\): \(\theta\) \(J\) 0 0.0000 5.0000 0.0000 5.0000 0.0000 5.0000 1 0.4000 3.5600 2.0000 1.0000 4.4000 6.7600 2 0.7200 2.6384 2.0000 1.0000 −0.8800 9.2944 3 0.9760 2.0486 2.0000 1.0000 5.4560 12.9439

The multipliers are \(1 - 0.2 = 0.8\), \(1 - 1 = 0\) and \(1 - 2.2 = -1.2\). For \(\alpha = 0.1\) the distance falls \(2 \to 1.6 \to 1.28 \to 1.024\). For \(\alpha = 0.5\) it is wiped out in one step. For \(\alpha = 1.1\) it goes \(-2 \to 2.4 \to -2.88 \to 3.456\): the sign flips each time and the size grows.

Step 4 — when does it converge?

The distance shrinks exactly when \(|1 - 2\alpha| < 1\), that is \(0 < \alpha < 1\). The best choice is \(\alpha = 0.5\), which equals \(1/J''\) since \(J'' = 2\). At \(\alpha = 1\) the multiplier is \(-1\) and \(\theta\) bounces between 0 and 4 for ever.

Answer. The minimiser is \(\theta^{*} = 2\). \(\alpha = 0.1\) converges slowly, \(\alpha = 0.5\) converges in one step, and \(\alpha = 1.1\) diverges, with \(\theta\) oscillating about 2 and \(J\) increasing at every step.

Comment. This one-parameter case is the whole story in miniature. For linear regression the same argument runs along each principal direction of the cost surface, with \(J''\) replaced by the eigenvalues of \(X^{T}X/m\): descent is stable only if \(\alpha\) is below \(2\) divided by the largest eigenvalue, and the smallest eigenvalue sets how long the slowest direction takes.

Example 4.10: The normal equation on four points

Problem. Use \(\theta = (X^{T}X)^{-1}X^{T}y\) to fit \(\hat{y} = \theta_{0} + \theta_{1}x\) to the points \((0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 5)\). Show \(X\), \(y\), \(X^{T}X\), \(X^{T}y\), the inverse and \(\theta\).

Step 1 — the design matrix

The first column of \(X\) is all ones so that \(\theta_{0}\) is the intercept.

\(X = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad y = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\)

Step 2 — the two products

\(X^{T}X = \begin{bmatrix} m & \sum x \\ \sum x & \sum x^{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad X^{T}y = \begin{bmatrix} \sum y \\ \sum xy \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12 \\ 24 \end{bmatrix}\)

since \(\sum x = 0+1+2+3 = 6\), \(\sum x^{2} = 0+1+4+9 = 14\), \(\sum y = 1+3+3+5 = 12\) and \(\sum xy = 0+3+6+15 = 24\).

Step 3 — the inverse of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix

\(\det = 4(14) - 6(6) = 56 - 36 = 20\), and swapping the diagonal and negating the off-diagonal gives

\((X^{T}X)^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix} 14 & -6 \\ -6 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\)

Step 4 — solve

\(\theta = \dfrac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix} 14(12) - 6(24) \\ -6(12) + 4(24) \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix} 168 - 144 \\ -72 + 96 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.2 \\ 1.2 \end{bmatrix}\)

Step 5 — check two ways

By the single-variable formulas: \(\bar{x} = 1.5, \ \bar{y} = 3, \ \sum(x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y}) = 6, \ \sum(x-\bar{x})^{2} = 5\), so \(\theta_{1} = 1.2\) and \(\theta_{0} = 3 - 1.2(1.5) = 1.2\). The same.

By orthogonality: the fitted values are \(1.2, 2.4, 3.6, 4.8\), so the residuals are \(-0.2, 0.6, -0.6, 0.2\). Their sum is 0, and \(\sum x\,e = 0 + 0.6 - 1.2 + 0.6 = 0\). The residual vector is perpendicular to both columns of \(X\), which is exactly what \(X^{T}(y - X\theta) = 0\) says.

Answer. \(\theta = (1.2, 1.2)\), that is \(\hat{y} = 1.2 + 1.2x\).

Comment. For \(2 \times 2\) systems the inverse formula is quick, but the habit worth keeping is the check: residuals that sum to zero and are orthogonal to every feature column.

Example 4.11: Two predictors, in deviation form

Problem. A response \(y\) is modelled on two predictors, \(y = b_{0} + b_{1}x_{1} + b_{2}x_{2}\).

\(x_{1}\) 1 2 3 4 5 \(x_{2}\) 2 1 4 3 5 \(y\) 9 8 19 18 26

Find \(b_{1}, b_{2}\) and \(b_{0}\), and predict \(y\) when \(x_{1} = 6\) and \(x_{2} = 4\).

Step 1 — centre everything

\(\bar{x}_{1} = 3, \ \bar{x}_{2} = 3, \ \bar{y} = 80/5 = 16\). Write \(d_{1} = x_{1} - 3, \ d_{2} = x_{2} - 3, \ d_{y} = y - 16\).

\(d_{1}\) \(d_{2}\) \(d_{y}\) \(d_{1}^{2}\) \(d_{2}^{2}\) \(d_{1}d_{2}\) \(d_{1}d_{y}\) \(d_{2}d_{y}\) −2 −1 −7 4 1 2 14 7 −1 −2 −8 1 4 2 8 16 0 1 3 0 1 0 0 3 1 0 2 1 0 0 2 0 2 2 10 4 4 4 20 20 \(\sum\) 10 10 8 44 46

Step 2 — the normal equations for the slopes

Writing \(S_{11} = 10, S_{22} = 10, S_{12} = 8, S_{1y} = 44, S_{2y} = 46\), the two equations are

\(S_{11}b_{1} + S_{12}b_{2} = S_{1y}: \quad 10b_{1} + 8b_{2} = 44\)

\(S_{12}b_{1} + S_{22}b_{2} = S_{2y}: \quad 8b_{1} + 10b_{2} = 46\)

Step 3 — solve by Cramer's rule

\(D = S_{11}S_{22} - S_{12}^{2} = 100 - 64 = 36\)

\(b_{1} = (S_{22}S_{1y} - S_{12}S_{2y})/D = (440 - 368)/36 = 2\)

\(b_{2} = (S_{11}S_{2y} - S_{12}S_{1y})/D = (460 - 352)/36 = 3\)

Step 4 — the intercept and the prediction

\(b_{0} = \bar{y} - b_{1}\bar{x}_{1} - b_{2}\bar{x}_{2} = 16 - 2(3) - 3(3) = 1\), so \(\hat{y} = 1 + 2x_{1} + 3x_{2}\).

At \((6, 4)\): \(\hat{y} = 1 + 12 + 12 = 25\).

Step 5 — check against the full normal equations

With the column of ones, \(X^{T}X = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 15 & 15 \\ 15 & 55 & 53 \\ 15 & 53 & 55 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(X^{T}y = (80, 284, 286)^{T}\). Substituting \(\theta = (1, 2, 3)\): \(5 + 30 + 45 = 80\), \(15 + 110 + 159 = 284\) and \(15 + 106 + 165 = 286\). All three hold.

Answer. \(b_{0} = 1, \ b_{1} = 2, \ b_{2} = 3\); the prediction at \((6, 4)\) is 25.

Comment. Three things to notice. First, the fit is exact here: for the row \((1, 2)\) the model gives \(1 + 2 + 6 = 9\), and likewise for all five rows, so every residual is zero. Second, \(b_{1} = 2\) is a partial effect. A regression of \(y\) on \(x_{1}\) alone has slope \(S_{1y}/S_{11} = 44/10 = 4.4\), more than twice as large, because \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\) rise together (their correlation is \(8/10 = 0.8\)) and the single-variable slope credits \(x_{1}\) with some of what belongs to \(x_{2}\). Third, \(D = S_{11}S_{22}(1 - r^{2}) = 100(1 - 0.64) = 36\); as \(r \to 1\) the determinant \(D \to 0\), which is multicollinearity seen in the arithmetic.

Example 4.12: A quadratic by least squares

Problem. Fit \(y = a_{0} + a_{1}x + a_{2}x^{2}\) to the data below by least squares, and estimate \(y\) at \(x = 6\).

\(x\) 1 2 3 4 5 \(y\) 5 12 23 38 57

Step 1 — the model is linear in \(a\)

Treat \(x\) and \(x^{2}\) as two features alongside the column of ones. The design matrix has columns \(1, x, x^{2}\), and the normal equations \(X^{T}X a = X^{T}y\) apply unchanged. Written out they read

\(n\,a_{0} + (\sum x)\,a_{1} + (\sum x^{2})\,a_{2} = \sum y\)

\((\sum x)\,a_{0} + (\sum x^{2})\,a_{1} + (\sum x^{3})\,a_{2} = \sum xy\)

\((\sum x^{2})\,a_{0} + (\sum x^{3})\,a_{1} + (\sum x^{4})\,a_{2} = \sum x^{2}y\)

Step 2 — the sums

\(x\) \(y\) \(x^{2}\) \(x^{3}\) \(x^{4}\) \(xy\) \(x^{2}y\) 1 5 1 1 1 5 5 2 12 4 8 16 24 48 3 23 9 27 81 69 207 4 38 16 64 256 152 608 5 57 25 125 625 285 1425 \(\sum\) 135 55 225 979 535 2293

with \(n = 5\) and \(\sum x = 15\). The three equations are

\(5a_{0} + 15a_{1} + 55a_{2} = 135 \qquad (1)\)

\(15a_{0} + 55a_{1} + 225a_{2} = 535 \qquad (2)\)

\(55a_{0} + 225a_{1} + 979a_{2} = 2293 \qquad (3)\)

Step 3 — eliminate \(a_{0}\)

\((2) - 3 \times (1)\): \(\ 10a_{1} + 60a_{2} = 130\), so \(a_{1} + 6a_{2} = 13 \qquad (A)\)

\((3) - 11 \times (1)\): \(\ 60a_{1} + 374a_{2} = 808\), so \(30a_{1} + 187a_{2} = 404 \qquad (B)\)

Step 4 — solve for \(a_{2}\), then back-substitute

From (A), \(a_{1} = 13 - 6a_{2}\). Into (B): \(390 - 180a_{2} + 187a_{2} = 404\), so \(7a_{2} = 14\) and \(a_{2} = 2\).

Then \(a_{1} = 13 - 12 = 1\), and from (1): \(5a_{0} + 15 + 110 = 135\), so \(a_{0} = 2\).

Step 5 — check and predict

\(\hat{y} = 2 + x + 2x^{2}\). At \(x = 3\): \(2 + 3 + 18 = 23\), which matches the data, and the other four points match too, so the SSE is zero.

At \(x = 6\): \(\hat{y} = 2 + 6 + 2(36) = 80\).

Answer. \(y = 2 + x + 2x^{2}\); the estimate at \(x = 6\) is 80.

Comment. A quadratic has three parameters and these five points were generated by one, so the fit is perfect. With noisy data a perfect fit would be a warning rather than a triumph: with five points, a quartic has five parameters and would pass through any five points exactly. The sums \(\sum x^{4}\) and \(\sum x^{3}\) also show why powers must be scaled: they grow far faster than \(\sum x\).

docs.title: 4.7 Common mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
Each of the following is a mistake that costs marks in an examination or accuracy in practice.

  • Do not update \(\theta _{0}\) and then use the new value inside the gradient for \(\theta _{1}\). The updates are simultaneous.
  • Do not blame a rising cost on anything but \(\alpha\). If \(J\) increases, \(\alpha\) is too large — nothing else produces that symptom.
  • Do not forget the 1/m in the gradient. Without it the effective learning rate grows with the size of your dataset.
  • Do not use the normal equation when \(n\) is large, and do not be surprised when it fails on duplicated columns — that is \(X^{T}X\) being singular, and it is a diagnosis, not a bug.
  • Do not compare raw coefficient sizes across features on different scales.
  • Do not extrapolate. A line fitted between 1 and 5 hours says nothing about 20 hours, however confidently it computes a number.
  • Do not read a coefficient as a cause. Regression measures association.

docs.title: 4.8 Summary
docs.text:
After working through this chapter you should be able to do the following.

  • Fit a line by least squares from the two sums, check it against \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\), read its slope in the language of the problem, and refuse to extrapolate beyond the data.
  • Write \(J(\theta )\), explain the 1/m and the ½, describe its bowl shape, and say why squaring — not summing, not absolute value — is the default and when it is the wrong default.
  • Run gradient descent by hand with simultaneous updates, diagnose \(\alpha\) from a cost curve without guessing, name the three batch variants, and explain why standardising the features changes the route to the minimum but not the minimum itself.
  • Move to many features in vector form, use the normal equation and say when its \(O(n^{3})\) inversion becomes impossible, and recognise a singular \(X^{T}X\) as redundant columns or \(n > m\) rather than as a bug.

docs.title: 4.9 Exercises
docs.text:
1. \(x = 1, 2, 3, 4\) and \(y = 2, 4, 5, 8\). Fit the least-squares line and predict at \(x = 5\).

    Answer

    \(\bar{x} = 2.5, \ \bar{y} = 4.75\). \(\sum(x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y}) = (-1.5)(-2.75) + (-0.5)(-0.75) + (0.5)(0.25) + (1.5)(3.25) = 9.5\) and \(\sum(x-\bar{x})^{2} = 5\). So \(\theta_{1} = 9.5/5 = 1.9\) and \(\theta_{0} = 4.75 - 1.9(2.5) = 0\) exactly. The line is \(\hat{y} = 1.9x\) and \(\hat{y}(5) = 9.5\).

  2. Show algebraically that the fitted line passes through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\).

    Answer

    At the minimum of \(J = \sum(\theta_{0} + \theta_{1}x_{i} - y_{i})^{2}\) the partial derivative with respect to \(\theta_{0}\) is zero: \(2\sum(\theta_{0} + \theta_{1}x_{i} - y_{i}) = 0\). Expanding, \(m\theta_{0} + \theta_{1}\sum x_{i} - \sum y_{i} = 0\). Dividing by \(m\) gives \(\theta_{0} + \theta_{1}\bar{x} - \bar{y} = 0\), that is \(\bar{y} = \theta_{0} + \theta_{1}\bar{x}\). The left side is the mean of \(y\) and the right side is the line evaluated at \(\bar{x}\), so the point \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\) lies on the line. The same equation says the residuals sum to zero.

  3. With data (1, 3), (2, 5) and \(\theta = (0, 0), \alpha = 0.2\), compute one gradient-descent step.

    Answer

    With \(\theta = (0, 0)\) the predictions are 0, so the errors \(h - y\) are \(-3, -5\) and \(m = 2\).

    \(\partial J/\partial\theta_{0} = (-3 - 5)/2 = -4, \qquad \partial J/\partial\theta_{1} = \left[(-3)(1) + (-5)(2)\right]/2 = -6.5\)

    \(\theta_{0} := 0 - 0.2(-4) = 0.8, \qquad \theta_{1} := 0 - 0.2(-6.5) = 1.3\)

    So \(\theta = (0.8, 1.3)\). (The cost falls from \(J = 8.5\) to \(J = 0.8425\).)

  4. Why does \(J\) for linear regression have exactly one minimum, while \(J\) for a neural network does not? Answer in two sentences.

    Answer

    For linear regression each prediction is a linear function of \(\theta\), so \(J\) is a sum of squares of linear terms: a convex quadratic bowl whose Hessian \(X^{T}X/m\) is positive semi-definite, so any stationary point is the global minimum (and it is a single point whenever \(X^{T}X\) is invertible). In a neural network the prediction is a composition of non-linear functions of the weights, which makes \(J\) non-convex, with many local minima, saddle points and equivalent copies of the same function (for instance by swapping hidden units), so where descent ends depends on where it starts.

  5. A model has 10 features and \(m = 12\) examples. What goes wrong with the normal equation, and name two fixes.

    Answer

    There are \(n + 1 = 11\) parameters (with the intercept) for only 12 rows, so just \(m - n - 1 = 1\) degree of freedom is left over. The model can bend to pass almost exactly through every point: training error is close to zero and the coefficients are unstable, changing wildly if one row changes (overfitting, high variance). \(X^{T}X\) is invertible only if the 11 columns are linearly independent; any near-dependence between columns makes it nearly singular, and with only 10 rows the 11 columns could not be independent at all, so it would be exactly singular and the normal equation would have no unique solution. Fixes: collect more rows, drop or select features (or reduce them with PCA), or add a ridge penalty so that \(X^{T}X + \lambda I\) is invertible and the coefficients are shrunk. Lasso also works and removes features as it fits.

  6. A fitted model is \(\hat{y} = 12 - 0.8x\), where \(x\) is hours of television per day and \(y\) is the exam score out of 100. Interpret the slope and the intercept. A friend concludes that watching less television causes higher marks. Is that justified? What does the model predict at \(x = 15\)?

    Answer

    The slope: each extra hour of television a day is associated with a score \(0.8\) marks lower. The intercept: the predicted score for someone who watches none is 12 out of 100, which is implausibly low and a hint that the model is poorly specified or that the units in the problem are off; it cannot be taken literally. The causal claim is not justified. Regression measures association; students who watch more television may also study less, sleep less or differ in other ways, and the fit cannot separate these. At \(x = 15\) the model gives \(12 - 0.8(15) = 0\), and beyond 15 hours it predicts negative scores, so it must not be extrapolated.

  7. The engine size \(x\) (litres) and fuel efficiency \(y\) (miles per gallon) of four cars are \((1.2, 35), (1.6, 32), (2.0, 28), (2.4, 24)\). Fit the least-squares line, interpret the slope, and predict for a 1.8 litre engine. Compute \(R^{2}\).

    Answer

    \(\bar{x} = 1.8, \ \bar{y} = 29.75\). Deviations of \(x\): \(-0.6, -0.2, 0.2, 0.6\); of \(y\): \(5.25, 2.25, -1.75, -5.75\). \(\sum(x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y}) = -3.15 - 0.45 - 0.35 - 3.45 = -7.4\) and \(\sum(x-\bar{x})^{2} = 0.8\). So \(\theta_{1} = -7.4/0.8 = -9.25\) and \(\theta_{0} = 29.75 + 9.25(1.8) = 46.4\). The line is \(\hat{y} = 46.4 - 9.25x\). Slope: each extra litre of engine size goes with 9.25 fewer miles per gallon. The intercept, 46.4 at zero litres, has no physical meaning. At 1.8 litres: \(46.4 - 16.65 = 29.75\), which equals \(\bar{y}\) because 1.8 is \(\bar{x}\). The residuals are \(-0.3, 0.4, 0.1, -0.2\), so \(\text{SS}_{\text{res}} = 0.09 + 0.16 + 0.01 + 0.04 = 0.30\), \(\text{SS}_{\text{tot}} = 68.75\), and \(R^{2} = 1 - 0.30/68.75 = 0.9956\).

  8. Five houses have bedrooms and cost (in lakh): H-1: 2, 12; H-2: 1, 6; H-3: 3, 14; H-4: 4, 16; H-5: 5, 20. Fit the regression line of cost on bedrooms, using the house label only to identify rows, and predict the cost of a house with 8 bedrooms. Comment on the prediction.

    Answer

    The labels H-1 to H-5 are identifiers, not a numerical feature, so they stay out of the calculation. \(\bar{x} = 3, \ \bar{y} = 13.6\); \(\sum(x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y}) = (-1)(-1.6) + (-2)(-7.6) + 0 + (1)(2.4) + (2)(6.4) = 1.6 + 15.2 + 2.4 + 12.8 = 32\) and \(\sum(x-\bar{x})^{2} = 10\). So \(\theta_{1} = 3.2\) and \(\theta_{0} = 13.6 - 3.2(3) = 4.0\), giving \(\hat{y} = 4.0 + 3.2x\). At 8 bedrooms \(\hat{y} = 4.0 + 25.6 = 29.6\) lakh. The data go only up to 5 bedrooms, so this is an extrapolation of three bedrooms beyond the data and should be treated as a rough guess at best. (\(R^{2} = 0.955\) on the five houses.)

  9. Data \((1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 4)\), starting point \(\theta = (0, 1)\) and \(\alpha = 0.1\). Compute the cost \(J\), both partial derivatives, the updated parameters, and the new cost. Did the cost fall?

    Answer

    With \(\theta = (0, 1)\) the predictions are \(1, 2, 3\), so \(h - y = -1, 0, -1\), and \(m = 3\).

    \(J = \dfrac{1}{6}\left[1 + 0 + 1\right] = 0.3333\)

    \(\partial J/\partial\theta_{0} = (-1 + 0 - 1)/3 = -0.6667, \qquad \partial J/\partial\theta_{1} = \left[(-1)(1) + 0 + (-1)(3)\right]/3 = -1.3333\)

    \(\theta_{0} := 0 + 0.1(0.6667) = 0.0667, \qquad \theta_{1} := 1 + 0.1(1.3333) = 1.1333\)

    New predictions \(1.2, 2.3333, 3.4667\); errors \(-0.8, 0.3333, -0.5333\); \(J = (0.64 + 0.1111 + 0.2844)/6 = 0.1726\). The cost fell from 0.3333 to 0.1726, as it should for a small enough \(\alpha\).

  10. Use the normal equation to fit \(\hat{y} = \theta_{0} + \theta_{1}x\) to \((1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 2), (4, 3)\). Show \(X^{T}X\), \(X^{T}y\) and the inverse, and check the answer with the two-sum formulas.

    Answer

    \(X^{T}X = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 10 \\ 10 & 30 \end{bmatrix}\) since \(\sum x = 10\) and \(\sum x^{2} = 30\); \(X^{T}y = \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ 23 \end{bmatrix}\) since \(\sum y = 8\) and \(\sum xy = 1 + 4 + 6 + 12 = 23\). \(\det = 120 - 100 = 20\), so \((X^{T}X)^{-1} = \frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix} 30 & -10 \\ -10 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(\theta_{0} = (30 \cdot 8 - 10 \cdot 23)/20 = 10/20 = 0.5\) and \(\theta_{1} = (-10 \cdot 8 + 4 \cdot 23)/20 = 12/20 = 0.6\). Check: \(\bar{x} = 2.5, \ \bar{y} = 2\), \(\sum(x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y}) = 3\) and \(\sum(x-\bar{x})^{2} = 5\), so \(\theta_{1} = 0.6\) and \(\theta_{0} = 2 - 0.6(2.5) = 0.5\). The line is \(\hat{y} = 0.5 + 0.6x\).

  11. Predict what happens to batch gradient descent in each case, and why. (a) \(\alpha\) is made 100 times too large. (b) \(\alpha\) is made 100 times too small. (c) Two features differ in scale by a factor of 1000 and are not scaled. (d) \(\theta_{0}\) is updated first and the new value is used in the gradient for \(\theta_{1}\).

    Answer

    (a) The steps overshoot the valley floor by more than they cover, so \(\theta\) oscillates with growing amplitude and \(J\) rises without limit: divergence. (b) It still descends, but each step is 100 times shorter, so it needs about 100 times as many iterations; the cost curve falls but is nearly flat. (c) The cost contours become a long narrow ravine. The gradient points mostly across the ravine, so descent zig-zags between the walls; \(\alpha\) must be small enough for the steep direction, which makes progress along the shallow direction very slow. The remedy is to standardise first. (d) The gradient for \(\theta_{1}\) is then evaluated at a point the algorithm has already left, so the step is not the steepest-descent step for \(J\) and the usual guarantee (a small enough \(\alpha\) always lowers \(J\)) no longer applies as stated. Both gradients must be computed from the old \(\theta\) and then both parameters assigned together.

  12. True or false, with a one-line reason. (a) The normal equation requires the features to be scaled. (b) Every update of batch gradient descent uses all \(m\) training examples. (c) If \(J\) rises from one iteration to the next, the learning rate is too large (or the sign of the update is wrong). (d) Polynomial regression is not a linear model, because the curve it draws is not a line. (e) The residuals of a least-squares line with an intercept always sum to zero. (f) Stochastic gradient descent with a fixed \(\alpha\) settles exactly at the minimum.

    Answer

    (a) False: it solves for \(\theta\) exactly in one step, so the answer does not depend on the scale (scaling matters for gradient descent and for penalties). (b) True: that is what makes it batch. (c) True: for a convex cost and a correct gradient, a rise means the steps overshoot. (d) False: it is linear in the parameters, which is all linear regression requires; the extra columns \(x^{2}, x^{3}, \ldots\) are just more features. (e) True: it is the first normal equation, \(\sum(y_{i} - \hat{y}_{i}) = 0\). (f) False: each update uses one example, so the path is noisy and keeps jittering around the minimum unless \(\alpha\) is reduced as training proceeds.

  13. A training set has \(m = 1200\) examples. How many parameter updates does one epoch consist of for batch gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent and mini-batch gradient descent with a batch size of 32? Why do practitioners usually choose mini-batches?

    Answer

    An epoch is one full pass through the data. Batch: 1 update per epoch (one step from the gradient over all 1200 examples). Stochastic: 1200 updates, one per example. Mini-batch of 32: \(1200/32 = 37.5\), that is 37 full batches and one final batch of 16, so 38 updates if the last partial batch is kept and 37 if it is dropped. Mini-batches are the practical compromise: each step is much cheaper than a full pass, the gradient is far less noisy than from a single example, and the arithmetic suits vectorised hardware. The batch size is itself a hyper-parameter.

  14. Five students have proficiency-test scores \(x = 95, 85, 80, 70, 60\) and course performance \(y = 85, 95, 70, 65, 70\). Fit the least-squares line and predict \(y\) for \(x = 90\). Then: two cost-versus-iteration curves are drawn for gradient descent on this problem. One falls steeply during the first few iterations and flattens early; the other falls slowly and is still falling after 100 iterations. Which curve belongs to the larger learning rate?

    Answer

    \(\bar{x} = 78, \ \bar{y} = 77\). \(\sum(x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y}) = (17)(8) + (7)(18) + (2)(-7) + (-8)(-12) + (-18)(-7) = 136 + 126 - 14 + 96 + 126 = 470\) and \(\sum(x-\bar{x})^{2} = 289 + 49 + 4 + 64 + 324 = 730\). So \(\theta_{1} = 470/730 = 0.6438\) and \(\theta_{0} = 77 - 0.6438(78) = 26.78\), giving \(\hat{y} = 26.78 + 0.6438x\) and \(\hat{y}(90) = 84.73\). (\(R^{2} = 0.48\), so the test score is only a modest predictor.) The curve that falls steeply and flattens early belongs to the larger learning rate, because larger steps cover more of the distance per iteration; the slowly falling curve belongs to the smaller one. The statement holds only while the larger rate is still below the stability limit: a rate that is too large would show a cost that oscillates or rises, not a smooth steep fall.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Logistic Regression and Multi-class Classification
docs.text: Naive Bayes counts; logistic regression fits. It keeps the straight-line score of linear regression and bends only the output, into a number between 0 and 1 that can be read as a probability. This chapter builds the model from the sigmoid and the log-loss, shows how gradient descent trains it, and then extends it from two classes to many, through the one-vs-rest and one-vs-one wrappers and through softmax regression.

docs.title: 8.1 Logistic regression
docs.text:
Why not just fit a straight line to a target that is 0 or 1? Because the line does not stop: it predicts 1.4 for a large \(x\) and −0.3 for a small one, and neither is a probability. Worse, a single far-away point drags the line and moves the boundary even though it was already being classified correctly.

The fix is to pass the linear score through a squashing function that maps the whole real line into (0, 1). The linear part stays exactly as it was; only the output is bent into shape.

\[ h_{\theta }(x) = \sigma (\theta ^{T}x) = 1 / (1 + e^{-\theta ^{T}x}) \]

the sigmoid, or logistic, function — the output is read as \(P(y = 1 \mid x)\)

Figure 8.1. The sigmoid maps every real number into (0, 1), passing through 0.5 at z = 0, and its derivative (lower curve) peaks at one quarter. The decision boundary is the straight line where the score is zero; the sigmoid only controls how confidence grows away from it. Figure 8.2. A logistic curve fitted to pass/fail outcomes against hours of revision. The decision boundary is where the curve crosses 0.5 (the vertical line); the dashes are the individual errors.

Definition: Log-loss (binary cross-entropy)

\(J(\theta ) =\) −(1/m) \(\sum\) [ \(y\) log \(h(x) + (1 - y) \log(1 - h(x))\) ]

Only one term is ever active: for \(y = 1\) the cost is −log \(h\), and for \(y = 0\) it is −log(1 \(- h\)).

Figure 8.3. The log-loss when the true label is 1, against the predicted probability. Predicting 0.9 costs 0.105, total ignorance (0.5) costs 0.693, and the cost grows without limit as the prediction goes to zero: confidence has to be earned.

Two reasons this cost and not squared error. It is convex in \(\theta\) — squared error on top of a sigmoid is not, and gradient descent can get trapped in a local minimum. And its gradient is remarkably clean:

\[ \partial J/\partial \theta _{j} = (1/m) \sum (h(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}) x_{j}^{(i)} \]

identical in form to linear regression — only \(h\) has changed

Odds and log-odds

Rearranging the sigmoid gives log[p/(1−p)] \(= \theta ^{T}x\). So logistic regression is a linear model of the log-odds, and a coefficient \(\theta _{j}\) means: a one-unit rise in \(x_{j}\) multiplies the odds by \(e^{\theta j}\). That is how the coefficients are reported in medicine and economics, where they are called odds ratios, and it is why the model remains popular despite being the simplest thing in this unit.

# logistic regression, with the two outputs that matter kept apart
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

proba = clf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]        # the score
pred  = (proba >= 0.5).astype(int)          # the decision — a separate choice

# the coefficients are log-odds; exponentiate them to get odds ratios
w = clf[-1].coef_[0]
print(np.exp(w).round(3))                   # "one sd more of this multiplies the odds by..."

Two details worth knowing. sklearn's C is the inverse of \(\lambda\), so a small \(C\) means strong regularisation — the opposite of the convention in Unit 3. And logistic regression is regularised by default, which is why the scaler is not optional here.

For more than two classes the same model is widened rather than replaced — the next section but one does that properly, and it turns out to need no new ideas at all.

Example 8.1: Deriving \(\sigma '(z)\) and the logistic gradient

Problem. Two results carry the whole of logistic regression and half of back-propagation: \(\sigma '(z) = \sigma (z)(1 - \sigma (z))\), and \(\partial J/\partial \theta _{j} = (1/m)\sum (h(x_{i}) - y_{i})x_{\text{ij}}\). Both are short.

Step 1 — differentiate the sigmoid

\(\sigma (z) = (1 + e^{-z})^{-1}\). By the chain rule, with the outer derivative of \(u^{-1}\) being \(-u^{-2}\) and the inner derivative of \(e^{-z}\) being \(-e^{-z}\):

\(\sigma '(z) =\) −(1 \(+ e^{-z})^{-2} \cdot (-e^{-z}) = e^{-z} / (1 + e^{-z})^{2}\)

Step 2 — recognise the two factors

Split the fraction deliberately:

\(\sigma '(z) = [1/(1 + e^{-z})] \cdot [e^{-z}/(1 + e^{-z})]\)

The first bracket is \(\sigma (z)\). For the second, add and subtract 1 in the numerator: \(e^{-z} = (1 + e^{-z}) - 1\), so the bracket is \(1 - 1/(1 + e^{-z}) = 1 - \sigma (z)\).

\(\sigma '(z) = \sigma (z)(1 - \sigma (z))\) — the derivative expressed entirely in terms of the output, which is why an implementation never needs to keep \(z\).

Step 3 — differentiate the log-loss

For one example, \(L =\) −[y ln \(h + (1 - y) \ln(1 - h)\)] with \(h = \sigma (z)\) and \(z = \theta ^{T}x\). Differentiate with respect to \(h\) first:

\(\partial L/\partial h =\) −y/h \(+ (1 - y)/(1 - h) = (h - y) / [h(1 - h)]\)

(put the two fractions over the common denominator \(h(1 - h)\) and the numerator collapses to \(h - y\)).

Step 4 — chain it through

\(\partial L/\partial \theta _{j} = (\partial L/\partial h)(\partial h/\partial z)(\partial z/\partial \theta _{j})\), and the three factors are

\((h - y)/[h(1 - h)] \times h(1 - h) \times x_{j}\)

The middle factor — which is \(\sigma '\) from step 2 — cancels the denominator exactly. That cancellation is not luck: log-loss is the loss for which it happens, which is one reason it is the loss we use.

Answer. \(\sigma '(z) = \sigma (z)(1 - \sigma (z))\) and \(\partial J/\partial \theta _{j} = (1/m) \sum (h(x_{i}) - y_{i}) x_{\text{ij}}\)

Comment. Compare the second result with the linear-regression gradient in Unit 3: identical in form, with \(h\) changed from \(\theta ^{T}x\) to \(\sigma (\theta ^{T}x)\). One optimiser serves both. And \(\sigma '\) has a maximum of 0.25 at \(z = 0\) — the number that later explains why deep sigmoid networks stop learning.

docs.title: 8.2 More than two classes
docs.text: Everything so far has answered yes or no. Most real problems do not: a digit is one of ten, an iris one of three, a support ticket one of forty. There are two honest ways to get there. Either build several two-class models and combine their answers, which needs no new mathematics at all, or widen the model so it produces one score per class and turn those scores into probabilities in one step. The second is softmax, and it is not a new algorithm — it is logistic regression with more than two outputs.

docs.title: Combining binary classifiers
docs.text: One-vs-rest (OvR) One-vs-one (OvO) Train \(c\) classifiers: class \(k\) against everything else. Train c(c−1)/2 classifiers, one per pair. Predict the class whose classifier scores highest. Every classifier votes; the class with most votes wins. \(c\) fits, each on the whole dataset. Many more fits, but each sees only two classes' worth of data. Every sub-problem is imbalanced by construction — one class against c−1. Cheaper overall when training cost grows faster than linearly with \(m\) — which is why SVC uses it. The \(c\) scores come from separate models, so comparing them is not entirely principled. Each sub-problem is balanced and usually easier. sklearn default for LogisticRegression(multi_class=“ovr”), Perceptron, SGDClassifier. 10 classes \(\to 45\) classifiers, so prediction is slower.

docs.title: Softmax regression
docs.text:
The direct route. Keep one weight vector per class, so the model produces \(c\) scores \(z_{k} = \theta _{k}^{T}x\), and convert them into probabilities that are positive and sum to one.

\[ P(y = k \mid x) = e^{z_{k}} / \sum _{j} e^{z_{j}} \]

the softmax function; \(z_{k} = \theta _{k}^{T}x\) is the score for class \(k\)

Why exponentiate rather than simply divide each score by the total? Because scores can be negative, and a negative probability is not one. The exponential sends every real number to a positive one first, so the ratios are always valid. It also makes the answer depend only on the differences between the scores, which is what the figure below is built to show.

Figure 8.4. Softmax turns three scores into three probabilities that sum to one. Adding the same constant to every score changes nothing, because only differences carry information.

Definition: Categorical cross-entropy

With the target written as a one-hot vector y (a 1 at the true class, zeros elsewhere),

\(L = - \sum _{k} y_{k}\) ln \(p_{k} = -\) ln \(p_{\text{true}}\)

Every term but one is multiplied by zero, so the sum collapses to a single logarithm: the cost is how surprised the model was by the right answer.

Example 8.2: Deriving the softmax gradient, and why binary logistic regression is a special case

Problem. Two claims: \(\partial L/\partial z_{k} = p_{k} - y_{k}\), the same (prediction \(-\) truth) shape as everywhere else in this course; and softmax with \(c = 2\) is the sigmoid.

Step 1 — differentiate the softmax itself

Write \(S = \sum _{j} e^{z_{j}}\), so \(p_{i} = e^{z_{i}}/S\). Differentiating with the quotient rule gives two cases, because \(z_{k}\) appears in the numerator only when \(i = k\), but in the denominator always:

\(\partial p_{i}/\partial z_{k} = p_{i}(1 - p_{i})\) if \(i = k\), and \(-p_{i}p_{k}\) otherwise.

Both cases are \(p_{i}(\delta _{\text{ik}} - p_{k})\), where \(\delta\) is 1 when the indices match and 0 when they do not.

Step 2 — chain it through the loss

\(L = -\sum _{i} y_{i}\) ln \(p_{i}\), so \(\partial L/\partial p_{i} = -y_{i}/p_{i}\), and

\(\partial L/\partial z_{k} = \sum _{i} (-y_{i}/p_{i}) \cdot p_{i}(\delta _{\text{ik}} - p_{k}) = -\sum _{i} y_{i}(\delta _{\text{ik}} - p_{k})\)

The \(p_{i}\) cancels — the same cancellation that made binary log-loss so clean.

Step 3 — collapse the sum

Split it: \(-\sum _{i} y_{i}\delta _{\text{ik}} + p_{k} \sum _{i} y_{i}\). The first sum picks out \(y_{k}\); the second is 1, because a one-hot vector sums to one. So

\(\partial L/\partial z_{k} = p_{k} - y_{k}\), and by the chain rule \(\partial L/\partial \theta _{k} = (p_{k} - y_{k})x\).

Step 4 — put \(c = 2\)

\(p_{1} = e^{z_{1}}/(e^{z_{1}} + e^{z_{2}})\). Divide numerator and denominator by \(e^{z_{1}}\):

\(p_{1} = 1/(1 + e^{-(z_{1} - z_{2})}) = \sigma (z_{1} - z_{2})\)

Two-class softmax is the sigmoid applied to the difference of the two scores. It also shows the model is over-parameterised — only \(z_{1} - z_{2}\) matters, so one of the two weight vectors is redundant, which is exactly why the binary model keeps just one.

Answer. \(\partial L/\partial z_{k} = p_{k} - y_{k}\); and softmax with two classes is \(\sigma (z_{1} - z_{2})\)

Comment. Line up the three gradients from this course: \((h - y)x\) for linear regression, \((h - y)x\) for logistic regression, and \((p - y)x\) here. One optimiser, three models. That is not a coincidence — it is what happens when each loss is chosen to match its output distribution.

docs.title: A straight line and an S-curve on the same data
docs.text:
The opening argument of this chapter is easy to state and easier to believe when it is drawn. In the figure, ten students are plotted as 0 (failed) or 1 (passed) against hours studied. The least-squares straight line is forced to leave the interval from 0 to 1 at both ends, and since a "probability" of 1.3 or \(-0.2\) means nothing, the line can only be used by chopping its ends off by hand. The S-curve flattens at 0 and at 1 by construction, and passes through 0.5 where the data change from mostly failing to mostly passing.

Figure 8.5. A straight line (linear regression) and an S-curve (logistic regression) fitted to the same pass/fail data. The shaded bands mark values that cannot be probabilities; only the S-curve stays out of them.

docs.title: Maximum likelihood: why log-loss is the natural cost
docs.text:
The log-loss was introduced as a cost with pleasant properties, but it can be derived rather than chosen. Suppose the model assigns the probability \(p_i = h_\theta(x^{(i)})\) to class 1 for example \(i\). The probability it gives to the label actually observed is \(p_i\) when \(y^{(i)} = 1\) and \(1 - p_i\) when \(y^{(i)} = 0\), which can be written in one expression as \(p_i^{\,y^{(i)}}(1 - p_i)^{1 - y^{(i)}}\). If the examples are independent, the probability that the model assigns to the whole set of observed labels is the product, the likelihood:

\[ L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{m} p_i^{\,y^{(i)}}(1 - p_i)^{1 - y^{(i)}} \]

Maximum likelihood estimation chooses the \(\theta\) that makes the data most probable under the model. A product of many numbers below 1 is awkward to work with and underflows on a computer, so we maximise its logarithm instead, which has the same maximiser because the logarithm is increasing. Negating turns the maximisation into a minimisation:

\[ -\ln L(\theta) = -\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bigl[\,y^{(i)}\ln p_i + (1 - y^{(i)})\ln(1 - p_i)\,\bigr] = m\,J(\theta) \]

So the log-loss cost \(J(\theta)\) is the negative log-likelihood divided by \(m\). Minimising log-loss and maximising likelihood are one and the same, which is the deepest reason for using it. Squared error has no such justification here: it is the negative log-likelihood of a model with Gaussian errors, which is the wrong noise model for a 0/1 label. There is no closed-form solution for the maximising \(\theta\), which is why logistic regression is trained iteratively, by gradient descent or by a quasi-Newton method such as L-BFGS.

docs.title: Regularised logistic regression
docs.text:
Logistic regression overfits in the same way that linear regression does, and for data that can be separated perfectly it does so in an extreme manner. If a straight line splits the two classes with no error, the likelihood can always be increased by making the S-curve steeper, so the best weights are infinitely large: gradient descent never stops growing them. (On the four-point data of the gradient descent example, \(\theta_1\) has already grown from 0.31 after two iterations to about 4.0 after two thousand and is still rising.) The cure is the one from Unit 3, a penalty on the size of the weights:

\[ J_{\text{ridge}}(\theta) = J(\theta) + \frac{\lambda}{2m}\sum_{j \ge 1}\theta_j^{2}, \qquad J_{\text{lasso}}(\theta) = J(\theta) + \frac{\lambda}{m}\sum_{j \ge 1}|\theta_j| \]

The sum starts at \(j = 1\): the intercept is not penalised. The gradient of the ridge cost changes only slightly, each weight gaining an extra term \(\frac{\lambda}{m}\theta_j\) that pulls it towards zero at every step. As \(\lambda \to 0\) the plain model returns, with low bias and high variance. As \(\lambda \to \infty\) every weight is squeezed to zero and the model predicts the same probability, the overall class fraction, for everybody: high bias and under-fitting. The lasso penalty can set weights exactly to zero, so it also performs feature selection.

Scikit-learn exposes this through the inverse parameter \(C = 1/\lambda\). On the four-point data (hours 1, 2, 4, 5 with results 0, 0, 1, 1), an L2-regularised fit gives:

\(C\) \(\theta_1\) \(P(\text{pass})\) at 1 h \(P(\text{pass})\) at 5 h 100 3.945 0.0004 0.9996 1 1.007 0.118 0.882 0.1 0.241 0.382 0.618 0.01 0.029 0.485 0.515

In every row the boundary is at 3 hours, because the data are symmetric about it, so regularisation does not move the boundary here at all. What it changes is the confidence: a strongly regularised model hedges, which is exactly what one should want from a model fitted to four students. Choose \(\lambda\) (or \(C\)) by cross-validation, as for any other hyper-parameter.

docs.title: Curved boundaries from a linear model
docs.text:
The decision boundary of logistic regression is always the hyperplane \(\theta^T x = 0\), so on the raw features it cannot separate a ring of one class from the points inside. The remedy is to add features, not to change the model: the model is linear in the parameters, and nothing requires the features to be the raw measurements. Take the features \((1,\ x_1,\ x_2,\ x_1^2,\ x_2^2)\) and the weights \(\theta = (4, 0, 0, -1, -1)\). Then

\[ z = 4 - x_1^{2} - x_2^{2} \]

and the boundary \(z = 0\) is the circle \(x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 4\) of radius 2. The point \((1, 1)\) has \(z = 2\) and \(p = 0.881\), inside, class 1; the point \((2, 2)\) has \(z = -4\) and \(p = 0.018\), outside, class 0. The boundary is a line in the five-dimensional feature space and a circle in the original plane. Products such as \(x_1 x_2\) tilt the ellipse. This is the idea that the support vector machine, later in this unit, automates with kernels, so that one does not have to write the extra features out.

docs.title: 8.4 Worked examples
docs.text:
The examples below work through the calculations of this chapter in full. Try each one on paper before reading the steps.

Example 8.3: Logistic regression, end to end on one example

Problem. A model has \(w = (0.8, -1.2)\) and \(b = 0.5\). Classify \(x = (2, 1)\), compute the log-loss if the true label is 1, and then give one gradient-descent update for \(w_{1}\) with \(\alpha = 0.1\).

Step 1 — the linear score

\(z = 0.8(2) +\) (−1.2)(1) \(+ 0.5 = 1.6 - 1.2 + 0.5 = 0.9\)

Step 2 — the probability

\(\sigma (0.9) = 1/(1 + e^{-0.9}) = 1/(1 + 0.4066) = 0.7109\)

\(0.711 \ge 0.5\), so predict class 1. Note that this follows from \(z \ge 0\) alone; the sigmoid was only needed for the probability.

Step 3 — the loss

\(y = 1\), so \(L =\) −ln(0.7109) \(= 0.3413\). For comparison, a hedged prediction of 0.5 would have cost 0.693, so being right and reasonably confident has halved the penalty.

Step 4 — the update

\(\partial L/\partial w_{1} = (h - y)x_{1} = (0.7109 - 1)(2) =\) (−0.2891)(2) \(= -0.5782\)

\(w_{1}\) := \(0.8 - 0.1(-0.5782) = 0.8 + 0.0578 = 0.8578\)

The weight increased, because the model was under-confident about a positive example with a positive \(x_{1}\). The next prediction for this example will be a little higher.

Answer. \(z = 0.9, p = 0.711\), predict 1, loss \(0.341, w_{1} \to 0.858\)

Example 8.4: Reading a fitted model: probability, boundary, odds and a target probability

Problem. A college has fitted \(z = -4 + 0.8h\), where \(h\) is the number of hours a student studied, and passes a student when \(P(\text{pass}) = \sigma(z) \ge 0.5\). (a) Find the probability of passing for \(h = 6\) and for \(h = 3\). (b) Where is the decision boundary? (c) By what factor does each extra hour multiply the odds of passing? (d) How many hours give a 90% chance of passing?

Step 1 — score and squash (part a)

For \(h = 6\): \(z = -4 + 0.8(6) = -4 + 4.8 = 0.8\), and \(e^{-0.8} = 0.4493\), so

\[ p = \frac{1}{1 + 0.4493} = \frac{1}{1.4493} = 0.690 \]

For \(h = 3\): \(z = -4 + 2.4 = -1.6\), \(e^{1.6} = 4.9530\), so \(p = 1/(1 + 4.9530) = 0.168\). Six hours predicts a pass at 69%; three hours predicts a fail with only a 17% chance of passing.

Step 2 — the boundary (part b)

\(\sigma(z) \ge 0.5\) exactly when \(z \ge 0\), so the boundary is \(-4 + 0.8h = 0\), that is \(h = 5\) hours. The sigmoid is not needed to find it.

Step 3 — odds (part c)

Because \(\ln\frac{p}{1-p} = z\), the odds are \(e^{z}\), and one more hour adds \(0.8\) to \(z\):

\[ \frac{\text{odds}(h+1)}{\text{odds}(h)} = \frac{e^{z + 0.8}}{e^{z}} = e^{0.8} = 2.2255 \]

Check against Step 1: at \(h = 5\) the odds are \(e^{0} = 1\) (even money), and at \(h = 6\) they are \(0.690/0.310 = 2.23\).

Step 4 — run the model backwards (part d)

A probability of 0.9 means odds of \(0.9/0.1 = 9\), so \(z = \ln 9 = 2.1972\). Then

\[ -4 + 0.8h = 2.1972 \;\Rightarrow\; h = \frac{6.1972}{0.8} = 7.75 \text{ hours} \]

Answer. \(p(6) = 0.690\) (pass), \(p(3) = 0.168\) (fail); boundary at 5 hours; each hour multiplies the odds by 2.23; about 7.75 hours for a 90% chance.

Comment. The effect on the odds is constant, the effect on the probability is not. From 5 to 6 hours the probability rises by 0.19 (0.50 to 0.69); from 7 to 8 hours it rises by only 0.085 (0.832 to 0.917). The log-odds is the scale on which the model is linear.

Example 8.5: Log-loss on four predictions, and the likelihood behind it

Problem. A spam filter gives these probabilities of "spam" to four e-mails.

E-mail True label \(y\) Predicted \(p\) E1 1 (spam) 0.9 E2 1 (spam) 0.7 E3 0 (not spam) 0.2 E4 0 (not spam) 0.6

Compute the loss of each e-mail and the average loss, say which e-mail hurts most, and relate the total to the likelihood of the four labels.

Step 1 — the probability given to the truth

Log-loss is \(-\ln\) of the probability the model assigned to the correct answer: \(p\) when \(y = 1\), and \(1 - p\) when \(y = 0\).

E-mail Probability given to the truth Loss \(= -\ln(\cdot)\) E1 \(0.9\) \(0.1054\) E2 \(0.7\) \(0.3567\) E3 \(1 - 0.2 = 0.8\) \(0.2231\) E4 \(1 - 0.6 = 0.4\) \(0.9163\)

Step 2 — total and average

\(0.1054 + 0.3567 + 0.2231 + 0.9163 = 1.6015\), so the average loss is \(1.6015/4 = 0.4004\).

Step 3 — the worst offender

E4 contributes \(0.9163/1.6015 = 57\%\) of the total although it is one e-mail in four. It is a genuine message that the model leaned towards calling spam, so the truth received only 0.4.

Step 4 — the link with likelihood

The probability that the model assigned to all four observed labels together is the product

\[ L = 0.9 \times 0.7 \times 0.8 \times 0.4 = 0.2016, \qquad -\ln L = 1.6015 \]

which is exactly the total loss. Minimising the sum of log-losses and maximising the likelihood are the same act, because \(-\ln\) turns a product into a sum.

Answer. Losses \(0.1054,\ 0.3567,\ 0.2231,\ 0.9163\); average \(0.4004\); E4 hurts most; \(L = 0.2016\) and \(-\ln L = 1.6015\).

Comment. Loss is lopsided on purpose. A prediction of 0.4 for the truth costs 0.92, but 0.01 would cost \(-\ln 0.01 = 4.61\), five times as much. The model is charged for being loudly wrong, not merely for being wrong.

Example 8.6: Two iterations of batch gradient descent

Problem. Four students studied \(x = 1, 2, 4, 5\) hours and had results \(y = 0, 0, 1, 1\) (1 = pass). Fit \(h(x) = \sigma(\theta_0 + \theta_1 x)\) by batch gradient descent from \(\theta_0 = \theta_1 = 0\) with \(\alpha = 0.5\). Do two iterations, report the cost each time, and predict the result for 3 hours.

Step 1 — the starting cost

With \(\theta = (0, 0)\) every score is 0 and every \(h = \sigma(0) = 0.5\), so each of the four losses is \(-\ln 0.5\):

\(J = \ln 2 = 0.6931\)

Step 2 — iteration 1

The error is \(e = h - y\), and the gradients are \(\frac{1}{4}\sum e\) and \(\frac{1}{4}\sum e\,x\).

\(x\) \(y\) \(z\) \(h\) \(e = h - y\) \(e \cdot x\) 1 0 0 0.5 0.5 0.5 2 0 0 0.5 0.5 1.0 4 1 0 0.5 \(-0.5\) \(-2.0\) 5 1 0 0.5 \(-0.5\) \(-2.5\) Sum \(0\) \(-3.0\)

\(\partial J/\partial\theta_0 = 0/4 = 0\) and \(\partial J/\partial\theta_1 = -3/4 = -0.75\). Updating simultaneously:

\(\theta_0 = 0 - 0.5(0) = 0\), \(\theta_1 = 0 - 0.5(-0.75) = 0.375\), and the new cost is \(J = 0.5948\).

Step 3 — iteration 2, with \(\theta = (0, 0.375)\)

\(x\) \(y\) \(z\) \(h\) \(e = h - y\) \(e \cdot x\) 1 0 0.375 0.5927 0.5927 0.5927 2 0 0.750 0.6792 0.6792 1.3584 4 1 1.500 0.8176 \(-0.1824\) \(-0.7297\) 5 1 1.875 0.8670 \(-0.1330\) \(-0.6648\) Sum \(0.9565\) \(0.5565\)

\(\partial J/\partial\theta_0 = 0.9565/4 = 0.2391\) and \(\partial J/\partial\theta_1 = 0.5565/4 = 0.1391\), so

\(\theta_0 = 0 - 0.5(0.2391) = -0.1196\), \(\theta_1 = 0.375 - 0.5(0.1391) = 0.3054\), and \(J = 0.5662\).

Step 4 — predict for 3 hours

\(z = -0.1196 + 0.3054(3) = 0.7966\), so \(p = \sigma(0.7966) \approx 0.689\): predict a pass.

Answer. \(\theta = (-0.1196,\ 0.3054)\) after two iterations; cost \(0.6931 \to 0.5948 \to 0.5662\); \(P(\text{pass} \mid 3\text{ h}) \approx 0.689\).

Comment. The cost falls at every step, so \(\alpha\) is suitable. The first step moved only \(\theta_1\), because at \(\theta = 0\) the errors on the two classes cancel in the bias gradient. The data are perfectly separable, so left to run indefinitely \(\theta_1\) keeps growing: the S-curve gets steeper and the cost creeps towards zero without ever reaching it. Regularisation, described later in this chapter, is what stops that.

Example 8.7: Reading a coefficient table: odds ratios

Problem. A hospital reports a logistic regression for the risk of a heart event within ten years.

Feature Coding Coefficient Intercept \(-5.0\) Age years \(\div\) 10 \(+0.4\) Smoker 1 = yes, 0 = no \(+1.2\) BMI BMI \(\div\) 10 \(+0.9\)

A patient is 50 years old, a smoker, with BMI 30. (a) Find the risk. (b) Find the odds. (c) What is the odds ratio for smoking? (d) Verify it by recomputing the patient as a non-smoker.

Step 1 — encode and score (part a)

Age \(= 50/10 = 5\), smoker \(= 1\), BMI \(= 30/10 = 3\).

\(z = -5.0 + 0.4(5) + 1.2(1) + 0.9(3) = -5.0 + 2.0 + 1.2 + 2.7 = 0.9\)

\(p = 1/(1 + e^{-0.9}) = 1/(1 + 0.4066) = 0.711\), a 71% risk.

Step 2 — odds (part b)

\(\text{odds} = p/(1 - p) = 0.7109/0.2891 = 2.46\), which equals \(e^{0.9} = 2.4596\) as it must.

Step 3 — odds ratios (part c)

The odds ratio of a feature is \(e^{\text{coefficient}}\).

Feature Coefficient Odds ratio Reading Age 0.4 \(e^{0.4} = 1.49\) each extra 10 years multiplies the odds by about 1.49 Smoker 1.2 \(e^{1.2} = 3.32\) smoking multiplies the odds by about 3.32 BMI 0.9 \(e^{0.9} = 2.46\) each 10 BMI points multiplies the odds by about 2.46

Step 4 — verify for smoking (part d)

As a non-smoker \(z' = -5.0 + 2.0 + 0 + 2.7 = -0.3\), so \(p' = 1/(1 + e^{0.3}) = 1/(1 + 1.3499) = 0.4256\) and the odds are \(0.4256/0.5744 = 0.7408\). Then

\[ \frac{2.4596}{0.7408} = 3.3201 = e^{1.2} \]

Answer. Risk \(0.711\), odds \(2.46\), odds ratio for smoking \(3.32\); the non-smoker version has risk \(0.426\) and odds \(0.741\).

Comment. An odds ratio is not a probability ratio. Smoking multiplied this patient's odds by 3.32, but the risk only went from 0.426 to 0.711, a factor of 1.67. Quoting "smoking more than triples the risk" from this table is the commonest misreading of logistic regression output, and it is wrong, most of all when the baseline risk is already high.

Example 8.8: Three classes with one-vs-rest, and what softmax would do

Problem. A fruit sorter has two features, redness \(x_1\) and length \(x_2\), and three one-vs-rest logistic models \(P(\text{class} \mid x) = \sigma(\theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1 + \theta_2 x_2)\).

Model \(\theta_0\) \(\theta_1\) \(\theta_2\) Apple \(-1\) \(1.5\) \(-0.5\) Banana \(0.5\) \(-1\) \(1\) Orange \(-2\) \(0.5\) \(1.5\)

(a) Classify the fruit \(x = (2, 1)\). (b) Rescale the three outputs to sum to 1. (c) How many binary models would one-vs-one need for 3 classes and for 10?

Step 1 — score each model (part a)

Apple: \(z = -1 + 1.5(2) - 0.5(1) = 1.5\), \(\sigma(1.5) = 0.8176\)

Banana: \(z = 0.5 - 1(2) + 1(1) = -0.5\), \(\sigma(-0.5) = 0.3775\)

Orange: \(z = -2 + 0.5(2) + 1.5(1) = 0.5\), \(\sigma(0.5) = 0.6225\)

The highest probability is Apple's, so the fruit is classified as apple.

Step 2 — normalise (part b)

The three outputs sum to \(0.8176 + 0.3775 + 0.6225 = 1.8176\), not 1, because each model was trained separately and answers its own yes-or-no question. Dividing each by the sum:

Apple \(0.8176/1.8176 = 0.450\), Banana \(0.3775/1.8176 = 0.208\), Orange \(0.6225/1.8176 = 0.342\)

Step 3 — count the models (part c)

One-vs-rest needs \(c\) models: 3 and 10. One-vs-one needs \(c(c-1)/2\): \(3 \cdot 2/2 = 3\) and \(10 \cdot 9/2 = 45\).

Answer. Apple (0.8176 against 0.3775 and 0.6225); normalised 0.450, 0.208, 0.342; one-vs-one needs 3 models for 3 classes and 45 for 10.

Comment. Softmax applied to the same three scores gives a different, properly constructed distribution: \(e^{1.5}, e^{-0.5}, e^{0.5} = 4.482,\ 0.607,\ 1.649\) with sum \(6.737\), so \(0.665,\ 0.090,\ 0.245\). The ranking is the same, but the numbers differ from the rescaled one-vs-rest outputs because softmax compares the scores themselves, not three separately squashed probabilities. (These weights were not trained under softmax, so this is only an illustration of the arithmetic.)

docs.title: 8.5 Common mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
Each of the following is a mistake that costs marks in an examination or accuracy in practice.

  • Do not fit a straight line to a 0/1 target and call it classification. The outputs are not probabilities and the cost is non-convex once you squash them.

docs.title: 8.6 Summary
docs.text:
After working through this chapter you should be able to do the following.

  • Derive logistic regression as a squashed linear model, explain why log-loss replaces squared error on both convexity and gradient grounds, locate the boundary at \(\theta ^{T}x = 0\), and read a coefficient as a log-odds ratio.

docs.title: 8.7 Exercises
docs.text:
1. \(w = (1, -1), b = 0\). Give the predicted probability and class for \(x = (3, 1)\).

    Answer

    \(z = 1(3) + (-1)(1) + 0 = 2\), so \(p = \sigma(2) = 1/(1 + e^{-2}) = 1/(1 + 0.1353) = 0.881\). Since \(0.881 \ge 0.5\) (equivalently \(z \ge 0\)), the class is 1.

  2. Show that \(\sigma '(z) = \sigma (z)(1 - \sigma (z))\), and state the maximum value of \(\sigma '\).

    Answer

    Write \(\sigma(z) = (1 + e^{-z})^{-1}\). The chain rule gives \(\sigma'(z) = -(1 + e^{-z})^{-2}\cdot(-e^{-z}) = \dfrac{e^{-z}}{(1 + e^{-z})^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\cdot\dfrac{e^{-z}}{1 + e^{-z}}\). The first factor is \(\sigma(z)\). For the second, \(e^{-z} = (1 + e^{-z}) - 1\), so it equals \(1 - \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} = 1 - \sigma(z)\). Hence \(\sigma' = \sigma(1 - \sigma)\). The product \(p(1-p)\) is largest at \(p = 0.5\), which is \(z = 0\), where \(\sigma' = 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\). This is the maximum, and it is why a sigmoid shrinks every gradient passing through it by at least a factor of four.

  3. A logistic model has \(\theta = (\theta_0, \theta_1, \theta_2) = (1, 2, -1)\). For the input \(x = (x_1, x_2) = (1, 4)\) compute \(z\), the probability of class 1, the predicted class at threshold 0.5, and write the equation of the decision boundary.

    Answer

    \(z = 1 + 2(1) + (-1)(4) = -1\). \(p = \sigma(-1) = 1/(1 + e^{1}) = 1/3.718 = 0.269\), so the predicted class is 0. The boundary is \(z = 0\), that is \(1 + 2x_1 - x_2 = 0\), or \(x_2 = 1 + 2x_1\): a straight line, with class 1 on the side where \(x_2 < 1 + 2x_1\).

  4. A model has \(\theta = (-4, 1, 1)\). Find the probability and class at \((x_1, x_2) = (3, 2)\), the equation of the decision boundary, and the side of it on which \((1, 1)\) falls.

    Answer

    At \((3, 2)\): \(z = -4 + 3 + 2 = 1\), \(p = \sigma(1) = 1/(1 + 0.3679) = 0.731\), class 1. The boundary is \(z = 0\), that is \(x_1 + x_2 = 4\). At \((1, 1)\), \(x_1 + x_2 = 2 < 4\), so \(z = -2\), \(p = \sigma(-2) = 0.119\), and the point is on the class-0 side.

  5. The model \(z = -4 + 0.8x\) (\(x\) = hours studied) is tested on four students.

    \(x\) (hours) 2 4 6 8 \(y\) (passed?) 0 1 1 1

    (a) Find each predicted probability and class at threshold 0.5, and the number of errors. (b) Find the boundary. (c) Compute the likelihood of the four labels and the average log-loss. (d) By what factor do the odds of passing change per extra hour?

    Answer

    (a) \(z = -2.4, -0.8, 0.8, 2.4\) give \(p = 0.0832,\ 0.3100,\ 0.6900,\ 0.9168\) and classes \(0, 0, 1, 1\). The student with \(x = 4\) passed but is predicted to fail: one error.

    (b) \(z = 0 \Rightarrow x = 5\) hours.

    (c) The probability given to the truth is \(1 - 0.0832 = 0.9168\), then \(0.3100\), \(0.6900\), \(0.9168\). Likelihood \(L = 0.9168 \times 0.3100 \times 0.6900 \times 0.9168 = 0.1798\). The losses are \(0.0868,\ 1.1711,\ 0.3711,\ 0.0868\), total \(1.7159 = -\ln L\), average \(1.7159/4 = 0.429\).

    (d) \(e^{0.8} = 2.2255\): each extra hour multiplies the odds by about 2.23.

  6. Using \(p(X) = \dfrac{e^{-6 + 0.005X}}{1 + e^{-6 + 0.005X}}\), two customers each have a balance of \(X = 8000\). Customer A defaulted (\(y = 1\)) and customer B did not (\(y = 0\)). Find the predicted probability for each and the likelihood of the two outcomes, and comment on the result.

    Answer

    \(z = -6 + 0.005(8000) = 34\), so \(p = \sigma(34) = 1 - 1.7\times 10^{-15}\), which is 1 for every practical purpose. Both customers receive this same probability. For A (defaulted) the probability given to the truth is \(p \approx 1\). For B (did not default) it is \(1 - p = e^{-34}/(1 + e^{-34}) \approx 1.7\times 10^{-15}\). The likelihood is the product, \(\approx 1.7\times 10^{-15}\), and B's log-loss is about \(34\), equal to \(z\). One confidently wrong prediction wipes out the likelihood, however many others are right. This is what log-loss is designed to punish, and why overconfident models are dangerous.

  7. Four points \((x_1, x_2)\) have labels: \((1,1) \to 0\), \((2,1) \to 0\), \((2,3) \to 1\), \((3,2) \to 1\). Train \(h = \sigma(\theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1 + \theta_2 x_2)\) by batch gradient descent from \(\theta = (0, 0, 0)\) with \(\alpha = 0.5\). Do two iterations and report the cost before and after each.

    Answer

    Start: every \(h = 0.5\) and \(J = \ln 2 = 0.6931\).

    Iteration 1: errors \(e = h - y = (0.5, 0.5, -0.5, -0.5)\). Gradients: \(\partial J/\partial\theta_0 = 0/4 = 0\); \(\partial J/\partial\theta_1 = (0.5 + 1.0 - 1.0 - 1.5)/4 = -0.25\); \(\partial J/\partial\theta_2 = (0.5 + 0.5 - 1.5 - 1.0)/4 = -0.375\). New \(\theta = (0,\ 0.125,\ 0.1875)\); \(J = 0.6378\).

    Iteration 2: \(h = (0.5775, 0.6077, 0.6926, 0.6792)\), so \(e = (0.5775, 0.6077, -0.3074, -0.3208)\). Gradients: \((0.1392,\ 0.0539,\ -0.0946)\). New \(\theta = (-0.0696,\ 0.0980,\ 0.2348)\); \(J = 0.6225\).

    The cost falls \(0.6931 \to 0.6378 \to 0.6225\), so training is converging.

  8. A logistic model with \(\theta = (0, 0, 0)\) sees a single training example \(x = (x_1, x_2) = (1, 2)\) with label \(y = 1\). Perform one gradient descent step with \(\alpha = 0.01\). What would be the effect of a much smaller, and of a much larger, \(\alpha\)?

    Answer

    At \(\theta = 0\) the prediction is \(h = 0.5\), so the error is \(h - y = -0.5\). The gradient is \((h - y)\times(1, x_1, x_2) = (-0.5, -0.5, -1.0)\). Then \(\theta_0 = 0 + 0.01(0.5) = 0.005\), \(\theta_1 = 0.005\), \(\theta_2 = 0.01\). The new score for the same example is \(0.005 + 0.005 + 0.02 = 0.03\), a slight rise in the right direction. A much smaller \(\alpha\) makes each step negligible, so training crawls and may need millions of iterations. A much larger \(\alpha\) overshoots the minimum: the cost zig-zags or even increases, and training diverges.

  9. Explain why squared error is not used as the cost function for logistic regression, and what is used instead.

    Answer

    With the sigmoid inside the model, \((h - y)^2\) is a non-convex function of \(\theta\): its surface has flat regions and local minima, so gradient descent can stall in a poor solution. It also punishes a confident wrong answer only mildly (the penalty is at most 1 however wrong the model is), and its gradient contains the factor \(\sigma'\), which is tiny when the unit is saturated. The log-loss \(-[y\ln h + (1-y)\ln(1-h)]\) is convex in \(\theta\), grows without limit for confident mistakes, is the negative log-likelihood of the Bernoulli model, and has the clean gradient \((h - y)x\) because the \(\sigma'\) cancels.

  10. A problem has 6 classes with 100 training examples each. How many binary classifiers do one-vs-rest and one-vs-one train, and how many examples does each classifier see? Give one drawback of each approach.

    Answer

    One-vs-rest: 6 classifiers, each trained on all 600 examples, with 100 positives against 500 negatives. One-vs-one: \(6 \cdot 5/2 = 15\) classifiers, each trained on only \(100 + 100 = 200\) examples, perfectly balanced. Drawbacks: one-vs-rest sub-problems are imbalanced, and the six scores come from separately trained models, so they are not on a common scale and do not sum to 1. One-vs-one needs many more models (45 for ten classes) and prediction needs a vote across all of them.

  11. Compute the softmax probabilities for the scores \(z = (2,\ 1,\ 0.1)\). Show that adding 10 to every score changes nothing.

    Answer

    \(e^{2} = 7.3891\), \(e^{1} = 2.7183\), \(e^{0.1} = 1.1052\); the sum is \(11.2125\). Probabilities: \(7.3891/11.2125 = 0.659\), \(2.7183/11.2125 = 0.242\), \(1.1052/11.2125 = 0.099\); they sum to 1. With \(z + 10\), every numerator and the denominator are multiplied by \(e^{10}\), which cancels: \(\dfrac{e^{z_k + 10}}{\sum_j e^{z_j + 10}} = \dfrac{e^{10}e^{z_k}}{e^{10}\sum_j e^{z_j}}\). Only the differences between scores matter.

  12. True or false, with a reason: "A logistic regression model needs the sigmoid in order to decide which class to predict at the 0.5 threshold."

    Answer

    False. Since \(\sigma(z) \ge 0.5\) exactly when \(z \ge 0\), the class is decided by the sign of the linear score alone, and the boundary is the straight line \(\theta^T x = 0\). The sigmoid is needed only to turn the score into a probability, for example to compare with a threshold other than 0.5, to rank cases, or to compute the loss.

  13. In regularised logistic regression the cost is \(J(\theta) + \dfrac{\lambda}{2m}\sum_{j \ge 1}\theta_j^2\) (ridge) or \(J(\theta) + \dfrac{\lambda}{m}\sum_{j\ge 1}|\theta_j|\) (lasso). What happens as \(\lambda \to 0\) and as \(\lambda \to \infty\)? Which penalty can set weights exactly to zero? Why is \(\theta_0\) left out, and how does scikit-learn's \(C\) relate to \(\lambda\)?

    Answer

    As \(\lambda \to 0\) the penalty vanishes and we recover the plain model: low bias, high variance. As \(\lambda \to \infty\) every weight except \(\theta_0\) is squeezed to zero, so the model gives the same probability to everyone (the overall class fraction): high bias, under-fitting. The L1 (lasso) penalty can set weights exactly to zero, so it also selects features. The intercept \(\theta_0\) is not penalised because it only shifts the boundary and is not a measure of how sensitively the model reacts to the features. In scikit-learn \(C = 1/\lambda\) (in the form where the data term is the summed loss), so a small \(C\) means strong regularisation.

  14. Compare linear regression and logistic regression on objective, cost function and the nature of the prediction, with an example of each.

    Answer

    Linear regression predicts a continuous number (for example a house price) by fitting a line or hyperplane; its cost is squared error, minimised in closed form or by gradient descent, and its output is unbounded. Logistic regression predicts the probability of a class (for example whether a customer defaults) by passing the same linear score through a sigmoid; its cost is the log-loss, minimised iteratively, and its output lies in \((0, 1)\) and is thresholded to give a class. Both have the gradient \((h - y)x\), with \(h\) the linear score in one and the sigmoid of it in the other.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Naive Bayes
docs.text: Decision trees ask a sequence of questions of the data. Naive Bayes takes a different route: it asks how probable each class is given everything observed, and answers with Bayes' theorem. The 'naive' assumption that the features are independent within a class turns an intractable estimation problem into a few counts, and the result is a classifier that is fast, needs little data and is the standard baseline for text. This chapter derives the rule, works it by hand on a small table, shows what to do about zero counts and numeric features, and states plainly where the assumption breaks.

docs.title: 7.1 Naïve Bayes
docs.text:
You want \(P(\text{spam} \mid \text{this} \text{email})\). Bayes' theorem turns that around into something you can count: \(P(\text{email} \mid \text{spam}) \times P(\text{spam})\), divided by a constant that is the same for every class and therefore cannot change which class wins. But \(P(\text{email} \mid \text{spam})\) is the probability of that exact combination of words, which you have almost certainly never seen before, so counting it is hopeless.

The naïve step is to pretend the features are independent given the class, which lets you multiply their individual probabilities. The assumption is false — words travel in company — and the classifier works anyway, because it only has to get the ranking of the classes right, not the probabilities.

\[ P(C \mid x_{1}\ldots x_{n}) \propto P(C) \cdot \Pi _{j} P(x_{j} \mid C) \]

the naïve Bayes rule: prior times the product of the per-feature likelihoods

The zero-frequency problem

A single unseen feature–class combination sets one factor to zero, and zero times anything is zero. One missing cell in a training table vetoes a class outright. Laplace smoothing adds \(\alpha\) to every count and \(\alpha \times\) (number of values) to each denominator, so nothing is ever impossible — only rare. \(\alpha = 1\) is the standard choice.

docs.title: What to do when a feature is a number
docs.text:
Counting works while the features are categories — Sunny, Overcast, Rain. It stops working the moment a feature is a measurement. Nobody in your training set has a glucose reading of exactly 137.4, so the count is zero and the class is vetoed, and rounding to the nearest whole number only hides the problem.

The fix is to stop counting and start assuming a shape. For each class, and each feature separately, assume the values follow a normal distribution, and estimate its two numbers from the training examples of that class.

Definition: Gaussian naïve Bayes

\(P(x_{j} = v \mid C) = (1 / \sqrt{2\pi \sigma _{\text{jC}}^{2}}) \cdot \exp(\) −(v \(- \mu _{\text{jC}})^{2} / (2\sigma _{\text{jC}}^{2}\)) )

\(\mu _{\text{jC}}\) is the mean of feature \(j\) among the training examples of class \(C\), and \(\sigma _{\text{jC}}^{2}\) is their variance. Two numbers per feature per class — that is the entire model.

Read the formula in three pieces and it stops looking forbidding. The bracket \((v - \mu )/\sigma\) is the z-score of Unit 2: how many standard deviations the value is from that class's average. Squaring and negating it means the further away, the smaller the result, and the fall is quick because it is squared inside an exponential. The factor in front, \(1/\sqrt{2\pi \sigma ^{2}}\), is only there to make the area under the curve equal to 1; it does no work in the comparison, because it appears for every class.

This is a density, not a probability

Its value can exceed 1 — with \(\sigma = 0.1\) the peak is about 4 — and \(P(x = 137.4)\) for a continuous quantity is strictly zero. What the number means is relative plausibility, and naïve Bayes only ever compares two of them for the same \(x\), so the distinction never affects the answer. It does affect what you may say about the number: never quote a density as “the probability of that reading”.

Figure 7.1. Gaussian naive Bayes on one feature: each curve is a class density multiplied by its prior, and the predicted class changes where the curves cross. With equal variances the boundary lies half-way between the means, and a larger prior for one class moves it towards the other.

Example 7.1: \(\cdot A\) worked value, so the formula is not just a picture

Among the healthy training examples a feature has mean \(\mu = 4.0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma = 1.2\). A new case reads \(x = 6.0\). Then

\(z = (6.0 - 4.0)/1.2 = 1.667\), so the exponent is \(-z^{2}/2 = -1.389\)

\(P(x \mid \text{healthy}) = (1/(1.2 \times 2.5066)) \cdot e^{-1.389} = 0.3325 \times 0.2494 = 0.0829\)

If among the diabetic examples \(\mu = 8.0\) with the same \(\sigma\), then \(z = -1.667\) and the density is the same 0.0829 — the two are equally plausible, which is why \(x = 6.0\) is exactly the boundary when the priors are equal.
