Adding \(\lambda I\) adds \(\lambda\) to every eigenvalue, so all are at least \(\lambda > 0\) and the matrix can be inverted. For nearly collinear features the smallest eigenvalues of \(X^{T}X\) are tiny, which makes its inverse huge and the coefficients unstable; adding \(\lambda\) lifts them, so the weights are shrunk and shared between the correlated features and their variance falls. Prefer ridge when you believe most features each contribute a little and want to keep them all; prefer lasso when you believe most are irrelevant and want selection.

  14. Design task. You must predict apartment rent from 40 features, many of them correlated and some irrelevant, using only 300 rows. Propose a pipeline: preprocessing, model, how to tune, how to avoid leakage, and which metrics to report.

    Answer

    One reasonable design. Hold out a test part (say 60 of the 300 rows) and do not touch it until the end. Preprocessing: one-hot encode categorical columns with \(c - 1\) columns each, and standardise the numeric features; if the residuals show a funnel, model the logarithm of rent. Model: an elastic net. The correlated features argue against plain lasso, which would keep one of each correlated group arbitrarily; the irrelevant features argue against plain ridge, which keeps them all; elastic net groups the correlated features and still sets the useless coefficients to zero. Tuning: \(k\)-fold cross-validation (5 or 10) on the 240 training rows over a grid of \(\lambda\) and of the L1/L2 mix, choosing the setting with the lowest mean validation RMSE. Leakage: put the scaler and the model in a single Pipeline so the scaler is refitted inside every fold. Finish by refitting on all 240 training rows at the chosen setting and scoring once on the test rows. Report RMSE and MAE in rupees and \(R^{2}\) on the test rows, with the cross-validation spread, and look at the residual plot for structure.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Perceptrons, Multilayer Networks and Back-propagation
docs.text: A logistic regression with a threshold is already a very small neural network: one neuron. This chapter starts from that neuron in its original form, the perceptron, shows what a single neuron can and cannot learn, and then stacks neurons into layers. The multilayer perceptron can represent curved boundaries, and the back-propagation algorithm is what makes it trainable: it computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight in a single backward pass.

docs.title: 10.1 The perceptron
docs.text:
Rosenblatt's 1958 model is the ancestor of every neural network. One unit takes a weighted sum of its inputs and fires if the sum crosses a threshold.

\[ \hat{y} = \text{step}(w^{T}x + b), \text{step}(z) = 1 \text{if} z \ge 0, \text{else} 0 \]

the bias \(b\) is the negative of the firing threshold

Definition: The perceptron update

For each example in turn: \(w\) := \(w + \eta (y - \hat{y})x\) and \(b\) := \(b + \eta (y - \hat{y})\).

If the prediction is correct, \(y - \hat{y} = 0\) and nothing changes. The perceptron learns only from its mistakes.

The rule's shape is not arbitrary. Suppose the true label was 1 and the unit answered 0. Adding \(x\) to \(w\) makes the new score for this same example larger by \(\eta (\Vert x\Vert ^{2} + 1)\), so the boundary has moved towards classifying it correctly. If the error is the other way, it subtracts, and the score falls.

Convergence theorem, and its limit

If the training data is linearly separable, the perceptron rule converges to a separating boundary in a finite number of updates, whatever the initial weights. If it is not separable, the rule never terminates and simply oscillates. It has no concept of “as good as possible” — which is precisely the gap that logistic regression (a differentiable loss with a real minimum) and the SVM (maximise the margin) each close in their own way.

XOR, and the winter it caused

A single perceptron computes AND and OR without difficulty, because each has a straight line separating its true and false cases. XOR does not: its true cases sit at opposite corners of a square. Minsky and Papert's 1969 book made this point precisely, funding collapsed, and neural network research stalled for over a decade. The resolution — a hidden layer — was known in principle but had no practical training algorithm until back-propagation was popularised in 1986.

docs.title: 10.2 Multilayer perceptrons and back-propagation
docs.text:
Stack the units. An input layer, one or more hidden layers, an output layer; each unit computes a weighted sum and passes it through a non-linear activation.

Why the non-linearity is not optional

A linear function of a linear function is linear. Without an activation, a hundred-layer network computes exactly what one layer computes, and the whole enterprise collapses into a single matrix. The squashing step is what makes depth mean anything.

Definition: Back-propagation

Forward: compute every \(z\) and a from input to output, then the loss.

Backward: compute \(\delta\) at the output, \(\delta = (\hat{y} - y)\cdot \sigma '(z)\), then pass it back layer by layer with \(\delta _{j} = (\sum _{k} \delta _{k}w_{\text{jk}})\cdot \sigma '(z_{j})\).

Update: every weight gradient has the same form — \(\delta\) at the far end times the activation at the near end — and each weight takes a gradient-descent step.

There is no new mathematics here: back-propagation is the chain rule, organised so that quantities computed for one layer are reused by the next, which is what makes it O(number of weights) rather than hopeless.

Figure 10.1. A small network: two inputs, two hidden units and one output, with the weights written on the connections. Chapter 10 returns to this network when it derives the backward pass. Activation Formula Derivative Comment Sigmoid \(1/(1+e^{-z})\) \(\sigma (1-\sigma )\), max 0.25 historically standard; saturates and kills gradients tanh \((e^{z}-e^{-z})/(e^{z}+e^{-z})\) \(1 - \tanh^{2}\), max 1 zero-centred, so usually better than sigmoid ReLU \(\max(0\), z) 1 for \(z > 0\), else 0 the modern default in hidden layers; no saturation for positive inputs Softmax \(e^{\text{zi}}/\sum e^{\text{zj}}\) — output layer for multi-class; the outputs sum to 1

Vanishing gradients, in one line of arithmetic

\(\sigma ' \le 0.25\) everywhere. Each layer the error signal passes through multiplies it by at most a quarter, so ten layers scale it by \(0.25^{10} \approx 10^{-6}\) and the early layers stop learning altogether. ReLU has derivative exactly 1 wherever it is active, so nothing shrinks — which is the single change that made deep networks trainable.

The universal approximation theorem

says a network with one hidden layer and enough units can approximate any continuous function to any accuracy. It is an existence result and nothing more: it does not say how many units, it does not say the weights can be found, and it does not say the result will generalise. Depth in practice buys efficiency — deep networks represent many functions with far fewer units than a shallow one would need.

# a multilayer perceptron — and the one line that decides whether it works
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier

net = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),                          # leave this out and it will not converge
    MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(16,), activation="relu",
                  max_iter=2000, random_state=42)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print("layers", [c.shape for c in net[-1].coefs_])   # the weight matrices
print("iterations", net[-1].n_iter_, "final loss", net[-1].loss_)

Example 10.1: Deriving the back-propagation rule

Problem. Why is every weight gradient \(“\delta\) at the far end times the activation at the near end”, and why does \(\delta\) travel backwards through the same weights it travelled forwards through?

Step 1 — name the quantities

For unit \(j\) in some layer: \(z_{j} = \sum _{i} w_{\text{ij}}a_{i} + b_{j}\) and \(a_{j} = f(z_{j})\), where the \(a_{i}\) are the activations arriving from the layer before. Define \(\delta _{j} = \partial L/\partial z_{j}\) — the sensitivity of the loss to that unit's input. Everything follows from this one definition.

Step 2 — the gradient for a weight

\(w_{\text{ij}}\) influences the loss only through \(z_{j}\), so the chain rule gives one factor:

\(\partial L/\partial w_{\text{ij}} = (\partial L/\partial z_{j})(\partial z_{j}/\partial w_{\text{ij}}) = \delta _{j} \cdot a_{i}\)

because \(z_{j}\) is linear in \(w_{\text{ij}}\) with coefficient \(a_{i}\). That is the rule: \(\delta\) at the far end, activation at the near end. Likewise \(\partial L/\partial b_{j} = \delta _{j}\), since the bias has coefficient 1.

Step 3 — \(\delta\) at the output

With the squared-error loss \(L = \tfrac{1}{2}(a_{\text{out}} - y)^{2}\):

\(\delta _{\text{out}} = \partial L/\partial z_{\text{out}} = (a_{\text{out}} - y) \cdot f'(z_{\text{out}})\)

For a sigmoid output that is \((\hat{y} - y)\cdot \hat{y}(1 - \hat{y})\), using the identity derived above.

Step 4 — \(\delta\) for a hidden unit

A hidden unit \(j\) affects the loss only through the units \(k\) it feeds, so the chain rule sums over all of them:

\(\delta _{j} = \sum _{k} (\partial L/\partial z_{k})(\partial z_{k}/\partial a_{j})(\partial a_{j}/\partial z_{j}) = (\sum _{k} \delta _{k} w_{\text{jk}}) \cdot f'(z_{j})\)

Read it: each downstream unit sends back its own \(\delta\), weighted by the very connection through which this unit influenced it. A unit that mattered a lot to a badly wrong output is charged a lot. That is the entire idea — the rest is bookkeeping.

Step 5 — why this is efficient

Computing each \(\partial L/\partial w\) separately would repeat the same partial products thousands of times. Back-propagation stores \(\delta\) once per unit and reuses it for every weight into that unit, which makes the whole gradient cost about the same as one forward pass — O(number of weights) rather than \(O(\text{weights}^{2})\). That is why the algorithm mattered enough to restart the field in 1986.

Answer. \(\partial L/\partial w_{\text{ij}} = \delta _{j}a_{i}\), with \(\delta _{\text{out}} = (\hat{y} - y)f'(z_{\text{out}})\) and \(\delta _{j} = (\sum _{k} \delta _{k}w_{\text{jk}})f'(z_{j})\)

Comment. Now the vanishing gradient is visible in the algebra rather than asserted: every backward step multiplies by another f′, and for the sigmoid f′ \(\le 0.25\), so ten layers scale \(\delta\) by at most \(0.25^{10} \approx 10^{-6}\). ReLU has f′ \(= 1\) wherever it is active, so nothing shrinks.

docs.title: Counting the parameters
docs.text:
“How many trainable parameters does this network have?” is a standard exam question, and it is arithmetic once the rule is stated. A fully connected layer with \(n\) inputs and \(k\) units holds nk weights and \(k\) biases. Input units hold nothing: they are values, not parameters.

\[ \text{parameters} = \sum _{\text{layers}} (n_{\ell } \times k_{\ell } + k_{\ell }) \quad \text{where} n_{\ell } \text{is} \text{the} \text{size} \text{of} \text{the} \text{previous} \text{layer} \]

Example 10.2: Two parameter counts

Problem. (a) A network with 10 inputs, a hidden layer of 8, a second hidden layer of 6 and an output layer of 3, all with biases. (b) A network with 3 inputs, one hidden layer of 2 and 1 output, all with biases.

(a) Layer by layer

Connection Weights Biases Subtotal \(10 \to 8\) \(10 \times 8 = 80\) 8 88 \(8 \to 6\) \(8 \times 6 = 48\) 6 54 \(6 \to 3\) \(6 \times 3 = 18\) 3 21 Total 146 17 163

\((b)\) The small one

\(3 \times 2 + 2 = 8\), then \(2 \times 1 + 1 = 3\). Total 11.

The check worth doing

The bias count is simply the total number of non-input neurons — \(8 + 6 + 3 = 17\) in (a), and \(2 + 1 = 3\) in \((b)\). If your bias count does not match that, you have either counted the input layer or missed a layer.

Answer. (a) 163 parameters; (b) 11 parameters

Why the number matters

It is the dimension of the space gradient descent is searching, and a rough guide to capacity: a network with more parameters than training rows can memorise the training set outright. The usual first response to a large train–test gap is to make this number smaller.

docs.title: Choosing the loss at the output
docs.text:
The derivation of back-propagation in this chapter used the squared error, which makes the output delta \(\delta = (\hat{y} - y)\,\hat{y}(1 - \hat{y})\). For classification this is rarely the best choice. If the output unit is a sigmoid and the loss is the binary cross-entropy of the logistic regression chapter, the slope factor \(\hat{y}(1 - \hat{y})\) cancels and the output delta becomes simply

\[ \delta_{\text{out}} = \hat{y} - y \]

the same "prediction minus truth" that appeared in logistic regression and in softmax regression. With several classes, a softmax output layer and categorical cross-entropy give \(\delta_k = \hat{y}_k - y_k\) for each output unit. The practical advantage is that the delta is large exactly when the network is badly wrong, even if the unit is saturated; with squared error a confidently wrong sigmoid unit has a tiny slope and learns very slowly. The rule of thumb: sigmoid or softmax output with cross-entropy for classification, a linear output with squared error for regression. Everything behind the output layer, the backward pass through the hidden layers, is unchanged.

docs.title: Training a network in practice
docs.text:
The worked examples update the weights once, on one example. A real run repeats this many times, and several practical decisions surround the loop.

Epochs and mini-batches. One pass over the whole training set is an epoch. Updating after every single example (stochastic gradient descent) is noisy; updating only after the full pass (batch gradient descent) is slow per update and memory-hungry. The usual compromise is the mini-batch: shuffle the data, split it into groups of \(B\) examples (commonly 32 to 256), average the gradient over each group, and update after every group. With \(m = 1000\) examples and \(B = 50\) there are \(1000/50 = 20\) updates per epoch. The noise in the mini-batch gradient is not only tolerated but useful, since it helps the search leave shallow dips.

Initialisation. Starting every weight at the same value, zero included, is fatal. All hidden units of a layer would compute the same output, receive the same delta and be updated identically, so they would stay identical forever and the layer would behave like a single unit. The weights are therefore started at small random values, which breaks the symmetry, and the inputs are scaled to comparable ranges so that no unit begins saturated.

The learning rate is the most important setting. If it is too small the loss falls smoothly but so slowly that training stalls long before the minimum. If it is too large, each step overshoots the valley, the loss zig-zags and may climb without limit. A value that gives a fast, smooth decay flattening near the bottom is the target, and it is found by trying a few values spaced by factors of about three or ten and watching the loss curve, exactly as in the gradient descent chapter of Unit 3.

docs.title: Controlling overfitting in networks
docs.text:
A network has far more parameters than a linear model, so it can memorise a training set. The training loss keeps falling while the loss on held-out data first falls and then rises. Four defences are standard.

  • Early stopping. Track the loss on a validation set after each epoch and stop when it starts to rise, keeping the weights from the best epoch.
  • L2 weight decay. Add \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum w^{2}\) to the loss. Every update then also shrinks each weight slightly towards zero, which favours smoother functions, exactly as in ridge regression.
  • Dropout. At each training step, switch off a random fraction of the hidden units (say half) and train the remaining network. No unit can then depend on a particular partner, so each has to learn a feature that is useful on its own. At test time all units are used, with their outputs scaled so that the expected input to the next layer is unchanged, and the result behaves like an average over many thinned networks, which lowers variance.
  • Data augmentation. Enlarge the training set with label-preserving changes to the inputs, such as flips, small shifts or added noise for images, so that the network sees more variety than the raw data hold.

These are the same bias-variance dials as elsewhere in the unit: weight decay strength, the fraction dropped and the stopping epoch all trade a little extra training error for a larger gain in generalisation.

docs.title: 10.4 Worked examples
docs.text:
The examples below work through the calculations of this chapter in full. Try each one on paper before reading the steps.

Example 10.3: Why the perceptron cannot learn XOR

Problem. Show that no single perceptron computes XOR, and give a two-unit hidden layer that does.

Step 1 — write down what would be required

XOR: \((0,0)\to 0, (0,1)\to 1, (1,0)\to 1, (1,1)\to 0\). A perceptron fires when \(w_{1}x_{1} + w_{2}x_{2} + b \ge 0\), so we need

(0,0): \(b < 0 \cdot (0,1): w_{2} + b \ge 0 \cdot (1,0): w_{1} + b \ge 0 \cdot (1,1): w_{1} + w_{2} + b < 0\)

Step 2 — derive the contradiction

From the second and third, \(w_{1} \ge\) −b and \(w_{2} \ge\) −b, so \(w_{1} + w_{2} \ge\) −2b.

The fourth requires \(w_{1} + w_{2} <\) −b.

Together: −2b \(\le w_{1} + w_{2} <\) −b, which needs −2b \(<\) −b, i.e. \(b > 0\). But the first condition says \(b < 0\). Contradiction, so no weights exist.

Geometrically: the two positive cases sit at opposite corners of the unit square, with the negatives at the other two. No straight line separates one diagonal pair from the other.

Step 3 — build it from two units

Note that XOR \(=\) OR AND NOT(AND). Both OR and AND are linearly separable, so use one hidden unit for each:

\(h_{1} = \text{step}(x_{1} + x_{2} - 0.5)\) — this is OR

\(h_{2} = \text{step}(x_{1} + x_{2} - 1.5)\) — this is AND

output \(= \text{step}(h_{1} - h_{2} - 0.5)\) — fires when OR is true and AND is not

Check \((1,1): h_{1} = 1, h_{2} = 1\), output \(=\) step(1 \(- 1 - 0.5) =\) step(−0.5) \(= 0\) ✓. Check \((0,1): h_{1} = 1, h_{2} = 0\), output \(=\) step(0.5) \(= 1\) ✓.

Answer. No single perceptron can do it — the four constraints are inconsistent. Two hidden units computing OR and AND, combined as OR \(-\) AND, solve it.

Comment. This is the whole argument for hidden layers in miniature. The hidden units transform the input into a new space — here, (OR, AND) coordinates — in which the problem is linearly separable. A trained network discovers such a transformation for itself instead of being handed one.

Example 10.4: One neuron under four activations

Problem. A neuron has inputs \(x_1 = 0.5\), \(x_2 = 0.8\), weights \(w_1 = -0.2\), \(w_2 = 0.5\) and bias \(b = -0.1\). Find the weighted sum \(z\), and the output under the step, sigmoid, tanh and ReLU activations. With a sigmoid, the output class is 1 if \(\sigma(z) \ge 0.5\).

Step 1 — the weighted sum

\(z = (-0.2)(0.5) + (0.5)(0.8) + (-0.1) = -0.10 + 0.40 - 0.10 = 0.20\)

Step 2 — apply each activation to \(z = 0.2\)

Activation Working Output Step \(z = 0.2 \ge 0\) \(1\) Sigmoid \(1/(1 + e^{-0.2}) = 1/(1 + 0.8187)\) \(0.5498\) tanh \(\tanh(0.2)\) \(0.1974\) ReLU \(\max(0, 0.2)\) \(0.2\)

Step 3 — the class

\(\sigma(0.2) = 0.5498 \ge 0.5\), so the sigmoid neuron outputs class 1; the step neuron agrees.

Answer. \(z = 0.2\); step \(1\), sigmoid \(0.5498\), tanh \(0.1974\), ReLU \(0.2\); class 1.

Comment. Every unit in every network of this chapter does exactly this: multiply, add, activate. With a sigmoid the neuron is a logistic regression, and with a step it is a perceptron. Only the last step differs.

Example 10.5: A perceptron learns the AND gate

Problem. Train a single perceptron to compute AND: \((0,0) \to 0\), \((0,1) \to 0\), \((1,0) \to 0\), \((1,1) \to 1\). Start from \(w_1 = 0.3\), \(w_2 = 0.3\), \(b = -0.15\), with \(\eta = 0.1\) and step activation (output 1 if \(z \ge 0\)). Present the rows in the order given and stop when a whole pass makes no error.

Rule. For each row: \(z = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b\), \(o = \text{step}(z)\), \(e = t - o\); then \(w_i \leftarrow w_i + \eta e x_i\) and \(b \leftarrow b + \eta e\). If \(e = 0\) nothing changes.

Step 1 — epoch 1, row by row

Row \((0,0)\), target 0: \(z = -0.15 < 0\), so \(o = 0\), \(e = 0\). No change.

Row \((0,1)\), target 0: \(z = 0.3(0) + 0.3(1) - 0.15 = 0.15 \ge 0\), so \(o = 1\) and \(e = 0 - 1 = -1\). Update: \(w_1 = 0.3 + 0.1(-1)(0) = 0.3\), \(w_2 = 0.3 + 0.1(-1)(1) = 0.2\), \(b = -0.15 + 0.1(-1) = -0.25\).

Row \((1,0)\), target 0, with the updated weights: \(z = 0.3(1) + 0.2(0) - 0.25 = 0.05 \ge 0\), so \(o = 1\) and \(e = -1\). Update: \(w_1 = 0.3 - 0.1 = 0.2\), \(w_2 = 0.2\), \(b = -0.25 - 0.1 = -0.35\).

Row \((1,1)\), target 1: \(z = 0.2 + 0.2 - 0.35 = 0.05 \ge 0\), so \(o = 1 = t\). No change.

Step 2 — epoch 2, a check pass with \(w = (0.2, 0.2)\), \(b = -0.35\)

\(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(z = 0.2x_1 + 0.2x_2 - 0.35\) \(o\) \(t\) Error 0 0 \(-0.35\) 0 0 0 0 1 \(-0.15\) 0 0 0 1 0 \(-0.15\) 0 0 0 1 1 \(+0.05\) 1 1 0

No errors, so training has converged.

Answer. \(w_1 = 0.2\), \(w_2 = 0.2\), \(b = -0.35\), after two corrections in the first epoch. The unit fires when \(0.2x_1 + 0.2x_2 \ge 0.35\), that is \(x_1 + x_2 \ge 1.75\), which only \((1,1)\) satisfies.

Comment. The perceptron changed its weights only twice, both times on a row it got wrong. Training it on XOR instead would never converge, for the reason in the figure.

Example 10.6: A forward pass through a 2–2–1 network

Problem. A network has two inputs, a hidden layer of two sigmoid neurons and one sigmoid output neuron. The inputs are \(x_1 = 0.5\), \(x_2 = 0.1\). Hidden neuron \(h_1\) has weights \((0.15, 0.20)\) and bias \(0.35\); \(h_2\) has weights \((0.25, 0.30)\) and bias \(0.35\); the output neuron has weights \((0.40, 0.45)\) from \((h_1, h_2)\) and bias \(0.60\). Compute the network's output.

Step 1 — hidden neuron \(h_1\)

\(\text{net}_{h_1} = 0.15(0.5) + 0.20(0.1) + 0.35 = 0.075 + 0.020 + 0.35 = 0.445\)

\(h_1 = \sigma(0.445) = 1/(1 + e^{-0.445}) = 1/(1 + 0.6408) = 0.6094\)

Step 2 — hidden neuron \(h_2\)

\(\text{net}_{h_2} = 0.25(0.5) + 0.30(0.1) + 0.35 = 0.125 + 0.030 + 0.35 = 0.505\)

\(h_2 = \sigma(0.505) = 1/(1 + 0.6035) = 0.6236\)

Step 3 — the output neuron

The hidden outputs now act as its inputs:

\(\text{net}_o = 0.40(0.6094) + 0.45(0.6236) + 0.60 = 0.2438 + 0.2806 + 0.60 = 1.1244\)

\(o = \sigma(1.1244) = 1/(1 + e^{-1.1244}) = 1/(1 + 0.3248) = 0.7548\)

Answer. \(h_1 = 0.6094\), \(h_2 = 0.6236\), output \(= 0.7548\); as a classifier with threshold 0.5, class 1 with 75.5% confidence.

Comment. Each hidden neuron is a logistic regression on the raw inputs, and the output neuron is a logistic regression on their answers. The next example trains this very network.

Example 10.7: One full back-propagation step

Problem. Take the network of the previous example, with target \(y = 1\), squared error \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}(y - o)^2\) and learning rate \(\alpha = 0.5\). Update all nine parameters once, and verify that the error falls.

Step 1 — forward pass and starting error

From the previous example, \(h_1 = 0.6094\), \(h_2 = 0.6236\), \(o = 0.7548\). Then \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - 0.7548)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.2452)^2 = 0.03006\).

Step 2 — the output delta

\(o - y = -0.2452\) and \(o(1 - o) = 0.7548 \times 0.2452 = 0.18507\), so

\(\delta_o = (o - y)\,o(1 - o) = (-0.2452)(0.18507) = -0.04538\)

Step 3 — gradients of the output layer

Each gradient is \(\delta_o\) times the signal that travelled along that connection:

\(\partial E/\partial v_1 = \delta_o h_1 = (-0.04538)(0.6094) = -0.02766\)

\(\partial E/\partial v_2 = \delta_o h_2 = (-0.04538)(0.6236) = -0.02830\)

\(\partial E/\partial b_3 = \delta_o = -0.04538\)

Step 4 — send the blame back, using the old weights

Each hidden delta is \(\delta_o\), times the weight on the connection to the output, times the hidden neuron's own slope \(h(1 - h)\).

\(h_1(1 - h_1) = 0.6094 \times 0.3906 = 0.23802\), so \(\delta_{h_1} = (-0.04538)(0.40)(0.23802) = -0.004320\)

\(h_2(1 - h_2) = 0.6236 \times 0.3764 = 0.23472\), so \(\delta_{h_2} = (-0.04538)(0.45)(0.23472) = -0.004793\)

The hidden deltas are about ten times smaller than \(\delta_o\) after a single layer.

Step 5 — gradients of the hidden layer (delta times input, with \(x_1 = 0.5\), \(x_2 = 0.1\))

Parameter Gradient Value \(w_{11}\) \(\delta_{h_1}x_1 = (-0.004320)(0.5)\) \(-0.002160\) \(w_{12}\) \(\delta_{h_1}x_2 = (-0.004320)(0.1)\) \(-0.000432\) \(b_1\) \(\delta_{h_1}\) \(-0.004320\) \(w_{21}\) \(\delta_{h_2}x_1 = (-0.004793)(0.5)\) \(-0.002396\) \(w_{22}\) \(\delta_{h_2}x_2 = (-0.004793)(0.1)\) \(-0.000479\) \(b_2\) \(\delta_{h_2}\) \(-0.004793\)

Step 6 — update all nine, new \(=\) old \(- 0.5 \times\) gradient

Parameter Old New \(w_{11}\) 0.1500 0.1511 \(w_{12}\) 0.2000 0.2002 \(b_1\) 0.3500 0.3522 \(w_{21}\) 0.2500 0.2512 \(w_{22}\) 0.3000 0.3002 \(b_2\) 0.3500 0.3524 \(v_1\) 0.4000 0.4138 \(v_2\) 0.4500 0.4642 \(b_3\) 0.6000 0.6227

Step 7 — forward pass with the new parameters

\(\text{net}_{h_1} = 0.1511(0.5) + 0.2002(0.1) + 0.3522 = 0.4478\), so \(h_1 = 0.6101\)

\(\text{net}_{h_2} = 0.2512(0.5) + 0.3002(0.1) + 0.3524 = 0.5080\), so \(h_2 = 0.6243\)

\(\text{net}_o = 0.4138(0.6101) + 0.4642(0.6243) + 0.6227 = 1.1650\), so \(o = 0.7622\)

\(E = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - 0.7622)^2 = 0.02827\)

Answer. The output rises from \(0.7548\) to \(0.7622\) and the error falls from \(0.03006\) to \(0.02827\), a reduction of about 6%.

Comment. Look at how unequal the changes are: the output-layer weights \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) each moved by about 0.014, the hidden weights by as little as 0.0002. Layers near the output learn fast and layers near the input learn slowly, because the delta shrinks at every layer it passes through, and here the inputs themselves are small. This is the vanishing-gradient effect visible in a two-layer network. Note too that \(\delta_{h_1}\) used the old \(v_1 = 0.40\): compute all the deltas before changing any weight.

Example 10.8: Activation functions compared, and a ReLU network

Problem. Five neurons have net inputs \(z = -2, -0.5, 0, 1, 2\). (a) Compute the output of each under sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and Leaky ReLU (slope \(0.01\) for \(z \le 0\)). (b) Compute the sigmoid's slope \(o(1 - o)\) at each point. (c) A small network has input \(x = (1, -2)\), a ReLU hidden layer and a sigmoid output; hidden neuron \(h_1\) has weights \((0.5, 0.3)\) and bias \(0.2\), \(h_2\) has weights \((-0.4, 0.6)\) and bias \(0.1\), and the output has weights \((1.0, 2.0)\) from \((h_1, h_2)\) and bias \(-0.05\). Compute the output.

Step 1 — the outputs (part a)

\(z\) Sigmoid tanh ReLU Leaky ReLU \(-2\) 0.1192 \(-0.9640\) 0 \(-0.020\) \(-0.5\) 0.3775 \(-0.4621\) 0 \(-0.005\) 0 0.5000 0.0000 0 0.000 1 0.7311 0.7616 1 1.000 2 0.8808 0.9640 2 2.000

Step 2 — the sigmoid slope (part b)

\(z\) \(o\) \(o(1 - o)\) \(-2\) 0.1192 0.1050 \(-0.5\) 0.3775 0.2350 0 0.5000 0.2500 1 0.7311 0.1966 2 0.8808 0.1050

The slope peaks at 0.25 at \(z = 0\) and falls towards zero on both sides.

Step 3 — the ReLU network (part c)

\(\text{net}_{h_1} = 0.5(1) + 0.3(-2) + 0.2 = 0.5 - 0.6 + 0.2 = 0.1\), so \(h_1 = \text{ReLU}(0.1) = 0.1\)

\(\text{net}_{h_2} = -0.4(1) + 0.6(-2) + 0.1 = -0.4 - 1.2 + 0.1 = -1.5\), so \(h_2 = \text{ReLU}(-1.5) = 0\)

\(\text{net}_o = 1.0(0.1) + 2.0(0) - 0.05 = 0.05\), so \(o = \sigma(0.05) = 1/(1 + 0.9512) = 0.5125\)

Answer. The tables above; the sigmoid slope never exceeds 0.25; the network outputs \(0.5125\), barely above 0.5, a very hesitant "class 1".

Comment. Two classic problems appear in this example. First, because the slope never exceeds 0.25, an error signal sent back through ten sigmoid layers is multiplied by at most \(0.25^{10} \approx 10^{-6}\), so the early layers stop learning; ReLU has slope exactly 1 for positive inputs, so it does not shrink the signal. Second, \(h_2\) output 0, and its ReLU slope there is also 0, so it receives no correction: a neuron whose input is negative for every example is stuck off for good (the "dying ReLU"). Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope for negative inputs so that such a neuron can recover.

Example 10.9: Why linear activations collapse, with numbers

Problem. A network has three inputs, a hidden layer of three ReLU units and one sigmoid output. Hidden-layer weights (row \(j\) holds the weights into \(h_j\)) and biases are

Unit from \(x_1\) from \(x_2\) from \(x_3\) bias \(h_1\) 0.5 0.4 \(-0.3\) 0.1 \(h_2\) \(-0.6\) 0.2 0.5 0.2 \(h_3\) 0.3 \(-0.5\) 0.4 \(-0.4\)

and the output unit has weights \(v = (0.6, -0.4, 0.5)\) and bias \(-0.2\). For \(x = (2, -1, 1)\) with label \(y = 1\): (a) count the parameters; (b) do the forward pass; (c) compute the binary cross-entropy loss; (d) show that if every activation were the identity the network would be a single linear unit, and find its weights.

Step 1 — count (part a)

Input to hidden: \(3 \times 3 + 3 = 12\). Hidden to output: \(3 \times 1 + 1 = 4\). Total 16.

Step 2 — forward pass (part b)

\(n_1 = 0.5(2) + 0.4(-1) - 0.3(1) + 0.1 = 0.4\), so \(h_1 = 0.4\)

\(n_2 = -0.6(2) + 0.2(-1) + 0.5(1) + 0.2 = -0.7\), so \(h_2 = \text{ReLU}(-0.7) = 0\)

\(n_3 = 0.3(2) - 0.5(-1) + 0.4(1) - 0.4 = 1.1\), so \(h_3 = 1.1\)

\(z = 0.6(0.4) - 0.4(0) + 0.5(1.1) - 0.2 = 0.59\), so \(\hat{y} = \sigma(0.59) = 1/(1 + 0.5543) = 0.6434\)

Step 3 — the loss (part c)

With \(y = 1\) the cross-entropy is \(-\ln \hat{y} = -\ln 0.6434 = 0.4410\).

Step 4 — the identity activation (part d)

If every activation is the identity, \(h = Wx + b\) and \(\hat{y}_{\text{lin}} = v^T(Wx + b) + c = (v^TW)x + (v^Tb + c)\). This is a single linear unit with weights \(v^TW\) and bias \(v^Tb + c\):

\(v^TW = 0.6(0.5, 0.4, -0.3) - 0.4(-0.6, 0.2, 0.5) + 0.5(0.3, -0.5, 0.4) = (0.69,\ -0.09,\ -0.18)\)

\(v^Tb + c = 0.6(0.1) - 0.4(0.2) + 0.5(-0.4) - 0.2 = -0.42\)

As a check at \(x = (2, -1, 1)\): \(0.69(2) - 0.09(-1) - 0.18(1) - 0.42 = 0.87\), the same as feeding the unclipped hidden values \((0.4, -0.7, 1.1)\) through the output unit: \(0.6(0.4) - 0.4(-0.7) + 0.5(1.1) - 0.2 = 0.87\).

Answer. 16 parameters; \(h = (0.4, 0, 1.1)\), \(z = 0.59\), \(\hat{y} = 0.6434\); loss \(0.4410\). Without non-linear activations the network is the single unit \(0.69x_1 - 0.09x_2 - 0.18x_3 - 0.42\).

Comment. Notice the difference the ReLU made: the true pre-activation of \(h_2\) is \(-0.7\), but the ReLU network replaces it by 0, so the network's \(z\) is \(0.59\) and not \(0.87\). That kink is the whole of the non-linearity, and it is what lets a network with enough units bend its boundary. A composition of linear maps is linear, so no number of linear layers could do more than the one unit above.

docs.title: 10.5 Common mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
Each of the following is a mistake that costs marks in an examination or accuracy in practice.

  • Do not expect the perceptron to converge on overlapping classes. It cannot, and it will not tell you so.
  • Do not build a network without a non-linear activation. Every layer collapses into one.
  • Do not update the weights during the backward pass and then keep using them for the remaining deltas of the same example. Compute all the deltas, then update.

docs.title: 10.6 Summary
docs.text:
After working through this chapter you should be able to do the following.

  • Run the perceptron rule, explain from its shape why it moves the boundary towards a misclassified point, state the convergence theorem with its separability condition, and prove that XOR is outside its reach.
  • Carry out a forward pass and a backward pass through a small network. You recognise that every weight gradient is \(“\delta\) at the far end times activation at the near end”. And you can explain vanishing gradients from the single fact that \(\sigma ' \le 0.25\).

docs.title: 10.7 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Perceptron with \(w = (0.5, -0.5), b = 0, \eta = 1\). Example (2, 1) with label 1. Give the new weights, and look before you compute.

    Answer

    Unchanged. \(z = 0.5(2) - 0.5(1) + 0 = 0.5 \ge 0\), so \(\hat{y} = 1 = y\) and \(y - \hat{y} = 0\): the update \(\eta(y - \hat{y})x\) is zero. The weights stay \((0.5, -0.5)\) and \(b\) stays 0, because the perceptron learns only from its mistakes.

  2. A network with a sigmoid output unit has \(\hat{y} = 0.7\) and target \(y = 1\). Compute \(\delta\) at the output for the squared-error loss \(\tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{y} - y)^2\).

    Answer

    \(\delta = (\hat{y} - y)\,\hat{y}(1 - \hat{y}) = (-0.3)(0.7)(0.3) = -0.063\). The negative sign says the output is too low, so the weights feeding it should increase.

  3. Prove that no single perceptron computes XNOR.

    Answer

    XNOR is 1 when the inputs agree: \((0,0) \to 1\), \((0,1) \to 0\), \((1,0) \to 0\), \((1,1) \to 1\). A perceptron outputs 1 when \(w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b \ge 0\), so we would need \(b \ge 0\), \(\ w_2 + b < 0\), \(\ w_1 + b < 0\), \(\ w_1 + w_2 + b \ge 0\). Adding the middle two gives \(w_1 + w_2 + 2b < 0\), so \(w_1 + w_2 + b < -b\). The first condition gives \(-b \le 0\), hence \(w_1 + w_2 + b < 0\), which contradicts the fourth condition. No weights exist. Geometrically, the two 1-cases lie on one diagonal of the unit square and the two 0-cases on the other, and no straight line separates two diagonals. (Two hidden units computing OR and NAND, combined by AND, give XOR; negating the output gives XNOR.)

  4. Train a perceptron (output 1 if \(z \ge 0\)) to compute NAND, starting from \(w_1 = 0.3\), \(w_2 = 0.2\), \(b = -0.1\) with \(\eta = 0.5\). Present the inputs in the order \((0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)\) and continue until a pass makes no error. NAND is 1 except for input \((1,1)\).

    Answer

    Epoch 1. \((0,0)\), target 1: \(z = -0.1\), \(o = 0\), \(e = +1\), so \(b = -0.1 + 0.5 = 0.4\) (weights unchanged, since the inputs are 0). \((0,1)\): \(z = 0.6\), \(o = 1\), correct. \((1,0)\): \(z = 0.7\), \(o = 1\), correct. \((1,1)\), target 0: \(z = 0.3 + 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.9\), \(o = 1\), \(e = -1\), so \(w = (0.3 - 0.5,\ 0.2 - 0.5) = (-0.2, -0.3)\) and \(b = 0.4 - 0.5 = -0.1\).

    Epoch 2. \((0,0)\): \(z = -0.1\), \(o = 0\), \(e = +1\), so \(b = 0.4\). \((0,1)\): \(z = 0.1\), correct. \((1,0)\): \(z = 0.2\), correct. \((1,1)\): \(z = -0.1\), \(o = 0\), correct.

    Epoch 3: no errors. Final \(w = (-0.2, -0.3)\), \(b = 0.4\): net inputs \(0.4,\ 0.1,\ 0.2,\ -0.1\) for the four rows, giving outputs \(1, 1, 1, 0\) as required.

  5. Train a perceptron on the OR gate (\(t = 0, 1, 1, 1\) for the inputs \((0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)\)), starting from \(w_1 = 0\), \(w_2 = 0.3\), \(b = 0.1\) with \(\eta = 0.2\). Give the final weights.

    Answer

    Epoch 1. \((0,0)\), target 0: \(z = 0.1\), \(o = 1\), \(e = -1\), so \(b = 0.1 - 0.2 = -0.1\). \((0,1)\): \(z = 0.2\), correct. \((1,0)\), target 1: \(z = -0.1\), \(o = 0\), \(e = +1\), so \(w_1 = 0.2\) and \(b = 0.1\). \((1,1)\): \(z = 0.6\), correct.

    Epoch 2. \((0,0)\): \(z = 0.1\), \(o = 1\), \(e = -1\), so \(b = -0.1\). The other three rows are correct (\(z = 0.2, 0.1, 0.4\)).

    Epoch 3: no errors. Final \(w = (0.2, 0.3)\), \(b = -0.1\), after three corrections. The boundary is \(0.2x_1 + 0.3x_2 = 0.1\), which cuts off only the corner \((0,0)\).

  6. A perceptron has \(w = (1, -1)\), \(b = 0.5\) and \(\eta = 1\). It sees \(x = (2, 3)\) with true label \(y = 1\). Find \(z\) and \(\hat{y}\); if the prediction is wrong, perform one update and check that the point is now classified correctly.

    Answer

    \(z = 1(2) - 1(3) + 0.5 = -0.5 < 0\), so \(\hat{y} = 0\): wrong. The error is \(y - \hat{y} = +1\), so \(w = (1 + 2,\ -1 + 3) = (3, 2)\) and \(b = 0.5 + 1 = 1.5\). Check: \(z = 3(2) + 2(3) + 1.5 = 13.5 \ge 0\), so \(\hat{y} = 1\), correct.

  7. How many trainable parameters (weights and biases) does a fully connected network have with layer sizes (a) 8–16–8–1 and (b) 784–128–10? State the quick check for the bias count.

    Answer

    (a) \(8 \times 16 + 16 = 144\); \(16 \times 8 + 8 = 136\); \(8 \times 1 + 1 = 9\). Total 289 (264 weights and 25 biases).

    (b) \(784 \times 128 + 128 = 100\,480\); \(128 \times 10 + 10 = 1\,290\). Total 101 770.

    The number of biases equals the number of non-input neurons: \(16 + 8 + 1 = 25\) in (a) and \(128 + 10 = 138\) in (b). Input units hold values, not parameters.

  8. A 2–2–1 network uses the sigmoid in every hidden and output unit. Hidden unit \(h_1\) has weights \((0.3, 0.4)\) and bias \(-0.1\); \(h_2\) has weights \((-0.2, 0.6)\) and bias \(0.2\); the output has weights \((0.5, -0.3)\) from \((h_1, h_2)\) and bias \(0.1\). For the example \(x = (1.0, 0.5)\) with target \(t = 1\), squared error \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}(t - o)^2\) and \(\eta = 0.5\): (a) do the forward pass and find \(E\); (b) find the three deltas; (c) update all nine parameters; (d) repeat the forward pass and check that \(E\) has fallen.

    Answer

    (a) \(\text{net}_{h_1} = 0.3 + 0.2 - 0.1 = 0.4\), \(h_1 = 0.5987\). \(\text{net}_{h_2} = -0.2 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.3\), \(h_2 = 0.5744\). \(\text{net}_o = 0.5(0.5987) - 0.3(0.5744) + 0.1 = 0.2270\), \(o = 0.5565\). \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.4435)^2 = 0.0983\).

    (b) \(\delta_o = (o - t)\,o(1 - o) = (-0.4435)(0.5565)(0.4435) = -0.1095\). \(\delta_{h_1} = \delta_o v_1 h_1(1 - h_1) = (-0.1095)(0.5)(0.5987)(0.4013) = -0.0131\). \(\delta_{h_2} = (-0.1095)(-0.3)(0.5744)(0.4256) = +0.0080\).

    (c) Output layer: \(v_1 = 0.5 - 0.5(-0.1095)(0.5987) = 0.5328\); \(v_2 = -0.3 - 0.5(-0.1095)(0.5744) = -0.2686\); \(b_o = 0.1 + 0.5(0.1095) = 0.1547\). Hidden layer: \(h_1\) weights \((0.3 + 0.5(0.0131)(1.0),\ 0.4 + 0.5(0.0131)(0.5)) = (0.3066, 0.4033)\), bias \(-0.1 + 0.5(0.0131) = -0.0934\); \(h_2\) weights \((-0.2 - 0.5(0.0080)(1.0),\ 0.6 - 0.5(0.0080)(0.5)) = (-0.2040, 0.5980)\), bias \(0.2 - 0.5(0.0080) = 0.1960\).

    (d) \(\text{net}_{h_1} = 0.4148\), \(h_1 = 0.6022\); \(\text{net}_{h_2} = 0.2910\), \(h_2 = 0.5722\); \(\text{net}_o = 0.3219\), \(o = 0.5798\); \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.4202)^2 = 0.0883 < 0.0983\).

  9. A 2–2–2 network uses ReLU in the hidden and output layers. Inputs are \((0.1, 0.5)\) and targets \((0.05, 0.95)\). Hidden unit \(h_1\) has weights \((0.1, 0.3)\) and \(h_2\) has \((0.2, 0.4)\), both with bias \(0.25\). Output \(o_1\) has weights \((0.5, 0.6)\) from \((h_1, h_2)\) and \(o_2\) has \((0.7, 0.8)\), both with bias \(0.35\). Biases stay fixed. With \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_k (t_k - o_k)^2\) and \(\eta = 0.5\): find the outputs and \(E\), the deltas, the eight updated weights, and the new \(E\).

    Answer

    Forward: \(h_1 = 0.1(0.1) + 0.3(0.5) + 0.25 = 0.41\) and \(h_2 = 0.2(0.1) + 0.4(0.5) + 0.25 = 0.47\) (both positive, so ReLU passes them). \(o_1 = 0.5(0.41) + 0.6(0.47) + 0.35 = 0.837\) and \(o_2 = 0.7(0.41) + 0.8(0.47) + 0.35 = 1.013\). \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}[(0.787)^2 + (0.063)^2] = 0.3117\).

    Deltas (ReLU slope 1 throughout): \(\delta_{o_1} = 0.787\), \(\delta_{o_2} = 0.063\); \(\delta_{h_1} = 0.5(0.787) + 0.7(0.063) = 0.4376\); \(\delta_{h_2} = 0.6(0.787) + 0.8(0.063) = 0.5226\), all computed with the old weights.

    Updates (\(w \leftarrow w - 0.5\,\delta \times \text{input}\)): output layer \(o_1\): \((0.5 - 0.5(0.787)(0.41),\ 0.6 - 0.5(0.787)(0.47)) = (0.3387, 0.4151)\); \(o_2\): \((0.7 - 0.5(0.063)(0.41),\ 0.8 - 0.5(0.063)(0.47)) = (0.6871, 0.7852)\). Hidden layer \(h_1\): \((0.1 - 0.5(0.4376)(0.1),\ 0.3 - 0.5(0.4376)(0.5)) = (0.0781, 0.1906)\); \(h_2\): \((0.2 - 0.5(0.5226)(0.1),\ 0.4 - 0.5(0.5226)(0.5)) = (0.1739, 0.2694)\).

    New forward pass: \(h = (0.3531, 0.4021)\), \(o = (0.6365, 0.9083)\), \(E = 0.1728\), a fall of about 44.5%.

  10. Explain why a network with 100 layers but only linear activations is no more powerful than a single layer, and say what that implies for the design of hidden units.

    Answer

    Two linear layers compose to \(W_2(W_1x + b_1) + b_2 = (W_2W_1)x + (W_2b_1 + b_2)\), which is again of the form \(Wx + b\). By induction any number of linear layers collapses into one, so the network can draw only straight-line boundaries and cannot even compute XOR. Hidden units therefore need a non-linear activation (ReLU, tanh, sigmoid); the bend in the activation is what makes extra layers add representational power.

  11. A deep network uses sigmoid activations in every layer. By what factor, at most, is the error signal multiplied on passing back through 5 layers? What happens with ReLU?

    Answer

    The sigmoid derivative is at most \(0.25\), so each layer multiplies the error signal by at most \(0.25\) (times a weight), and five layers by at most \(0.25^5 = 0.000977\), about \(10^{-3}\). The early layers receive a signal a thousand times weaker than the output layer and barely learn: the vanishing-gradient problem. ReLU has derivative exactly 1 for positive inputs, so on active paths nothing shrinks, which is the main reason ReLU replaced the sigmoid in hidden layers.

  12. A sigmoid output unit has \(\hat{y} = 0.7\) and \(y = 1\). Compute \(\delta\) at the output if the loss is the binary cross-entropy \(-[y\ln\hat{y} + (1-y)\ln(1-\hat{y})]\), and compare with the squared-error value of \(-0.063\).

    Answer

    For \(y = 1\) the loss is \(-\ln\hat{y}\), so \(\partial L/\partial\hat{y} = -1/\hat{y}\). Multiplying by the sigmoid slope \(\hat{y}(1 - \hat{y})\) gives \(\delta = -(1 - \hat{y}) = \hat{y} - y = -0.3\). The factor \(\hat{y}(1 - \hat{y})\) cancels. With squared error \(\delta = (\hat{y} - y)\hat{y}(1 - \hat{y}) = -0.063\), nearly five times smaller. Under squared error a badly wrong but saturated unit (for example \(\hat{y} = 0.01\), \(y = 1\)) gets a vanishing delta, so it learns slowly exactly when it is most wrong; with cross-entropy the delta stays large. This is why classification networks use cross-entropy.

  13. Name three techniques that reduce overfitting in a neural network and say in one line how each works.

    Answer

    Early stopping: watch the validation loss and stop training when it starts to rise although the training loss is still falling. L2 weight decay: add \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum w^2\) to the loss, which shrinks the weights towards zero and so prefers smoother, simpler functions. Dropout: at each training step randomly switch off a fraction of the units, so that no unit can rely on a particular partner; at test time all units are used, which behaves like averaging many thinned networks. (Data augmentation, which enlarges the training set with label-preserving transformations, is a fourth.)

  14. What happens to the loss during training if the learning rate is far too high, and what if it is far too low? How would you recognise each from a plot of loss against iteration?

    Answer

    Too high: each step overshoots the valley, so the loss zig-zags, oscillates or even grows without bound, and training diverges; the curve rises or jumps up and down. Too low: the loss decreases smoothly but extremely slowly, so training takes very long and may stop far from the minimum; the curve is a nearly flat gentle slope. A good value gives a fast, smooth decay that flattens near the bottom.

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
A course in five units

This book is a textbook for a first university course in machine learning. It follows the five units of the Machine Learning syllabus of the University of Delhi (DSC17 / DSC-A5 / GE7c, NEP UGCF 2022): the learning problem, data preprocessing and dimensionality reduction, regression, classification, and clustering. It assumes a pass in Class XII mathematics and some programming in Python; the mathematics used is school algebra, a little calculus (derivatives and partial derivatives) and a little linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues of a 2 × 2 matrix), and each is recalled where it is first needed.

docs.title: Who the book is for
docs.text: The book is written for the student who will sit the examination and for the teacher who must plan the lectures. The student will find each idea explained in plain words before any notation, every formula derived or at least motivated, and every calculation of the syllabus worked out line by line. The teacher will find the units broken into chapters of about one to two lectures each, with worked examples ready for the board and exercises with answers for tutorial sessions.

docs.title: How the book maps to the syllabus
docs.text:

Regression Linear regression with one variable and with multiple variables, gradient descent, over-fitting, regularisation, regression evaluation metrics 12 4, 5 4. Classification Decision trees, naive Bayes, logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, perceptron, multilayer perceptron, neural networks, back-propagation, support vector machines, classification evaluation metrics 12 6 to 12 5. Clustering Approaches for clustering, distance metrics, k-means clustering, hierarchical clustering 8 13, 14

The syllabus also prescribes twelve practical programs. They are listed below with the chapter that supplies the theory behind each; the practical work itself, done in Python on public data sets, is outside this book.

Practical Theory in chapter Naive Bayes classifier 7 Simple linear regression; multiple linear regression 4 Polynomial regression; lasso and ridge regression 5 Logistic regression 8 Artificial neural network 10 k-NN classifier 9 Decision tree classification 6 SVM classification 11 K-means clustering; hierarchical clustering 13, 14 Evaluation protocol: train/test split, k-fold cross-validation, MSE and \(R^2\) for regression, accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 and AUC for classification 5, 12

docs.title: How the chapters are built
docs.text:
Every chapter opens with a short introduction and, for the first chapter of a unit, the learning outcomes of that unit. The numbered sections that follow explain the topic in continuous prose. Four kinds of box recur:

  • Definitions and notes state a term precisely.
  • Key ideas pick out the one thing in a section that must not be forgotten.
  • Cautions mark the traps that cost marks and accuracy.
  • Examples work a problem completely, with every step shown. Derivations of the important results are presented in the same form.

Each chapter ends with a list of common mistakes, a summary of what you should now be able to do, and exercises. Every exercise has its answer in a box that stays closed until you open it: attempt the exercise on paper first.

docs.title: How to use the book
docs.text:
Read a chapter once for the idea, then read it again with pencil and calculator, redoing every worked example before looking at its steps. The examples deliberately use small numbers, so that the arithmetic can be done by hand and the structure of the method is not hidden by the numbers. Then do the exercises and check them. Three habits pay for themselves throughout the course:

  1. State, before computing anything, what is being predicted and how the result will be judged.
  2. Keep the test data sealed. Anything that is learned from data (a scaler, a selected feature, a threshold, a number of clusters) is learned from the training part alone.
  3. Compare every model with a trivial baseline before believing it.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text: The symbols are the same throughout. \(m\) is the number of examples and \(n\) the number of features; \(x^{(i)}\) is the \(i\)-th example and \(x_j\) its \(j\)-th feature; \(y\) is the target and \(\hat{y}\) the model's prediction; \(\theta\) (or \(w\) and \(b\)) are the parameters, learned from data, while \(\alpha\), \(\lambda\), \(k\) and \(C\) are hyper-parameters, chosen on validation data. The appendix Formula Sheet and Notation lists every symbol with the usual pitfalls, followed by the formulas of each unit for revision, and a glossary closes the book.

docs.title: A note on units and chapters
docs.text: The word unit always refers to one of the five syllabus units; the book is divided into chapters, which are shorter. Where the text says "Unit 3" it means the regression material of Chapters 4 and 5.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Preparing the Data: Scaling, Encoding, Outliers and Balance
docs.text:
Suppose you are asked which two of three people are most alike, given their height in centimetres and their annual income in rupees. Person A is 170 cm earning ₹500 000; B is 195 cm earning ₹501 000; \(C\) is 171 cm earning ₹900 000. Any distance you compute is going to be dominated by the income difference, because income is measured in numbers that are thousands of times larger. The algorithm will report that A and B are practically identical and that \(C\) is far away — entirely because of the units somebody happened to choose. Change income to lakhs and the answer changes.

That is the whole motivation for feature scaling, and it generalises. Learning algorithms do arithmetic on the numbers you hand them. They cannot see that one column is a length and another is money. They cannot see that a 999 in the age column means “not recorded”, that three of your forty features are copies of each other, or that 99% of your rows belong to one class. Preprocessing is the work of making the numbers mean what you think they mean.

One more thing, which is the axis this whole unit turns on. Every step here learns something from the data — a minimum, a mean, a set of eigenvectors, a list of columns to keep. Anything learned must be learned from the training set alone. Break that and your reported accuracy becomes a number about your notebook rather than about the world.

Learning outcomes of Unit 2

  • Apply min–max normalisation, z-score standardisation and robust scaling by hand, and say which one a given situation calls for — including the situations that call for none.
  • State exactly which algorithms are sensitive to feature scale and why, rather than remembering a list.
  • Detect outliers with the \(1.5 \times\) IQR rule and the z-score rule, explain why the two disagree, and decide what to do with what you find.
  • Distinguish filter, wrapper and embedded feature selection, and choose between selection and extraction.
  • Carry out PCA on a small covariance matrix: eigenvalues, eigenvectors, proportion of variance explained, and how many components to keep.
  • Recognise class imbalance, explain the accuracy paradox, and compare undersampling, oversampling, SMOTE and class weights.
  • Order a pipeline so that no information leaks from the test set into the training process.

docs.title: 2.1 Why raw data is rarely usable
docs.text:
Real datasets arrive with several distinct problems, and each has its own remedy. It is worth being able to name them separately, because the fixes are not interchangeable.

Problem What it looks like Remedy Incomparable scales age in years next to income in rupees scaling — this unit's first topic Missing values blanks, NaN, or a sentinel like −1 or 999 drop, impute, or flag as missing Categorical text “Mumbai”, “Delhi”, “Chennai” one-hot, ordinal or target encoding Outliers one value ten times everything else investigate; then keep, cap, or remove Too many features 200 columns, 300 rows selection, or extraction with PCA Redundant features “height in cm” and “height in inches” correlation filter, PCA, or a regulariser Class imbalance 99.7% negative resampling, class weights, and a better metric Skew income, city population, word counts log or Box–Cox transform

Key idea

Preprocessing is not tidying-up done before the real work. It is part of the model. A scaler is fitted, has parameters, and must be shipped and versioned with the model — if the values used at prediction time differ from those used at training time, the model receives inputs in a coordinate system it has never seen, and its output is meaningless rather than merely inaccurate.

docs.title: 2.2 Feature scaling
docs.text:
Definition: The two workhorses

Min–max normalisation maps a feature onto a fixed interval, usually [0, 1]:

x′ \(= (x -\) min) / (max \(-\) min)

Z-score standardisation re-centres to mean 0 and rescales to standard deviation 1:

\(z = (x - \mu ) / \sigma\)

Mean normalisation is min–max recentred on the mean, so the values land in [−0.5, 0.5] with an average of zero:

x′ \(= (x - \mu ) /\) (max \(-\) min)

Min–max preserves the shape of the distribution exactly and guarantees the range; it is completely at the mercy of the extreme values, because they are the parameters. Standardisation is far more robust to a single large value: an outlier moves \(\mu\) a little and \(\sigma\) a little, rather than redefining the whole scale. But it bounds nothing, so a standardised feature can perfectly well take the value 12.

Figure 2.1. The same eight salaries on three scales: raw, min-max and z-score. The pattern of the points is unchanged, only the axis differs. One extreme value would squeeze the other seven into a huddle under min-max scaling, whereas z-scores merely stretch.

docs.title: Which algorithms care, and why
docs.text:
Do not memorise a list — the reason predicts the list.

Scale-sensitive

Anything that computes a distance or a dot product, or descends a gradient. k-NN, k-means, SVM, PCA — because a distance is a sum over features and the biggest-numbered feature dominates the sum. Linear and logistic regression trained by gradient descent, and neural networks — because unequal scales make the cost surface a long thin ravine that gradient descent zig-zags down instead of walking straight to the bottom. Ridge and lasso — because the penalty \(\lambda \sum \theta ^{2}\) punishes a coefficient for being large, and a coefficient is large partly because its feature is measured in small units.

Scale-indifferent

Anything that considers one feature at a time and only compares values within that feature. Decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting — a split asks “is \(x <\) t?”, and any increasing transformation of \(x\) leaves the ordering, and hence every possible split, unchanged. Also naïve Bayes on categorical features, and linear regression solved by the normal equation, which finds the exact optimum regardless of conditioning.

Definition: Robust scaling and the log transform

Robust scaling replaces \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) with the median and the IQR: x′ \(= (x -\) median) / IQR. Both are rank statistics, so an extreme value cannot drag them. Use it whenever the feature is heavy-tailed.

Log transform \(x \to \log(1 + x)\) is not scaling but reshaping: it pulls in a long right tail so that a variable like income or city population becomes roughly symmetric. Apply it before standardising, and only to positive quantities.

Figure 2.2. The only correct order for a learned transformation: split first, fit on the training rows only, then apply the same stored numbers to both parts. Any arrow from the test side back to the training side would be a leak.
  1. Raw dataset. Everything you have. Nothing has been computed from it yet.
  2. 1 Split. FIRST. Before any statistic is computed from any row. Everything that follows depends on this ordering.
  3. 2 Fit on train (μ, σ, min, max, PCs). Every number the transformation needs is computed from the training rows only. scaler.fit(X_train).
  4. 3 Apply to both. scaler.transform(X_train) and scaler.transform(X_test) — the same stored numbers for both. The test set is transformed, never consulted.
  5. 4 Train the model. On the transformed training set.
  6. 5 Evaluate once. On the transformed test set, at the very end. This number is now an honest estimate.

Why fitting the scaler on everything is wrong, concretely

Suppose the test set happens to contain the largest salary in the dataset. If min and max were computed over all rows, that value defines the top of the scale, and the model has been trained in a coordinate system that only exists because of a row it was not supposed to see. The effect is usually small and always in the same direction: your reported score is better than the truth. It costs nothing to do it correctly — in scikit-learn, put the scaler and the model in a Pipeline and the correct order becomes automatic.

# scaling, done the only correct way: inside a pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

# WRONG — the scaler has seen every row, the test rows included
X_all = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X_all, y, random_state=42)

# RIGHT — split first; the pipeline refits the scaler inside every fold
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=42)
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), model)
print(cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean())

# the stored statistics — these must travel with the model to production
sc = StandardScaler().fit(X_tr)
print(sc.mean_, sc.scale_)      # mu and sigma, learned from training data alone

The first version is not slower or uglier — it is wrong, and it will report a slightly better score than the model deserves. That is the whole reason Pipeline exists.

docs.title: Missing values
docs.text:
First find them, including the ones in disguise: a coded 999, a −1, an empty string, a zero in a column where zero is impossible. Then choose.

  • Drop the rows — fine when few rows are affected and the missingness is unrelated to the target. Dangerous otherwise: if income is missing mainly for the unemployed, dropping those rows removes exactly the group you care about.
  • Drop the column — when most of it is missing and the rest is not clearly informative.
  • Impute — fill with the mean (symmetric numeric data), the median (skewed or with outliers), the mode (categorical), or a model-based value (k-NN imputation). Every one of these is a statistic, so compute it on the training fold and reuse it.
  • Flag it — add a binary was_missing column. Often the fact of absence carries real information, and this keeps it while still letting you fill the value.

docs.title: Encoding categories
docs.text:
Method What it does Use when Risk One-hot one binary column per value unordered categories, few values column explosion with high-cardinality features Dummy (drop one) \(c - 1\) columns linear and logistic regression none; avoids the dummy-variable trap Ordinal map to 0, 1, 2 … in order genuinely ordered: low \(<\) medium \(<\) high invents an order where there is none Label arbitrary integers the target of a classifier never use on an unordered input feature

The mistake worth naming: encoding city as Mumbai \(= 0\), Delhi \(= 1\), Chennai \(= 2\), Kolkata \(= 3\) tells a linear model that Kolkata is three times Delhi and that Delhi sits between Mumbai and Chennai. The model will happily act on that fiction. A decision tree suffers less, because it can carve the integers into arbitrary groups, but it still has to spend splits doing so.

docs.title: 2.4 Outliers: finding them, and deciding what they are
docs.text:
An outlier is a value far from the rest. That is a statement about the data, not about the truth. It might be a typo — a weight of 700 kg. It might be a real, rare case — a genuine ₹5-crore transaction. Or it might be the very thing you are trying to detect, as in fraud or fault detection, where the outliers are the signal and everything else is background. Detection is arithmetic; deciding what to do is judgement.

Definition: IQR and z-score

Tukey's rule. With quartiles Q1 and Q3 and IQR \(= Q3 - Q1\), flag any value outside [\(Q1 -\) 1.5·IQR, \(Q3 +\) 1.5·IQR]. Values beyond 3·IQR are “far out”.

Z-score rule. Flag any value with |z| \(=\) |x \(- \mu |/\sigma > 3\).

The two disagree, and the disagreement is instructive. Quartiles are computed from ranks, so no single monstrous value can move them. But \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) are computed from the values themselves, so a large outlier inflates \(\sigma\) — and then hides inside the wider band it created. This is called masking, and it is why the IQR rule catches things the z-rule misses.

Figure 2.3. A box plot of twelve values with the interquartile-range fences (dashed). The point beyond the upper fence is flagged; removing it would change every statistic and move the fences.

What to do with one you have found

Investigate first — a negative age is an error, a ₹5-crore transaction may be real. Correct if it is an error you can fix. Cap (winsorise) at the 1st and 99th percentile to limit its influence without discarding the row. Remove only when you are confident it is not a real case. Or keep it and use a robust method — median instead of mean, MAE instead of MSE, a tree instead of a linear model. Removing points because they are inconvenient is how you end up with a model that fails precisely on the cases that matter.

docs.title: 2.5 Class balancing
docs.text:
Figure 2.4. An imbalanced dataset: 95 majority-class points against 8 minority-class points.

The accuracy paradox

With 99.7% negatives, the model that answers “negative” for every input scores 99.7% accuracy and detects nothing. Any real classifier that finds some positives at the cost of a few false alarms will score lower on accuracy — so optimising accuracy actively pushes you towards the useless model. Report precision, recall, F1 and the confusion matrix instead, and always quote the majority-class baseline next to whatever number you claim.

Remedy What it does Cost Random undersampling discard majority examples until balanced throws away real information; only viable when the majority class is huge Random oversampling duplicate minority examples no new information; a flexible model memorises the repeats SMOTE synthesise new minority points along lines joining nearest neighbours plausible but invented; can blur the boundary if the classes overlap Class weights tell the loss function that a minority mistake costs more none — usually the first thing to try, and it changes no data at all Move the threshold keep the model, lower the cut-off for “positive” none; often the whole solution, since the model already ranks correctly

Resample the training fold only

SMOTE applied before the split puts synthetic points built from training data into the test set, so the model is graded on near-copies of what it studied. Recall will look wonderful and will collapse in production. Test sets keep the real, imbalanced distribution — that is what the world looks like.

# class imbalance: try the cheapest remedy first
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# 1. costs nothing and changes no data: tell the loss a rare mistake costs more
clf = LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced").fit(X_tr, y_tr)

# 2. resampling — inside the training fold only, never before the split
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE          # pip install imbalanced-learn
from imblearn.pipeline import make_pipeline as imb_pipeline

pipe = imb_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SMOTE(random_state=42), LogisticRegression())
print(cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring="f1").mean())

Note the import

imblearn's pipeline, not sklearn's — because a resampler must act on the training fold and be skipped when the fold is scored, and only imblearn's version knows that. Using sklearn's pipeline with SMOTE resamples the validation fold too, which is the same leak in a different costume. And scoring="f1", not accuracy: that is the whole reason you are resampling.

docs.title: Scaling to any interval
docs.text:
Min–max normalisation is usually quoted for the interval \([0, 1]\), but the same idea maps a feature onto any chosen interval \([a, b]\):

\[ x' = a + \frac{(x - \min)(b - a)}{\max - \min}. \]

For \(a = 0\) and \(b = 1\) this is the formula already given. Many neural networks work best with inputs centred on zero, so \([-1, 1]\) is a common choice: for the column \(10, 20, 30, 40, 50\) the formula gives \(x' = -1 + (x - 10)(2)/40\), that is \(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1\). Image pixels, which lie between 0 and 255, are the standard case: dividing by 255 gives \([0, 1]\), and \(2x/255 - 1\) gives \([-1, 1]\). As always, \(\min\) and \(\max\) are the training-set values (or, for pixels, the known limits of the measurement), and a later value outside them simply lands outside the interval.

docs.title: Target encoding, and the leak it invites
docs.text:
One-hot encoding fails when a feature has hundreds or thousands of values (a postcode, a shop identifier): the number of columns explodes. Target (or count) encoding replaces each category by a summary of the target for that category, most simply the mean of \(y\) over the training rows that have it. It turns one high-cardinality column into one numeric column, at a price: the encoding is computed from the labels, so it is the one preprocessing step in which the answer itself is used.

city rows in training defaults (\(y = 1\)) mean of \(y\) Delhi 4 3 \(0.75\) Mumbai 3 1 \(0.33\) Chennai 1 1 \(1.00\)

The overall default rate is \(5/8 = 0.625\). Notice Chennai: one row, one default, so the encoded value is \(1.00\) and the feature reproduces that row's label exactly. For a rare category the mean is mostly noise, yet it looks like a strong predictor, and a flexible model will use it to memorise the training set. Two safeguards are standard. Smooth towards the overall rate: with a weight \(m\) (here \(m = 2\)),

\[ \text{encoded} = \frac{n\cdot \bar{y}_{\text{category}} + m\cdot \bar{y}_{\text{all}}}{n + m}, \]

which gives Delhi \(0.708\), Mumbai \(0.45\) and Chennai \(0.75\); the single-row category is pulled most strongly towards the overall rate. And compute the encoding out of fold: each training row is encoded using only the other folds, so that its own label never feeds into its own feature. Like every learned transformation, the encoding must be fitted on the training part only and applied unchanged to the test part, with a category unseen in training given the overall rate.

docs.title: 2.7 Worked examples
docs.text:
The examples below work through the calculations of this chapter in full. Try each one on paper before reading the steps.

Example 2.1: Scale a feature, then scale a new value

Problem. Training salaries (₹ thousand) are 20, 35, 40, 55, 100. Standardise them using the population \(\sigma\). A test example arrives with salary 70 — give its z-score. Then give the min–max value of the same test example.

Step 1 — training statistics, from training data only

\(\mu = (20 + 35 + 40 + 55 + 100)/5 = 250/5 = 50\)

deviations: −30, −15, −10, 5, 50; squares: 900, 225, 100, 25, 2500; sum 3750

\(\sigma = \sqrt{3750/5} = \sqrt{750} = 27.386\)

Step 2 — the training set, transformed

\(z = (-30, -15, -10, 5, 50)/27.386 = (-1.095, -0.548, -0.365, 0.183, 1.826)\)

Check: these sum to 0, as standardised values must.

Step 3 — the test example

\(z = (70 - 50)/27.386 = 0.730\). The stored \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) are used; the test value takes no part in computing them.

Step 4 — min–max, for contrast

min \(= 20\), max \(= 100\) from the training set, so x′ \(= (70 - 20)/(100 - 20) = 50/80 = 0.625\).

Now notice what happens with a test salary of 120: x′ \(= (120 - 20)/80 = 1.25\), outside [0, 1]. That is not a mistake — it is min–max being honest about a value beyond the training range, and it is exactly why min–max is fragile when the future is larger than the past.

Answer. \(z = 0.730\); min–max \(= 0.625\)

Example 2.2: The two outlier rules disagree

Problem. Values: 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18, 95. Apply the \(1.5 \times\) IQR rule and the |z| \(> 3\) rule, and explain the disagreement.

Step 1 — the IQR rule

Sorted, \(n = 8\). With linear interpolation, \(Q1 = 12.75, Q3 = 16.5\), IQR \(= 3.75\).

Fences: \(12.75 - 1.5(3.75) = 7.125\) and \(16.5 + 1.5(3.75) = 22.125\).

\(95 > 22.125\), so the IQR rule flags 95.

Step 2 — the z-score rule

\(\mu = (10+12+13+14+15+16+18+95)/8 = 193/8 = 24.125\)

Squared deviations sum to \(5782.9\), so \(\sigma = \sqrt{5782.9/8} = \sqrt{722.9} \approx 26.89\).

\(z\) for \(95 = (95 - 24.125)/26.89 = 2.64\), which is less than 3. The z-rule does not flag it.

Step 3 — why

The outlier is inside both statistics it is being tested against. It pulled \(\mu\) up from about 14 to 24, and it inflated \(\sigma\) from about 2.4 to 27 — more than ten times. Having widened its own goalposts, it now sits comfortably inside them. This is masking.

The quartiles cannot be moved this way, because they depend on the ranks of the values, not their sizes. Replace 95 by 950 and Q1, Q3 and the fences do not change at all.

Answer. IQR flags 95; the z-rule does not, because 95 inflated \(\sigma\) to 26.9 and so hid inside its own band. Prefer the IQR rule, or use a robust \(z\) built on the median and MAD.

Example 2.3: Order a pipeline correctly

Problem. You have 1 000 rows, 30 features, 4% positives, some missing values and features on wildly different scales. Write the correct order of operations and say what would go wrong if the split came last.

The order

  1. Split — stratified, so both parts keep the 4% positive rate. Nothing has been computed from any row yet.

  2. Impute — medians computed on the training fold, then applied to both.

  3. Encode categories — the category list comes from the training fold; an unseen category in the test set maps to all zeros.

  4. Scale — \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) from the training fold.

  5. Select or reduce — correlation filter or PCA fitted on the training fold.

  6. Balance — SMOTE or class weights, applied to the training fold only. The test set keeps the real 4%.

  7. Train, tuning hyper-parameters by cross-validation inside the training fold.

  8. Evaluate once on the test set, using precision, recall and F1 rather than accuracy.

What goes wrong if the split comes last

Every statistic — medians, \(\mu , \sigma\), the correlation ranking, the principal components — has then been computed with the test rows included, so the test set has influenced the model without being used to train it. The reported score is optimistic and there is no way to say by how much.

With SMOTE the damage is worse and easy to see: synthetic points are built by interpolating between real minority points. If that happens before the split, a synthetic point in the test set may be a near-copy of a real training point. Recall on the test set can approach 1.0 and mean nothing at all.

Answer. Split \(\to\) impute \(\to\) encode \(\to\) scale \(\to\) select/reduce \(\to\) balance (train only) \(\to\) train \(\to\) evaluate once.

Example 2.4: Scaling can change which point is nearest

Problem. A model uses salary (range ₹20 000 to ₹200 000 in the data) and age (range 20 to 60 years). A query person has salary ₹50 000 and age 30. Candidate P has salary ₹50 100 and age 55; candidate Q has salary ₹60 000 and age 30. Which candidate is nearer to the query by Euclidean distance (i) on the raw numbers, and (ii) after min–max scaling each feature to \([0, 1]\) using the stated ranges?

Step 1 — the raw differences

P: \(\Delta \text{salary} = 100\), \(\Delta \text{age} = 25\). Q: \(\Delta \text{salary} = 10\,000\), \(\Delta \text{age} = 0\).

Step 2 — raw distances

\(d(P) = \sqrt{100^{2} + 25^{2}} = \sqrt{10\,625} = 103.1\)

\(d(Q) = \sqrt{10\,000^{2} + 0^{2}} = 10\,000\)

On the raw numbers P is nearer by a factor of about 100. The 25-year age gap is invisible because it is added to a salary gap measured in the tens of thousands.

Step 3 — scale each difference by the feature's range

A min–max-scaled difference is the raw difference divided by the range. The salary range is \(200\,000 - 20\,000 = 180\,000\) and the age range is \(60 - 20 = 40\).

P: \(\Delta \text{salary}' = 100/180\,000 = 0.00056\), \(\Delta \text{age}' = 25/40 = 0.625\)

Q: \(\Delta \text{salary}' = 10\,000/180\,000 = 0.0556\), \(\Delta \text{age}' = 0/40 = 0\)

Step 4 — scaled distances

\(d(P) = \sqrt{0.00056^{2} + 0.625^{2}} = 0.625\)

\(d(Q) = \sqrt{0.0556^{2} + 0} = 0.0556\)

After scaling Q is nearer, by a factor of more than 11.

Answer. Raw: P is nearer (\(103.1\) against \(10\,000\)). Scaled: Q is nearer (\(0.0556\) against \(0.625\)). The nearest neighbour reverses.

Comment. Neither answer is "true" in the abstract; the point is that the raw answer is decided by the units. Someone 25 years older is a large difference in age terms, someone ₹10 000 richer is a small difference in salary terms, and scaling lets the distance reflect that. A k-NN classifier would have used different neighbours, and so made different predictions, with and without scaling.

Example 2.5: Four ways to rescale one skewed column

Problem. Household wealth (₹ lakh) in a small sample is \(8, 10, 12, 15, 18, 400\). Rescale the column by (i) min–max, (ii) z-score with the population \(\sigma\), (iii) robust scaling \((x - \text{median})/\text{IQR}\), and (iv) the transform \(\ln (1 + x)\). Compare how well each one separates the five ordinary values.

Step 1 — min–max

\(\min = 8\), \(\max = 400\), range \(= 392\), so \(x' = (x - 8)/392\):

\(0,\ 0.0051,\ 0.0102,\ 0.0179,\ 0.0255,\ 1\)

The five ordinary households are squeezed into an interval of width \(0.0255\), a fortieth of the scale.

Step 2 — z-score

\(\mu = (8 + 10 + 12 + 15 + 18 + 400)/6 = 463/6 = 77.17\)

The squared deviations are \(4784.0, 4511.4, 4246.7, 3864.7, 3500.7, 104\,221.4\), which sum to \(125\,128.8\).

\(\sigma = \sqrt{125\,128.8/6} = \sqrt{20\,854.8} = 144.41\)

\(z = (-0.479,\ -0.465,\ -0.451,\ -0.431,\ -0.410,\ 2.236)\)

The outlier has inflated both \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\); the five ordinary values now sit within \(0.07\) of each other.

Step 3 — robust scaling

Sorted, with linear interpolation: the median is \((12 + 15)/2 = 13.5\); \(Q1\) is at position \(0.25 \times 5 = 1.25\), so \(Q1 = 10 + 0.25(12 - 10) = 10.5\); \(Q3\) is at position \(3.75\), so \(Q3 = 15 + 0.75(18 - 15) = 17.25\). \(\text{IQR} = 17.25 - 10.5 = 6.75\).

\(x' = (x - 13.5)/6.75 = (-0.815,\ -0.519,\ -0.222,\ 0.222,\ 0.667,\ 57.26)\)

The ordinary values now cover a range of \(1.48\) and are easy to tell apart. The outlier is still extreme, which is honest: it is.

Step 4 — the log transform

\(\ln (1 + x) = (2.197,\ 2.398,\ 2.565,\ 2.773,\ 2.944,\ 5.994)\)

The ordinary values span \(0.75\), and the outlier is now only \(3.05\) above the largest of them instead of \(382\). The ratio of one household to another has become a difference, which is what a long right tail needs.

Answer.

Method Width covered by the five ordinary values Outlier min–max \(0.026\) \(1.00\) z-score \(0.07\) \(2.24\) robust \(1.48\) \(57.3\) \(\ln (1 + x)\) \(0.75\) \(5.99\)

Comment. Min–max and z-score are both linear maps, so neither can change the shape of the data: a skewed column is still skewed after both. Only robust scaling, which takes its centre and its scale from rank statistics, and the log transform, which is nonlinear, deal with the outlier. In practice take the log first and then standardise. Note also a general fact about the z-score: with the population \(\sigma\), no value in a sample of \(n\) can have \(|z|\) larger than \(\sqrt{n - 1}\) (here \(\sqrt{5} = 2.236\), and the outlier reaches \(2.2355\)). For \(n \le 10\) the rule "\(|z| > 3\)" can therefore never flag anything.

Example 2.6: Impute, then scale, using training statistics only

Problem. A numeric training column has the observed values \(4, 6, 8, 10, 12\) and one missing entry. Two test examples arrive: one with the value missing, and one with the value \(14\). Fill the missing entries by the mean, standardise with the population \(\sigma\), and give the processed values of both test examples.

Step 1 — the imputation value, from the training column only

Mean of the observed training values: \((4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12)/5 = 40/5 = 8\). The missing training entry becomes \(8\), and so will every missing entry in the test data. The test examples take no part in computing it, and the target \(y\) is not used.

Step 2 — the training column after imputation

\(4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 8\). Its mean is \(48/6 = 8\), unchanged, because we filled with the mean.

Step 3 — the scaler, fitted on this filled training column

Squared deviations from 8: \(16, 4, 0, 4, 16, 0\); sum \(= 40\).

\(\sigma = \sqrt{40/6} = \sqrt{6.667} = 2.582\)

The training column becomes \((-1.549,\ -0.775,\ 0,\ 0.775,\ 1.549,\ 0)\).

Step 4 — transform the two test examples with the stored numbers

Test example with the value missing: filled with \(8\), then \(z = (8 - 8)/2.582 = 0\).

Test example with the value \(14\): \(z = (14 - 8)/2.582 = 2.324\).

Answer. The imputation value is \(8\); \(\mu = 8\) and \(\sigma = 2.582\). The processed test values are \(0\) (the missing entry) and \(2.324\) (the value 14).

Comment. Two things to notice. First, mean imputation followed by standardisation maps every filled entry to exactly \(0\), the centre of the scale: the model sees "average" for every unknown, which is why a separate was-missing indicator is worth adding when missingness may mean something. Second, imputation shrinks the spread: the five observed values alone have \(\sigma = \sqrt{40/5} = 2.828\), against \(2.582\) after filling. The order impute-then-scale, both on the training fold, is the order of the pipeline set out earlier in this chapter.

Example 2.7: Why integer codes for a city mislead, in numbers

Problem. A feature city takes the values Delhi, Mumbai and Chennai, and is fed to a distance-based model. Compare the distances between the cities when they are coded \(\text{Delhi} = 0\), \(\text{Mumbai} = 1\), \(\text{Chennai} = 2\) and when they are one-hot encoded.

Step 1 — the integer code

The distance between two cities is the absolute difference of the codes:

Pair \(\lvert \text{difference} \rvert\) Delhi, Mumbai \(\lvert 0 - 1 \rvert = 1\) Mumbai, Chennai \(\lvert 1 - 2 \rvert = 1\) Delhi, Chennai \(\lvert 0 - 2 \rvert = 2\)

The code says Delhi and Chennai are twice as far apart as any other pair, and that Mumbai lies between them. None of this is a fact about cities; it came from the order in which someone wrote the names.

Step 2 — the one-hot code

Delhi \(= (1, 0, 0)\), Mumbai \(= (0, 1, 0)\), Chennai \(= (0, 0, 1)\). Any two different cities differ in exactly two positions, by \(1\) in each:

\(d = \sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2}} = \sqrt{2} = 1.414\)

for every pair.

Step 3 — count the columns

One-hot encoding turns one column into \(c = 3\) columns. A linear model with an intercept needs only \(c - 1 = 2\) of them (Delhi is then the case where both are zero), otherwise the three indicator columns add up to the intercept column and the design matrix is singular.

Answer. Integer code: distances \(1, 1, 2\), a made-up order and spacing. One-hot: all three distances equal \(\sqrt{2}\), so no city is closer to another. A linear model needs \(c - 1 = 2\) indicator columns.

Comment. Label coding is correct for a genuinely ordered feature (low \(<\) medium \(<\) high), and for the target of a classifier. It is wrong for an unordered input of a distance-based or linear model.

Example 2.8: The accuracy paradox, class weights and one SMOTE point

Problem. A data set has 1 000 rows, of which 40 (4%) are positive. (i) A model that always answers "negative" is compared with one whose confusion counts are \(TP = 30, FN = 10, FP = 60, TN = 900\). Compute accuracy, precision, recall and \(F_{1}\) for each. (ii) Compute the "balanced" class weights \(w_{c} = n/(k\, n_{c})\) for \(k = 2\) classes. (iii) Generate one synthetic minority point by SMOTE from the minority points \(a = (2, 4)\) and \(b = (5, 8)\) with the interpolation fraction \(\lambda = 0.25\).

Step 1 — the always-negative model

It is right on all 960 negatives and wrong on all 40 positives: \(TP = 0, FN = 40, FP = 0, TN = 960\).
